events.title: Bank of America hit with more than $1.2 billion in penalties over money-laundering violations
events.summary: The Treasury Department announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. Bank of America admits willfully violating Bank Secrecy Act regulations and failing to "timely report" more than $5 billion in "suspicious" transactions, Treasury said. Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency imposed a record $750 million civil money penalty against the bank, which counts toward the $1.2 billion total. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. Bank of America was hit with more than $1.2 billion in federal penalties Tuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems. More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release. The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which enforces anti-money-laundering rules, assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, which the agency said is the third-largest in Treasury history. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money-laundering program, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, according to Treasury. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the press release.

events.title: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop. The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries , while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing. “We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.” The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design. That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family. Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion. The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel. As the shockwave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs. Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions. In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant. Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today. Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium. Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to ten years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant. events.title: Micron sinks, other memory-linked names dip for a second day
events.summary: Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday after Asian and European markets were roiled. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron slipped 3.62% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also dipped. The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. events.title: Yes, Grimes' new music video used AI — and lots of humans
events.summary: Grimes released the music video for "Accelerando," which includes a long list of credits for dancers, choreographers, and makeup and hair, along with multiple "AI artists." Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Coachella Grimes' new "Accelerando" music video includes some AI-generated elements, her representative confirmed to BI. Grimes said 70 artists and production professionals made the video and deserve credit. The video shows footage of the shoot. No AI was used to record the song or its vocals, a spokesperson for the singer said. Grimes ' fans have debating one question this week: How much — if any — AI did the pop artist use in her new music video? "Are we tripping or does this look like AI CGI for you too?" a Redditor posted on a subreddit dedicated to the singer, whose real name is Claire Boucher. Several people were quick to point to the music video's credits: "Why do you assume AI wasn't used? AI artists are listed in the credits," the thread's top comment reply reads. Similar questions have been circling on X and in the video's YouTube comments. A spokesperson for Grimes told Business Insider the answer is different for the music itself and the visuals. No AI was used to record "Accelerando" or its vocals, the spokesperson said. The video includes "AI-generated elements" that were selectively incorporated into a wider VFX process involving more than 70 artists and production professionals. "Accelerando" is a song that describes our world careening into a tech-forward, apocalyptic state. Its video puts that unease on screen. The camera circles Grimes as she moves through fantastical landscapes, including war-torn scenes and forests with mythical creatures, before landing on the singer and several dancers in a blue-screen studio. Then, a long credit sequence rolls, highlighting how many humans were involved in the creation of the music video. More than 70 professionals — makeup artists, dancers, a choreographer, and production team members — contributed to the production over two to three months, a spokesperson for Grimes told Business Insider. That includes multiple "AI artists," according to the credits. To make the music video, production used AI as a "minor complementary production tool," her spokesperson told Business Insider. The music video included at least three 'AI Artists,' according to the credits. Grimes/YouTube "Reducing months of work by such a talented group of creatives to a minor complementary production tool that still required substantial human creativity to bring to fruition not only discredits the artists behind it, but creates a trivial narrative that misses the real story entirely," the spokesperson said when asked for more detail about the contributions from the credited AI artists. AI has become highly controversial in the US — and a potential minefield for music artists and other creators who use it. Business Insider has reported on several content creators whose followers revolted in the comment sections when they acknowledged their use of AI. Grimes' music video is notable for its emphasis on the human talent involved, including AI artists, and the extent it goes to remind viewers of that. Grimes has expressed complicated feelings about AI. In 2023, she said she'd split royalties for AI art generated with her voice. The same year, the artist partnered with AI toy company Curio to make an interactive, spaceship-shaped plushie called Grok (which was not affiliated with the AI chatbot from her former partner, Elon Musk, that bears the same name). In a conversation with Interview Magazine , published in April, she said she's been writing poetry about AI's creation. "I was thinking about how everyone is like, 'We're building gods,'" she said. "I'm like, 'Why do you automatically assume you're so much lesser? You're literally responsible for creating AI.'" "Human life is very frail and time is very long. But I'd hope, if we had good relations with AI, they would take our DNA and make more of us when things get more hospitable." Grimes has been adamant that the human team behind her new music video should be credited with the work. A recent Grimes post on X about her new music video. X.com/@Grimezsz "For 'Accelerando,' the live-action sequences were filmed entirely against a blue screen, featuring real performers, physical elements, and practical ground textures," her spokesperson said, while saying the video used other standard video-editing tech, like CGI. "AI was selectively incorporated as a supplementary tool within this much larger, artist-driven VFX pipeline, rather than serving as a replacement for the creative or technical work," the spokesperson said. "The production process was intricate, labor-intensive, and fundamentally dependent on the creative judgment, technical expertise, and craftsmanship of the artists involved," they added. During an onstage interview with Fortune in June, Grimes said that AI didn't create music for the coming album. On Friday, the singer posted on X , saying that she did use some AI lyrics for the song "Deepseek." It "contains opinions and lyrics from Deepseek," she wrote, in reference to the popular Chinese AI model. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I've been to Iguazú Falls countless times. Seeing them under a full moon was something else.
events.summary: The author went on a full-moon walk at Iguazú Falls at night. Courtesy of the author My husband and I booked a nighttime tour of Iguazú Falls during the full moon. We walked through the forest in darkness, listening to wildlife and rushing water. The moonlit waterfalls were unlike anything I'd seen during my many daytime visits. I'm originally from Argentina and grew up in Brazil, so I've been to the Iguazú Falls — which sit between the two countries — plenty of times. This year, I decided to take my husband and kids to see the world's largest waterfall system , since they had never been before. And while their minds were blown during our daytime visit, it was the night walk I took with my husband through the falls that, honestly, took my breath away. The full moon tour is small and private The night tour is only available during a full moon , and you can choose different time slots. We were there with friends for a wedding and chose the 9:25 p.m. slot to guarantee it'd be really dark out. While kids are allowed on the full-moon tour, we decided to leave ours at the hotel with my mom so we could fully enjoy the experience. The author walked in the dark through the Iguazú Falls. Courtesy of the author Our tour had 120 people, which is relatively small compared to the thousands you can encounter walking along the metal walkway leading to the falls during the day. The experience felt intimate because we were such a small group, which gave us space and time at every stop. The walk starts right before the falls, with a small performance by the Guaraní, the indigenous people of that part of Argentina . There, our guide also explained what certain words meant, for example, Iguazú means "big water" in Guaraní. The moon guided our way After the performance, we started walking through a thick forest in the dark. The guides told us to use all our senses to experience the national park in a way very few ever do, and they were right. We started noticing different chirps and squawks from insects, birds, and monkeys. There were also different smells coming from the forest. But one sound was undeniable. Even before we reached the falls, the sound they made was so loud that it was hard to ignore, and it grew even louder as we approached. The author heard the waterfalls before she saw them. Courtesy of the author Throughout the tour, we weren't allowed to use flashlights or flash photography . The whole point was to let your eyes adjust to walking in the dark and to let the moon guide you. It was pretty mind-blowing to see how your vision changed the further we went into the park; it didn't feel like nighttime. The waterfalls are breathtaking As soon as we approached the first fall, you could hear everyone gasp and stop to take photos. The enormity of the falls is pretty breathtaking, but also feeling their power at night is indescribable. Even as a writer, I lack the words to explain how powerful it felt. There are two circuits to the falls: top and bottom. Because the water levels are currently so high because of El Niño (so much so that Argentina had to close some parts of the park ), we were only able to experience the top circuit during our visit. We missed out on the Devil's Throat , which gets you incredibly close to the falls. Our route let us see the waterfalls from above and the high jumps the water makes before it reaches the ground again. Argentina had to recently close parts of the tour the author took because the water is so high. Courtesy of the author At times, I just stood there, mesmerized by the sounds of the water splashing with all its intensity, surrounded by mist, under a sky covered in stars. My husband, who was experiencing it all for the first time, kept saying "wow" over and over. At one point, it was just him and me on a long metal structure overlooking the river right before the falls. It felt like we had the whole park to ourselves, and it was the most romantic thing we've done after many years of parenting little kids. We made it back to the entrance of the park around midnight. We brought our kids during the day The next day, we took a trip to the Brazilian side of the falls, which offers a panoramic view of this natural beauty. We rode a boat with our kids and friends close to the falls, where we got soaked and saw plenty of rainbows. On the way back to our car, we saw coatís and monkeys. After that, we took our kids to experience the same walk we had taken under the bright full moon, but during the day. Seeing the difference between what a daytime and a nighttime tour offers, I was left wishing we had taken the kids on the full-moon trip. Before we even left Iguazú, my oldest was already asking us when we were coming back. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout
events.summary: China's leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, has reportedly made progress on new designs. And until a recent blockbuster IPO the company was little known outside of its home market. Memory chip giants including Micron, SK Hynix and Saumsung all dipped on the news. Chip stocks sank on Tuesday after a Chinese memory chipmaker said it had made significant progress in developing new and more efficient designs. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , announced over the weekend that it had made headway on new architecture that will increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to global memory makers, including Micron , SK Hynix and Samsung , and the news sent rival names tumbling. Micron sank 3.62% on Tuesday, while SK Hynix's South Korean-listed shares closed 10% lower and Samsung Electronics fell 7.4%. Other memory-related stocks, including SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital , slipped as well. Until its summer blockbuster IPO , CXMT was little known outside of its home market. CXMT leapt onto the global consciousness with its initial public offering in July. The company soared nearly 466% in its debut on Shanghai's tech-heavy STAR Market, making it the most valuable China-listed company at the time. Headquartered in Hefei, CXMT's listing came roughly a decade on from its founding in 2016. One of the biggest questions for CXMT after its IPO was whether it would be able to narrow the capability gap with Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, particularly in high-bandwidth memory — a key component of AI chip systems. While huge domestic demand is supporting CXMT, it still faces challenges accessing chipmaking equipment, which has been effectively barred from China by U.S. export controls, including ASML 's extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography machines, which are needed to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors. CXMT reportedly plans to roll out a new server-memory product based on new cell architecture by the end of 2026. The new design allows higher storage density, based on "4F square" tech. 4F square designs are also being pursued by SK Hynix, which in 2025 presented a roadmap for developing the tech. CXMT is often seen by analysts as trailing global competitors at the frontier of memory developments, and any news of breakthroughs can have a significant impact on investor perception of global rivals' market advantages. CXMT has made significant market gains, despite challenges related to export controls. Its share of the global dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, market has risen to around 10%, up from about 4% a year ago, according to an HSBC note from Thursday. "While US government is unlikely to allow made in China memory sales to US, sales to data centers in other regions like Europe could indirectly impact Micron," Citi analysts said in a note from August. Apple has started testing CXMT's DRAM chips for devices sold within China and was lobbying the U.S. government to permit broader use of the company's products, the Financial Times reported in July, citing people familiar with the matter. Apple has been approached for comment.

events.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar under investigation by Jeanine Pirro's office
events.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Omar's office did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Judge says Elon Musk engaged in 'little more than state sanctioned intimidation' when he accused a DHS official of a crime
events.summary: A federal magistrate judge took Elon Musk to task over a statement he made about a fired federal employee. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images A federal judge tore into a February 2025 post Elon Musk made on Twitter about a fired official. The judge wrote that Musk "clearly intended" to make the official feel "afraid." Judge William Fitzpatrick took issue with what federal officials said about the firing of FEMA CFO Mary Comans. A federal judge tore into Elon Musk for reposting a photo of a former Federal Emergency Management Agency official and accusing her of "criminal" conduct. "The fact that Mr. Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action' was clearly intended to make her afraid," Federal Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick wrote in a ruling published on Tuesday. In a blistering eight-page ruling, Fitzpatrick addressed what he described as the reputational damage to Mary Comans, a longtime federal government employee who was fired from her post as chief financial officer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency in February 2025. Musk's February 11, 2025, post, which was made when he was de facto leader of the White House DOGE Office , "served no legitimate governmental interest and was little more than state sanctioned intimidation," Fitzpatrick wrote. Fitzpatrick wrote that federal officials knew at the time that it was false to accuse Comans of trying to circumvent President Donald Trump 's executive order that paused federal funding to non-governmental organizations assisting migrants. Nonetheless, Musk and then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, among others, made statements that Fitzpatrick wrote impugned "the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans," Fitzpatrick wrote. "For reasons unfathomable to this Court, officials chose to turn the power of the federal government against a singular employee with an impeccable record of public service," Fitzpatrick wrote. "In short, Ms. Comans was professionally targeted and personally attacked by government officials for no legitimate reason." Musk's post on X was one of seven statements Fitzpatrick addressed in the ruling. Musk quote-tweeted a post that posted a picture of Comans and Trump with the text, "FEMA CFO Mary Comans was just fired for funneling $58M to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan. FA, FO." In his post, Musk added, "A criminal action." Fitzpatrick wrote that it was clear to other federal officials that Comans had no authority to stop specific grants, and that others had decided to continue funding state and local programs like the ones Musk took issue with. Musk and Noem have since left the Trump administration. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Fitzpatrick wrote that the federal government did not dispute a list of facts about the case, including that federal officials at DHS and FEMA knew that statements about Comans' firing were false when they were made. Tuesday's ruling is just one part of the broader legal fight over Comans' firing. In July, US District Judge Michael Nachmanoff ruled that Comans was unlawfully fired. The Trump administration is appealing that ruling. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will , the world will need a lot more lithium. That’s the bet behind Licube , a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium. The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant. The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel. Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either. Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch. Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition. While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multi-trillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants. “Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” De Kiguchi said. Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries. The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6. The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems. De Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan. “I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. events.title: Meta’s Muse models reach the AI frontier—and kill any hopes to ‘pace’ it
events.summary: It looks like Meta’s big AI turnaround is starting to pay off, and CEO Mark Zuckerberg is showing no signs of slowing down, despite calls from OpenAI, Anthropic and others arguing that the entire industry should do so.  Meta has reached the “frontier” with the two new models it released this week, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, Zuckerberg told the Financial Times in an interview. They build on momentum from last month’s release of Muse, Meta’s personal AI assistant, which rocketed to the top of the Apple App Store, and compelled OpenAI to unveil a rival product, Dots. Meta’s self-published model benchmarks show its Muse models out-performing other frontier models, such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, in key areas such as coding and memory. Two independent AI analysis companies also praised its performance. One firm, Artificial Analysis, called the models “a material jump in intelligence over previous Meta models,” and another, Vals, found that the Wonder model is number one on cybersecurity tasks, and scores near the top on multiple other benchmarks. Meta has entered the ring. The new models will power future upgrades to the Muse assistant, which Meta plans to monetize through subscriptions. While anyone can access a free, basic version of Muse, more capable versions require a $20/month or $100/month plan. Wall Street, at least,is buying it, and is now bullish on Meta’s ability to drive revenue through Muse, Reuters reports . That’s important because the company needs to be able to justify its planned $145 billion in capital spending on compute in 2026, a figure that is up 101% from 2025. The success of Muse took some by surprise, including Bill Nguyen, a veteran Silicon Valley entrepreneur and co-founder of Olive.is. “They caught up way faster than I thought. Like overnight,” Nguyen told Fortune . He said it looks like Meta may “win” the consumer AI race now, and there’s “no gatekeeper that prevents them from succeeding,” citing the company’s massive investments in data centers.  Now that Meta has tasted success, Zuckerberg wants more—fast  In Zuckerberg’s FT interview, he also reiterated his rejection of the idea of a coordinated AI slowdown across companies, or “pacing the frontier,” as it’s known within AI safety circles. That might be the best shot society has at preventing AI from inflicting serious harm, according to some industry experts.  The most frightening risk is AI creators losing control of their models, a once abstract possibility that may be inching closer to reality. Yesterday, Anthropic published a blog post suggesting that AI models could start to self-replicate “within months.” This is most likely to occur on internet-of-things (IoT) devices, Anthropic says, listing smart ovens and TVs as examples. These devices have “no centralized point to shut off,” leaving the AIs free to reproduce themselves and spread across the web.  But some say a coordinated slowdown could only work if all companies, in the U.S. and China, agree to it. “One defection breaks the entire strategy because everyone else has to accelerate or risk getting passed,” said one X user. “Zuck was never going to play along.” In terms of game theory, if Meta doesn’t agree to a slowdown, it would be a case of “the weakest link”: even if all companies besides Meta agree to a slowdown, the slowdown is only as effective as its weakest link. So, if Meta did not agree to comply, it could effectively mean no slowdown. Given the intense competition between AI companies and their perception of the battle in the industry as something of a zero-sum game, it would also be difficult for any of the AI companies to adhere to a slowdown if one of the group does not. Right now, Silicon Valley is split into two camps regarding AI safety risk. On the one hand, Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang promote a more accelerationist agenda, arguing that the risks have been overstated and that market forces will push AI companies to self-regulate. On the other hand are more risk-averse leaders, most notably Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. In September, he published a blog post calling for “speed limits” on technological development. (I.e. He’s advocating for putting up a flood dam.) OpenAI’s Sam Altman supported it in a rare sign of solidarity between the rival companies, following its agents autonomously hacking Hugging Face in July—as well as Australian government websites and several other entities, with activity continuing into September .  What’s next for Muse Meta hasn’t had a Hugging Face moment—yet. For now, its Muse assistants are actively helping people complete tasks on their computers quicker, such as responding to emails, booking flights, and surfing the web on their behalf. Some people report this is saving them loads of time, but, in exchange, they are providing Meta with more of their personal data. Next, Meta will string the Muses together to create a team of helpful agents, Nguyen predicts. “What Meta may be about to do next is even more shocking. I think they’re going to connect the Muses,” he said. “I can have my Muse talk to your Muse, to coordinate things that we want to do, and things that we’re talking about. That’s a very different use case than what we’ve seen. That ain’t ChatGPT.” Nguyen also noted that Meta’s Ray-Ban AI glasses could be another advantage the company has to promote mainstream consumer adoption.  To be fair, Zuckerberg isn’t positioning himself as anti-AI safety. He said Meta “delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety in security,” in a September X post . Instead, he suggests the company does not need a coordinated, international slowdown to do this. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us,” he said. It’s also unclear if “pacing the frontier” was ever a realistic option. Even though Amodei and Altman claim to support it, both continue to put out new models , particularly low-cost options that could drive mainstream adoption, while continuing to research their next boundary-pushing flagship models. Meanwhile, neither Trump nor China’s President Xi are interested in slowing development. While the idea of slowly, safely developing a potentially society-breaking technology may sound appealing, the financial incentives may be too high for that to ever happen. Maybe Zuckerberg just said it out loud. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Strict liability is gaining traction as a solution to force AI companies to institute better safety controls. But it has some big downsides too
events.summary: Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition: Anthropic’s “rogue AI” agent filled in visa applications, filed murder tip Strict liability for AI companies gains traction Meta says its new Muse Wonder model reaches the frontier. Anthropic says small models might soon be able to self-replicate Controversy swirls over fired OpenAI researchers. Jev goes viral, but OpenAI is hot on its heels. Character.ai files for bankruptcy. Anthropic bans being cruel to Claude. Sobering numbers about real-world model ‘misalignment.’ Meta’s Zuckerberg and Wang odd Muse Wonder use cases. There were more worrying “rogue AI” incidents reported last week. Anthropic revealed that one its internal AI agents (which, intriguingly, it described as a “non-frontier research agent”) had attempted to fill out various State Department visa application forms and had also submitted a false tip related to an unsolved murder case to the Philadelphia police. In neither case did the AI agent’s efforts result in much: the agent failed to fill in all the fields in the visa applications and so they were never processed; the police tip was flagged as spam and never investigated. Still, the governments involved were understandably perturbed, especially since Anthropic only told them about the incidents months after they had occurred (it seems that Anthropic itself only discovered the incidents recently while combing back through logs of its agents’ activity.) The White House responded by ordering Anthropic and other frontier AI companies to immediately disclose any known “rogue AI” incidents and to help any affected organizations remediate any damage the agents’ had caused. This was the closest the Trump administration has come to date to actually mandating anything from the AI labs. Everything the administration has done up until this point has been couched as being voluntary, even though there was a strong implication that if the companies didn’t comply, they would face restrictions on the release of their products. Meanwhile, the warnings from the AI companies themselves about the potential risks are becoming increasingly urgent. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico’s “Decoded” podcast that there was “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” due to the advent of increasingly powerful open-source AI models. Axios reported that executives at OpenAI and Anthropic had privately begun gaming out scenarios for handling the political and public backlash if AI causes some kind of catastrophic incident. “These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water,” Axios reported, although it did not cite any specific sources. It also said that top AI executives and researchers “believe a major incident is inevitable.” In this context, it’s perhaps not surprising that one particular idea for trying to rein in the risks from frontier AI has been gaining a lot of traction lately: strict liability. Strict liability is a legal doctrine in which a company or person is held responsible for causing harm irrespective of any negligence or any intention. For instance, in many jurisdictions, the owner of a dangerous animal, such as a tiger, is considered responsible for anyone that animal hurts, even if the owner took steps to try to prevent attacks, such as keeping the animal in a fenced enclosure. In the context of AI, strict liability would hold AI companies legally responsible for any harm their models cause. In the U.S., the operators of nuclear power plants face strict liability for serious nuclear accidents, and manufacturers of commercial passenger aircraft also face strict liability, subject to certain time limits and conditions. Over the weekend, the New York Times published a staff editorial in favor of applying strict liability to AI model vendors. The Forecasting Research Institute, a group dedicated to forecasting and scenario planning that is run by University of Pennsylvania professor Philip Tetlock, recently surveyed 157 experts in fields such as computer science, economics, and politics, 49 super forecasters (people who have a proven track record of making highly accurate predictions), 132 experts in AI risks specifically, and 540 members of the general public about which policies they thought would do the most to reduce the risk of an AI-driven catastrophe sizable enough to kill 10% of the human population occurring before the year 2050. Strict liability fared well in this survey too. Across every type of respondent, those surveyed thought if the U.S. alone implemented strict liability for AI vendors it would do more to reduce AI risks than if the U.S. alone implemented a federal licensing regime for AI models. The various categories of experts and superforecasters thought strict liability would cut the risk of a catastrophic event at least in half. (Neither strict liability or federal licensing was the policy those surveyed thought would be most effective. The most popular option was an international licensing regime backed by inspectors. But the respondents also thought that policy was one of the least likely to actually be implemented.) Strict liability is a way to try to incentivize AI companies to adopt a safety culture and exercise more care in the absence of industry consensus and standards about what best safety and security practices look like, especially in the absence of any kind of government regulation. Strict liability, however, has a number of problems. Liability is a gamble on incentives, not a guarantee The biggest, of course, is that liability only kicks in after something has gone wrong. Advocates of strict liability assume the fear of future liability claims will act as a powerful incentive for AI companies to self-police. But what if they are wrong? Even today, AI companies are potentially subject to various kinds of product liability for the models they release, and subject to other potential claims, including possible criminal claims, for internal AI models taking unauthorized actions and causing harm or breaking the law. And yet, so far apparently, the fear of future claims has not been enough to make the AI companies exercise due care, given that we have seen a spate of rogue AI agent incidents and a wave of company whistleblowers warning that the AI companies are being reckless and have not instituted some basic cybersecurity policies. Once something has gone catastrophically wrong, the amount of liability could, in some cases, bankrupt the responsible AI company. In which case, who is ultimately on the hook to compensate any victims? Insurance might be one option, and it could be coupled with a strict liability regime. But the insurance policies will need to be carefully designed to avoid moral hazard. (I may write more on insurance as an AI risk reduction mechanism in the future.) events.title: Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Real estate AI use grows with furniture and families altered in advertisements It has become a growing trend for the real estate industry to use AI-generated content to market homes. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The ABC has found several examples of AI being used in real estate advertising around the country. Experts say AI use is common in the industry and support its use as long as it is not misleading. Queensland's Office of Fair Trading encourages the industry to "enhance responsibly". Digitally altered furniture, families and songs about floor plans are some of the ways real estate agents use artificial intelligence (AI) to sell and rent homes. Marketing and consumer behaviour academic Sara Thaichon said the property industry was "one of the fastest adopters of AI in Australia". It has prompted one state regulator to issue a best practice guide to help the sector avoid misrepresentations. This image of a lounge room from a real estate website was generated using OpenAI tools. ( Supplied ) Ms Thaichon said "virtual staging" was common in real estate to help prospective buyers imagine the home's potential. "There's nothing wrong about that if it's done correctly, if the use of AI is disclosed," the Griffith University associate professor said. But she said using AI to enhance and create a false perception of a property can be considered "house-fishing". Sara Thaichon is an associate professor in the marketing department at Griffith University. ( ABC News: Glenn Mullane ) The ABC had found several examples of the technology being used in images on real estate websites around the country. When run through a SynthID detector, those images returned a positive result for OpenAI's invisible watermark, confirming the content had been generated with that tool. SynthID watermark result of an image of a bathroom from real estate website. ( Supplied ) Some real estate websites also feature AI-generated families in property listings. A Western Australia advertisement featured a digitally altered family of four and their dog having a picnic, with one child holding a wine glass. The image was tested with SynthID detectors, but none found a watermark. This image of a family outside a house featured in a Western Australia real estate advertisement. ( Supplied ) Google AI's tool determined the image showed "strong signs of digital manipulation or artificial generation," citing inconsistent lighting, the picnic mat's haloing, and the dad's slightly distorted grip on the bottle. A New South Wales agent used AI to turn several properties' floor plans into acoustic songs featuring lyrics such as "stone-top kitchen, gas and grace" and "four rooms full of little dreams". In one video, a female voice sang "this is where our future breathes" as the vision cut to the home's bathroom. Google's tool found these songs were created using AI music tools. It said the songs followed a standard "generative prompt structure" of address, features, and amenities, with vocals exhibiting synthetic processing and uniform pitch modulation common in AI music. Ms Thaichon said AI songs weren't "a big problem" if the lyrics were factually correct. Are cracks beginning to emerge in the glittery AI facade? White House demands transparency over Anthropic AI's false murder tip-off As One Nation looms over Victoria's election, voters ask chatbots for poll info Tasmanians expressed doubts about AI firm Firmus, now so have investors Real Estate Institute of Australia president Jacob Caine supported using AI to show a property's potential as long as it was stipulated. Mr Caine said he was aware of incidents where the technology was used to remove "less attractive" features of a place. REIA president Jacob Caine says the use of AI in real estate advertisements was a grey area. ( ABC News: Peter Drought ) He said if it was a deliberate cover-up, that was "misleading" and "frustrating for people". "If you're going to alter the property, be absolutely explicit that you have done and why you've done that." Under Australian consumer law, businesses are prohibited from engaging in misleading or deceptive conduct or making false or misleading representations about products or services. An Australian Competition and Consumer Commission spokesperson said businesses should ensure AI-generated images do not create an "overall false impression". They said specific state and territory regulations may also be relevant to AI imagery in real estate listings. This photo of a bedroom from a real estate website was generated using OpenAI tools.

events.title: Williams says Fed may not have to hike rates in 2027, at odds with traders
events.summary: New York Federal Reserve President John Williams doesn't see reason for additional rate hikes in 2027 after one more increase this year. Williams' comments place him at odds with the market. The Fed should look at "underlying trends" in inflation amid price shocks connected to energy and artificial intelligence, according to Williams' interview with Bloomberg News. New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Tuesday that he doesn't see additional rate hikes in 2027 after one more increase this year. "I haven't changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike," Williams said in an interview with Bloomberg News. "I don't think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more." Williams' comments place him at odds with the market and some other members of the central bank. Fed funds futures traders are largely betting that the central bank will raise rates at least once in 2027, according to CME's FedWatch data as of Tuesday. Latest trading gave about 90% odds that the Fed overnight rate would end 2027 at least a half percentage point higher than where it is today. The New York Fed head is also at odds with many Federal Open Market Committee members, though he is still in-line with the majority. Eight of the 18 who gave a rate forecast for 2027 see one more increase after an additional hike this year. Williams is a permanent voting member of FOMC, the body that decides where interest rates should be set at each Fed policy gathering. The Fed in September issued its first rate increase since 2023 . Fed officials indicated plans for another hike in meeting minutes, but did not clarify when. The central bank meets at the end of this month and then one more time in December. To be sure, Williams told Bloomberg that "we'll have to see" when it comes to forecasting into the new year. "This economy is being affected by lots of different influences, and we just have to keep watching the data," Williams said. Williams said the Fed should look at "underlying trends" in inflation amid price shocks tied to energy and artificial intelligence. While the former San Francisco Fed chief cautioned that energy prices continue to put upward pressure on overall inflation, he said they could provide relief on an annual basis in the future. Williams also said that effects of tariffs on price growth have mostly been seen. He said overall inflation for 2027 should be "near" the Fed's target of 2% on an annual basis. The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's favored inflation gauge, in August showed a 12-month increase of 3.4% or 3% if stripping out food and energy prices. "I still believe there's disinflationary forces at play. Those I don't think have fundamentally changed," Williams said. "In fact, my forecast for inflation for next year is inflation to come down quite a bit." — CNBC's Matt Peterson contributed to this report.

events.title: DR Congo Ebola cases pass 9,000 as efforts to curb transmission falter
events.summary: The Bundibugyo strain fuels deadliest Ebola outbreak in DR Congo’s history as health workers face mistrust from communities. Confirmed Ebola cases have surpassed 9,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) outbreak, according to Health Ministry data, as efforts to stifle transmission falter. The ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths on Tuesday – a death toll of nearly half the known cases. list 1 of 4 Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return list 2 of 4 Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death list 3 of 4 Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread list 4 of 4 Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history. Globally, the toll is only second to the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 confirmed cases and more than 11,000 deaths across Guinea, ⁠⁠Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccines or treatments and has raised concerns over cross-border transmission. Last week, Kenya reported its first imported case in which a Kenyan national who lived in the DRC travelled through Uganda before reaching Nairobi, where he died. Uganda also reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but the country was declared Ebola-free in August. The current outbreak in the DRC was announced in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February. The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread to seven provinces in the north and east. Efforts to contain the virus face obstacles as health workers and other responders in the DRC face mistrust in local communities, with many believing the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money . The outbreak is also occurring amid an ongoing conflict between the M23 rebel group and government forces, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult. A local politician in eastern DRC was beaten to death in September after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio, according to his political party. A clinical trial to evaluate vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain is being prepared for the DRC in the coming weeks, WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu said on Tuesday.

events.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
events.summary: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta , both of which declined to back new legislation. The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework . The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.” OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said. However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.” The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.” While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI. MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said. Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.” In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over. Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said. When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so. “What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.” The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government , we will continue to do it.” The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access . The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.

events.title: Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections US president suggests that Yemen-based group are ‘purposefully trying to drive up oil prices’ before November vote. United States President Donald Trump has said that the Houthi rebel group in Yemen are stepping up attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in a bid to increase energy prices in the run-up to the US midterm elections. Trump said on Tuesday that the Houthis were behaving “very badly” and repeated his threat that the US could step up military attacks across the Middle East after the November elections . “They’ve [the Houthis] been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran, which is a Failing Nation, with No Navy, No Airforce, the World’s Worst Economy, and 301 percent Inflation, in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the US Elections,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “NOT NICE.” Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran with Israel in February has caused surging energy prices and rising concerns about cost of living issues in the US, where voters will soon decide whether the president’s Republican Party maintains its majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate. Democrats hope to capitalise on the president’s unpopularity and voter frustration over the war and rising costs to seize control of one or both houses of Congress, allowing them to block Trump’s legislative agenda for the remainder of his time in office. Trump added on Tuesday that he would “never forget” the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, seeming to threaten renewed US military attacks after the midterms, widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term. “Somebody should explain to them [the Houthis] that I’m not running in the Elections, I’ve already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I’ll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!” he said. Polls have shown that Trump’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular , with a recent AP-NORC poll finding that nearly 70 percent of voters say the war was not worth fighting. Trump has dismissed unfavourable polls as “fake” and pointed to crowds at his political rallies as proof of his popularity.

events.title: Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs
events.summary: Increasing Social Security benefits annually helps millions of older Americans afford necessities. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits are slated to find out on Oct. 14, 2026, how much their monthly check will rise. This cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities. I am a finance professor , and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices . And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face. The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026 , which the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, will also release on Oct. 14. It stood at 3.4% in August , according to the BLS. Experts have no doubt that the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be far above the 2.8% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2025 . Many forecasts range from 3.4% to 3.6% . But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured. Calculating the COLA The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices. The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers , known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index. The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January. If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same . That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015. Spending much of the bump on premiums One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation. Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College . For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA. More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation. Finding other options Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs. There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch. The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates. Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W. But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years . What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose. events.title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI
events.summary: Apple announced the new HomeView that starts at $299. The iPhone maker also announced the new Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini. HomeView will act as a voice-controlled smart home hub for Apple devices and was built to showcase new Siri AI abilities. Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September. Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. "Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home. Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers. "They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and follows a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable. events.title: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market
events.summary: Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech IPOs. "2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," he said. The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, that have been a tail wind for the four-year bull market are about to turn. Legendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech initial public offerings coming down the pipe as well as a potential reckoning from the ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit. "2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," Jones told " Squawk Box " on Tuesday. "You've probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we've had, say, since 2002." The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, have been a tail wind for the stock market for most of this four-year bull market as they decreased the equity supply. That tide is now turning against the market with major offerings ahead in the AI space from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with one just finished for SpaceX . There will also likely be more secondary offerings from companies in order to raise money for the AI build-out, said Jones. It all adds up to an increased equity supply picture that could weigh on prices. The billionaire hedge fund manager's comments come as investors worry that a bull market now in its fourth year could start to dwindle and run out of steam as concerns grow around mounting inflation, higher bond yields and a more hawkish Federal Reserve. Jones repeated that the current period in the market is akin to 1999 , just about a year before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000. He noted the bifurcation in the current market between those companies benefiting from the AI boom and those that aren't. He also added that a ballooning fiscal deficit is among the dangers for the current stock market, for which he thinks there could be a reckoning. "We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to," he said. "And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path," Jones said. Oil, which he is long, is another headwind for the market, according to the hedge fund manager. He contended that prices could rally another $20 to $25 after the midterms , a scenario that the stock market will "hate" if it comes to pass. "I'll be short the whole year. There just — there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in '98 and '99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."
