events.title: It pays to switch jobs again, but not everyone has that luxury
events.summary: Job switchers are getting bigger raises than job stayers again. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Job switchers are experiencing better wage growth than job stayers. Last year, both groups saw similar increases, defying historical trends. Still, not everyone can leave their job or find a new opportunity right now. It's once again better to switch jobs than stay in your current gig if you want a raise. "Wage growth for workers who change jobs is picking up again in 2026, even as raises for those who stay put keep slowing," Nicolas Petrosky-Nadeau, vice president for macroeconomic research at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, said in a LinkedIn post. That's based on 12-month moving averages of median wage growth for job switchers and stayers tracked by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta using Current Population Survey data. Year-over-year wage growth for job switchers has been 4.4% for four straight months, while growth for job stayers falls short, with September's estimate at 3.5%. The gap between the two groups shrank last year, including a brief period where stayers actually saw slightly better wage growth than switchers. The recent trend could be the start of a return to the historical norm of a healthy job-switching premium. "The first half of this year was the anomaly, and the low-hire environment is to blame," said Chris Martin, senior economist at Glassdoor. "Job seekers had to take what they could get, and that often meant compromise: fewer promotions and lower wages." However, some workers don't have the luxury to switch jobs right now. The quits rate has been bouncing between 1.9% and 2% for a little over a year now, far below the 3% rate a few years ago during the " Great Resignation ," suggesting lower confidence among workers. Openings have been similarly sluggish and are substantially down from the March 2022 record of 7.5%. "The return of this premium for job switchers is an early sign of improving prospects for job seekers, though the hiring rate remains low and job searches are taking longer," Martin said. With job openings basically in line with the unemployment level, AI making it easier to send out résumés, and job losses in white-collar sectors , workers might find it tough to say goodbye to their current role. "While job hopping still comes with higher pay, which is especially helpful for workers feeling the squeeze of inflation, the opportunities to job hop are few and far between," said ZipRecruiter economist Nicole Bachaud. People can improve their experience while stuck in their role. Bachaud suggests learning AI skills, which may be helpful in your current position or to note on your résumé. "For workers who are feeling stuck in their current position, it's important not to fall into the complacency trap," Bachaud said. "Beyond wages, the labor market is shifting rapidly as AI reshapes jobs." Whether you're applying for a new higher-paying job or seeking a raise from your current employer, it's not a bad idea to broadcast your accomplishments. People can " loud work " and boast their achievements and contributions to their manager and colleagues as well as beyond the workplace, such as through LinkedIn posts. "We stop ourselves from self-promotion because we think it's bad, but self-promotion is the breadcrumbs that lead to the titles and the promotions and the pay raises ," said Jasmine Escalera, a career expert with MyPerfectResume. events.title: EU watchdog urges smart glasses to clearly signal when recording
events.summary: Advisory comes amid growing concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women. The European Union’s data watchdog has called for smart glasses to clearly show when they are recording, saying bystanders have the right to know when they are being photographed or filmed. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued the non-binding recommendation on Tuesday, amid mounting concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women. list 1 of 3 Trump threatens tariffs for countries that levy digital tax on US firms list 2 of 3 EU hits Google with new $1bn fine, saying it broke digital antitrust rules list 3 of 3 Trump threatens EU will pay ‘big price’ after Brussels fines Google $1bn It said the use of smart glasses – which can resemble ordinary glasses but also take photos and videos, make phone calls and translate text when connected to the internet – raises “serious privacy concerns”. EDPB chair Anu Talus said the glasses should have clear signals when they are recording, such as “bright LED lights, audio signals or voice activation cues, privacy-friendly smartphone notifications, or unique designs”. “These warnings need to be reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date,” said Talus. “Even in public spaces, bystanders should clearly understand that someone is filming or photographing them.” The devices carry greater risks in “sensitive” spaces like schools and hospitals, as well as public spots like beaches, and raised concerns about children who are “more vulnerable to covert or intrusive processing of their personal data”, the EDPB warned. The advisory comes amid campaigns in several European countries to ban or restrict smart glasses over privacy concerns. Norway’s government said last week it was also worried about privacy invasions and wants a temporary ban on the use of smart glasses in certain public places. The capital Oslo already opted to ban glasses equipped with cameras in schools. France’s e-Enfance association, which operates the national hotline for victims of online abuse, has also sounded the alarm about videos recorded with camera-equipped glasses and shared online. Last month, French prosecutors said they had opened a criminal probe ⁠following sexual harassment complaints related to a social media trend of using smart glasses to film women on the street, without their consent, and posting the videos online. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, a “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign has launched a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale. It reached more than 10,000 signatures, which means the UK government must respond.

events.title: Walmart US workers are getting some new health care benefits in the new year
events.summary: Walmart workers will have access to a broader set of health care benefits in 2027. Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto via Getty Images Walmart plans to expand health benefits available to its 1.6 million employees. Eligible plan participants will have coverage for insulin, inhalers, and other medications. The company is also covering specialized care for rare conditions and premature births. Walmart, America's largest private employer, said it will expand the health benefit options for its 1.6 million-strong workforce . The retail giant said Tuesday that health plan participants will have several new benefits starting in 2027, including about 250 prescription drugs at no cost, including some insulin and inhalers. A spokesperson also told Business Insider that associates with type 2 diabetes and new prior authorization will have coverage for GLP-1 medications . That policy is similar to Starbucks, which recently cut back its coverage of the medications when they are prescribed for weight loss, though they may still be covered for other conditions. GLP-1 drugs have become highly sought-after treatments for obesity , but soaring costs are prompting some employers to limit eligibility. Walmart's list of covered drugs also includes hemophilia medications and a multiple sclerosis drug, each of which can cost thousands of dollars per month, the spokesperson said. In addition to the prescription benefits, Walmart is expanding its coverage of rare conditions to include no-cost access to specialists for evaluation and treatment review of multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). And starting next month, Walmart employees will have up to 12 weeks of paid leave if their newborn needs admission to a neonatal intensive care unit. That NICU leave can be combined with up to 16 weeks of existing paid maternity and parental leave available to frontline workers. Walmart's 2027 health plans start at $39.80 per pay period, a $1.50 increase from 2026, the spokesperson said. events.title: Michael Dell says AI needs safeguards and controls, and government has a role to play
events.summary: Michael Dell said AI models need "safeguards and controls," and the government has a role to play. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have backed efforts to pace frontier AI development as safety concerns intensify. Opposition to AI data centers has become a key issue in the run-up to the 2026 midterm election. Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell said that artificial intelligence models "have to have safeguards and controls" as the debate rages on over the threats the rapidly evolving technology could pose to humans. "I think we've always had technology that can do great things and maybe do some not-so-great things. You know, fire can heat your home. It can also burn down your whole village. So that's not good. So we have to have safeguards and controls," Dell told CNBC's David Faber in an interview Tuesday. Dell said "there's a role for government to play" and that the companies building AI tools need to also set "bounded permissions." He declined to give specifics about what that government role could look like, only saying he's "not a policymaker." In recent weeks, researchers and industry experts have debated the catastrophic possibilities that could come from self-improving AI models. The outcry was sparked by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who quit his job and warned in a Sept. 8 post that frontier labs were " gambling with our lives " in the race towards superintelligence. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI Since then, tech CEOs, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have endorsed calls for more regulation and an industry-wide slowdown in frontier model development. But the Trump administration has remained staunchly against a coordinated slowdown or other regulations. President Donald Trump hosted a lunch on Sept. 29 with AI leaders that ended with executives signing a "morally binding" document to self-regulate their products' safety with the help of outside evaluators. The White House document has made any further federal-level regulation unlikely ahead of November's midterm election, which is only weeks away. The backlash against AI and the data center build-out has reached a fever pitch and is a key issue that could help decide which party controls Congress in the final two years of Trump's term. Dell also addressed the rise in opposition to data centers and said the more active discussion about them was "a good thing." "We talk to our customers about it and hear what they're doing to address it, and certainly there are things we can do to make the systems more efficient, to reduce the energy consumption," Dell said. "So we're all working together to address this. I don't see it as a big impediment to 2027."

events.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days. How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause. Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines. Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today. “It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.” “Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha. Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model. “None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data. Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid). He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers. events.title: Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 may be above average. Some say it's not enough
events.summary: The Social Security Administration is expected to announce the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 on Wednesday. The benefit increase may be higher than average, ranging from 3.5% to 3.6%, according to the latest projections. Older Americans worry the increase may not be enough to cover rising consumer costs. Millions of Social Security beneficiaries may see a larger-than-average cost-of-living adjustment in 2027, according to experts' estimates. The Social Security Administration is expected to announce the COLA for 2027 on Wednesday with the release of new government inflation data. Social Security experts estimate that the COLA may raise benefits by 3.5% to 3.6% next year, which would be the largest increase in three years. Yet, even with an above-average increase, beneficiaries may still struggle to cover everyday costs . More than three-quarters of adults 50 years and older — 76% — said they do not think a projected 3.5% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 would be enough, according to an AARP survey published Monday. The poll of 1,023 adults ages 50-plus was fielded between Sept. 17 and 21. The survey had a 4.25% margin of error. "I would love it if the cost-of-living increase was more generous," said Donna Dalrymple, a 70-year-old retiree in Manchester, New Hampshire. Dalrymple retired at age 65 following a cancer diagnosis, she said, which prompted her to claim Social Security benefits and start 401(k) withdrawals five years earlier than she had planned. Today, she worries that other rising costs, particularly those for Medicare, may outpace the annual Social Security benefit increase, she said. Cost-of-living adjustments have averaged about 3.1% over the past decade, according to the Social Security Administration. In September, estimates showed the Social Security COLA may be the highest in three years. The Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan senior advocacy group, and Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, both forecast a 3.5% COLA for 2027. Meanwhile, AARP forecasts a 3.6% increase to benefits. The last time beneficiaries saw a larger increase was in 2023, when the COLA jumped to 8.7% — the highest in four decades — as a result of soaring inflation. In 2022, beneficiaries saw a 5.9% rise as the inflation rate began to climb. In 2026, Social Security beneficiaries received a 2.8% boost to their benefits. A 3.5% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 would increase the average benefit check by $67.90 per month — to around $2,008 per month from $1,940 — according to the Senior Citizens League. AARP's recent survey found that 7 in 10 adults ages 50-plus said an increase between 5% and 8% would be sufficient to help keep up with the daily cost of living. The official Social Security COLA announcement expected Wednesday may differ from September's estimates, since it will include an additional month of inflation data. A "very stiff jump in inflation" could push the Social Security COLA to 3.6%, Johnson said. But if inflation comes in lower than expected, the COLA may be 3.4%, she said. Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment is automatically applied to benefits to help keep pace with inflation. Since 1975, COLAs have been calculated annually for both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits. However, in some years when there was little to no inflation, the COLAs have been zero. "People are very, very grateful for it, and they look forward to it," Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano said Monday of the upcoming COLA announcement during an interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Rising Medicare costs in 2027 may limit how much of an increase Social Security beneficiaries see in their monthly checks. Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B, which are typically automatically deducted from Social Security checks, are projected to be $209.50 in 2027 , up from $202.90 in 2026. Medicare Part B covers certain medically necessary and preventive services. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, if their incomes exceed certain thresholds. Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to an analysis by KFF , a nonpartisan health policy research group. Part D premiums may also be deducted directly from Social Security checks. Social Security claiming ages may soon get new names. events.title: Walmart to cover some GLP-1s, inhalers and insulin for employees at no cost as it expands benefits
events.summary: Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees, in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers ahead of open enrollment. Walmart will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6. Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs. The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's years-long effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026. In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year. The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's. Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said. "The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC.

events.title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts
events.summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of rogue agents operating at scale and said the bank is building defensive tools. The bank is piloting Smart Cash, an internal tool to forecast cash flow and move funds to maximize yield. Dimon said customers using outside agents must understand the risks and potential transfer of responsibility. JPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. "Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said. "We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, like customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, CFO Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer." Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts.

events.title: Cornell suspends fraternity parties after alleged campus gang rape case
events.summary: Chapters face immediate emergency suspensions for violations amid a sweeping ban tackling fraternity parties at the US university. Cornell University has suspended fraternity parties for the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus. The Ivy League university announced the major changes on Tuesday, as it sought to reassure the rattled campus community amid the ongoing outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024. The accusations came to light after the former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month. In addition to the blanket suspension of all parties and social events at fraternity houses through the 2026-27 school year, Cornell President Michael I Kotlikoff announced a new “zero-tolerance” policy for violations, noting that any fraternity chapter that breaks the ban will face an immediate freeze. “These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter addressed to the campus community on Tuesday. The university president pledged to strengthen Cornell’s sexual misconduct response by adding a dedicated case manager to the Office of Civil Rights to guide survivors through the reporting process. Kotlikoff affirmed that he will be transferring investigative authority from the university police to independent, trauma-informed investigators with the New York State Police in an effort to reform the handling of sexual abuse cases on campus and restore community trust. Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk. Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programmes, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus”. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said. Doe’s lawsuit was brought against the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell University and seven of its members, accusing them of drugging and gang raping her during a party on the night of October 19, 2024. Following her initial allegations in 2024, Cornell shut down the fraternity and temporarily suspended the accused male students, two of whom were later expelled. But critics have said the university’s response was too lenient, prompting it to launch an independent review into its handling of the case, led by a former top US prosecutor. “We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Kotlikoff said. “Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

events.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
events.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program. Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site. Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes. Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant. A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said. But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now. "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said. Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders. Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call. Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment. It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical. The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said. In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join. Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher. The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions. "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said. "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added. Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

events.title: Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? As Israel moves Gaza’s Yellow Line westward, displaced families in Shujayea face renewed danger, and nowhere safe to go. Shujayea, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Harzeen is pitching a tent about 200 metres from the yellow concrete blocks marking Israel’s so-called Yellow Line , preparing for his sixth move. Each time the line inches closer, the 35-year-old packs up and moves further back, trying to keep his family away from danger. But every move offers only temporary relief. list 1 of 3 Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing list 2 of 3 Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears list 3 of 3 Israeli academic and Al Jazeera contributor Ori Goldberg dies at 50 “Every time they move forward a little, we move back a little,” Harzeen told Al Jazeera. The Yellow Line divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Israeli forces withdrew behind the line, but have continued to move the demarcation deeper into Gaza. They now control about 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed a year ago. On October 11, Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres westward in Shujayea, in eastern Gaza City. More of the neighbourhood was brought under Israeli military control and Palestinian families were forced to flee again, with Israel’s shifting boundaries further restricting where they can live and move. For Harzeen, who supports a family of 10, the latest move is part of a year-long search for somewhere his family can live. He can’t remember the dates of each displacement. Instead, he recalled the places, one after another: Zeitoun, Sahat al-Shawa, al-Muntazah. “About six times – every time the line advanced a little – I would feel that it was dangerous, so I would move back a little and try to live there for a while,” he explained. His most recent move barely lasted one night. After spending time setting up the tent, he slept in it once before Israeli forces moved the Yellow Line forward again, getting too close for Harzeen’s liking. “I pitched the tent and slept in it for one night,” he said. “The next morning, we took our bedding and our things and left.” The threat extends beyond the movement of the blocks themselves. Harzeen described living amid drones, helicopters, artillery fire and stray bullets, with shrapnel posing a constant danger to people sheltering nearby. The nights when the line advances are particularly frightening, he said, recalling tanks, troops and heavy shelling as the blocks were moved. Israel has continued its attacks despite the “ceasefire”, killing nearly 1,500 Palestinians in the last year. Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the war started in October 2023. “The night they move the line, there are tanks, infantry coming down, and shells being fired,” he said. “All of that happens just so they can move the yellow block a little further forward.” Most people in Gaza have been displaced multiple times as a result of Israel’s genocidal war and the accompanying large scale destruction of buildings across the enclave. That leaves little space to pitch tents in safer areas and soaring rent that Harzeen can’t afford. Now he is preparing for the possibility of moving again. “They will probably move it forward again,” he said. “Every time we have to flee, we have to move closer to it. We keep moving.” Fleeing at night, returning in the morning For Asma Ali, 32, the Yellow Line’s advance has turned displacement into a cycle of fleeing at night and returning in the morning, never knowing how long her family can stay in one place. Ali, a mother of three from Shujayea, said her family has been displaced seven or eight times since the ceasefire began. After staying in central Gaza City, they returned to Shujayea hoping to settle in the al-Mantar area. But then, a month later, renewed shelling and evacuation fears forced them to move again. The family sought shelter at a school before moving to a house near a bus stop. After a night of heavy shelling, they left in the early hours of the morning and went to stay with family back in the centre of Gaza City. But the advance of the Yellow Line has left Ali uncertain about where her family could go next. “Every night, we would flee, then come back in the morning,” Ali said. “You spend the night trying to find somewhere to stay, then return the next morning.” “The night the Yellow Line advances is terrifying,” she said. “The shooting continues from the beginning of the night until dawn. You live in fear.” Ali said her family lost their belongings – including gold, household items and her children’s clothes – when the dwelling they were staying in was destroyed. Among the items lost was a brace for her son, who has a disability. She only had the brace for two days.

events.title: Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
events.summary: Several attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport are highlighting how commercial aviation has become a greater target in global conflicts. Airlines suspended or postponed service to Riyadh after the attacks, which were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. The conflicts have also cut off swaths of airspace in the Middle East, mainly over Iran, which means airlines have to fly longer routes. Deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport over the past week are highlighting how conflicts in the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale. Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quickly cancel flights throughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether. "It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others. The Saudi airport attacks , claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones. Iran war threatens $11.7 trillion global travel industry as passengers get caught in crossfire As Iran strikes disrupt flights, why travel insurance may fall short Airlines divert, cancel more Middle East flights after Iran attacks U.S. military base Airlines cancel Israel flights, tour operators scramble to change trips after attacks Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is driving up air cargo costs "Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant. The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces. "There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving." King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country. Delta Air Lines , meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching an Atlanta-Riyadh route , the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier. But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March. The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment. Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks. events.title: Rivian’s startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics . Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding. Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field. Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale. Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human . The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer. Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation. “Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said. Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024 . He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.” “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also , a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized. Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026 . events.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says.

events.title: Consumers say regulators must 'lift their game' after solar battery delays
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lux Solar investigated by watchdog as consumers claim they were ripped off Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Bob Emery took his complaint to a consumer protection body and industry groups without resolution. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) Consumers are raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs. A government spokesperson said it had empowered the Clean Energy Regulator to monitor the industry closely. After waiting a year for a battery system that never showed up, Bob Emery's frustration boiled over. He claims the installer, Lux Solar, "can't be trusted". Mr Emery paid a $1,000 deposit last October for a 48kwh system which he hoped would slash his power bills at his Perth home. After lengthy delays, he unsuccessfully requested a refund. The retired electrician also pursued his case with a consumer protection body and industry groups without resolution. He joins a growing number of customers raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The program has sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025. Over four years, the scheme has covered estimated costs of more than $7.2 billion. There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs with the NSW energy and water ombudsman saying complaints in that jurisdiction had doubled since last year. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has several investigations underway and South Australia has announced a crackdown on "dodgy solar companies". Queensland's Office of Fair Trading confirmed Lux Solar is under investigation. It is the second solar company in as many months being probed for allegedly charging customers for deposits to install battery systems under the federal scheme that were never delivered. Bob Emery is still waiting for his solar battery. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) In June, Lux Solar was kicked out of the voluntary industry-run consumer protection scheme, the New Energy Tech Consumer Code (NETCC) for "major failures," including continuing to take payments without showing it could deliver the systems. The company has continued to advertise itself as an "approved seller" on its website, despite the Clean Energy Council requesting that wording be removed. Consumer advocate and CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre, Erin Turner, has called for the ad to be investigated. "That's really potentially misleading and I hope a regulator looks at it because that's a part of the consumer law where we can see really significant court actions with fines of up to $100 million," Ms Turner said. 'I don't have any trust in anyone installing it' In November 2025, Mr Emery was told the installation of his battery system was two to four weeks away. Two months later there was still no progress, so he emailed the salesman and asked for a refund. Bob Emery has waited over a year for his solar battery from Lux Solar. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) Again, he was told the "install team" would make contact within a week or two. Mr Emery grew alarmed when the salesman stopped answering his calls and voice messages with Lux Solar weren't returned. Lux Solar is based in Western Australia but also operates in Queensland and New South Wales. Mr Emery made a complaint to Consumer Protection WA but the watchdog said it was up to him to take the matter to court. "The government bodies need to lift their game," he said. "It's put me off the whole (federal battery) program, I don't have any trust in anyone installing it," he said. Lux Solar told customer Justin Albin that installer issues were the reason for delays getting his solar battery. ( ABC News: Brigham Edgar ) His frustration is shared by Brisbane man Justin Albin and his Queensland work colleague who both waited about a year after paying deposits to Lux Solar last October. In January, a salesman told Mr Albin there had been "some installer issues" but he would get his system as promised. He received an email which said Lux Solar had more installation teams "ramping back up" and confirmation would come soon. He sent a legal letter demanding Lux Solar install the system or he would start court proceedings. Justin Albin has waited about a year after paying a deposit last October. ( ABC News: Brigham Edgar ) Lux Solar offered him a refund which he rejected.

events.title: US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from freedom of information requirements. The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). The high court is intervening on Tuesday for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (CREW) in Washington’s case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of US President Donald Trump’s second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case. list 1 of 3 Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives list 2 of 3 Musk vows ‘affordable’ Starlink in India as he escalates feud with Ambani list 3 of 3 Elon Musk spends $366m to bolster Republican Party in US midterm elections Last year, the high court reined in a district court’s order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court’s conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group. CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body. Cooper ruled in CREW’s favour and ordered expedited processing of the group’s records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW. The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court’s direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the “autonomy and confidentiality” of presidential advisers. “Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach,” US Department of Justice lawyers wrote. The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorised the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason. CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court’s previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025. “Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President’s statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” CREW lawyers wrote. In a statement Tuesday, CREW lawyer Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act. “We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government,” Sus said in the statement. DOGE said it had slashed tens of billions of dollars in expenditures, but its claims were difficult for outside financial experts to verify. Federal auditors found that some of DOGE’s reported savings across contract, grant and ⁠lease terminations were incorrect, lacked supporting evidence or included terminations that were already under way when DOGE was established, according to ⁠a report by the Government Accountability Office.

events.title: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
events.summary: More Republicans are speaking out against President Donald Trump's decision to let Vladimir Putin's Russia temporarily export diesel fuel on the global market. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Kentucky's Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn of Texas joined six Democrats urging Trump to cancel the arrangement. Trump claims the deal will help bring diesel prices down, but oil analysts don't think it will be enough to make a meaningful impact. More Republicans are speaking out against President Donald Trump 's decision to let Vladimir Putin 's Russia temporarily export diesel fuel on the global market, expanding the bipartisan blowback over the deal. Six GOP senators joined six of their Democratic colleagues in a letter Tuesday urging Trump to cancel the arrangement allowing Russia to supply 4.8 million metric tons, or nearly 36 million barrels, of diesel through mid-April. "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the lawmakers wrote. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Kentucky's Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn of Texas signed on, adding to the list of of GOP Congress members who had earlier questioned the deal Trump announced Friday. Armstrong has roots in the energy industry, having been CEO of Williams Companies , the largest natural gas-focused company in the U.S. They joined Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, New Hampshire's Jeanne Shaheen , Richard Durbin of Illinois, Delaware's Chris Coons and Rhode Island's Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed . The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the letter. Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had already spoken out, joining a statement with Democrats on Sunday that urged Trump not to "provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians." Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah had also joined that statement. Trump announced the Russia diesel deal after a call with Putin. The announcement quickly drew an unusually critical response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who counts on continued U.S. support for his military. Trump, in turn, slammed Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should get a new president . Trump claimed in Friday's announcement that the deal will help quickly and sharply bring record-high diesel prices down. But oil analysts don't think the Russian supply will be nearly enough to make a meaningful impact on prices. The 12 senators who signed Tuesday's letter to Trump agreed, writing that the deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans." "Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans," the senators told Trump. "It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea," they wrote. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' The senators also alleged, as other critics already have, that the diesel deal contradicts the bipartisan Russian sanctions law that Trump signed into law a few weeks before announcing the deal, which required lifting existing sanctions on Russia. "These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," their letter read. "Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," they wrote. "Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world." Trump has doubled down on his decision . "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" he wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

events.title: Outcry over council's 'extortionate' fee hike on short-stay homes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bass Coast short-stay holiday home owners call for rethink of council fee hike Phillip Island holiday home owner Lisa has described the council fee hike on her property as extortionate. ( ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams ) Holiday home owners in Victoria's south-east are urging a council to overturn an increase to its short-stay accommodation levy. The Bass Coast Shire Council says the extra fees are needed to cover the costs associated with tourism, including rubbish collection. More than 1,000 properties are registered as short-term rentals in the shire, but industry data has identified more than 2,300 listings on platforms such as AirBnB and Stayz. A coastal Victorian council has defended its move to increase fees for providers of short-stay rental accommodation as hundreds of community members urge it to rethink the decision. The Bass Coast Shire, which takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island on Victoria's south-east coast, is one of just a handful of Victorian areas with local laws regulating short-stay accommodation. The council says the extra fees are necessary to cope with additional costs created by the holiday accommodation industry, but tourism advocates warn it may deter holiday home owners from renting at all, meaning more homes will stay empty for longer. Lisa, who did not want her last name published, bought her Phillip Island holiday home with her partner two years ago and said they worked very hard to afford it. Lisa says she and her partner have worked hard to afford their Phillip Island holiday home. ( ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams ) The couple is currently renting the property using an online platform at a base rate of about $220 per night. "We thought we could just share the home with other people and let them enjoy it until we're fully ready to move down here full time," she said. Earlier this year, Bass Coast Shire Council increased its annual registration fee to short-stay providers like Lisa from $324 to $600 — or $900 for homes with more than five bedrooms. The fee hike caught Lisa off guard. "It seems a bit extortionate really," she said. The Bass Coast Shire takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island. ( Supplied ) While governments across Australia have taken different approaches to regulating the short-stay sector, a statewide levy of 7.5 per cent came into effect in Victoria in 2025 . Some councils, like Warrnambool, scrapped local fees after the levy was introduced, but a handful retained local laws. That includes the Bass Coast, which has had a registration process in place since 2023 and now has the highest fees in the state . The retention of the local fees has led some short-stay providers to accuse governments of "double-dipping". However, University of Sydney housing expert Nicole Gurran said the state booking levy was likely also being paid by consumers. "It may be a bit of both: a bit of a provider absorbing the cost and a bit of them adding them on to the fee paid by the customer," she said. Professor Nicole Gurran says local councils are facing several challenges with tourism population booms. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Dr Gurran said short-stay rentals and sudden population booms over holiday periods were difficult for regional councils to deal with. "You've got increased costs associated with waste collection, for instance, associated with managing beaches, parks, public spaces," she said. Bass Coast Shire mayor Brett Tessari agreed, saying the fee was introduced to "control" issues related to short-stay accommodation, including complaints from permanent residents about disruptive behaviour. Bass Coast Mayor Brett Tessari says the new fee is an attempt to address issues associated with short-stay accommodation. ( ABC News ) "The waste, the rubbish, the anti-social behaviour — it's our regular permanents that put up with all that," he said. "The cost is quite significant and we realised before this increase that we were just nowhere near where we needed to be." While Victoria's statewide levy raised $85.8 million in 2025 , that money is directed towards social housing investment rather than being used used to cover local costs. Rental shortage after pandemic migration More than 1,000 short-stay properties in the Bass Coast region have registered with the council. However, data collected by AirDNA, a company that provides analytics on the short-term rental industry, identified more than 2,300 listings advertised across Airbnb and Stayz in the area in August.

events.title: Man City charges: Any political interference and I’ll quit, says regulator
events.summary: English football regulator insists there will be no political pressure in Manchester City’s appeal over guilty verdict. The chair of English football’s regulatory body said Tuesday he would resign if there were any political interference over potential sanctions for Manchester City. City has been found guilty of widespread breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules which could result in punishments including a massive fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England’s top flight. list 1 of 4 Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa list 2 of 4 Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ NBA Finals jersey sells for record $14m list 3 of 4 Canelo Alvarez ‘will fight in Riyadh’ despite Saudi airport attacks list 4 of 4 Verstappen wins chaotic Singapore GP F1 sprint after Russell crashes Separately, the government’s Independent Football Regulator has the powers to force club owners to sell and can withhold a license to operate if they are deemed unfit. An independent panel found United Arab Emirates-backed City had artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1bn over nearly a decade, circumventing fair-play rules. Football regulator chair David Kogan said it was still awaiting the outcome of City’s appeal against the verdict. The UAE is a big investor in the United Kingdom. Asked about the regulator’s ability to remain independent given wider relations between the governments, Kogan said “any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role and I stand by that completely”. “We’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic. And I don’t expect to in the future,” he said. Kogan’s comments came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s current ownership. Burnham also said he would not get “directly involved in the process”. City is accused of providing misleading information about its finances over a nine-year period from 2009-2018. During that time, it won three titles and signed some of the world’s best players. It went on to enjoy a period of unprecedented dominance of English football. The guilty verdict represents the biggest scandal in Premier League history and raises questions over the future of the club, which is owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, UAE deputy prime minister and a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family. The Independent Football Regulatory was established by the UK government last year to set governance standards in English football. Part of that includes the issuing of licenses for clubs to be able to operate, which will begin from November. Kogan suggested the guilty verdict would not impact the issuing of a license to City because its appeal is ongoing. “A verdict once it’s gone through an appeal process will certainly be something that we would clearly be taking into account when looking at awarding a license or looking at the owners, directors and senior executives,” he said.

events.title: Man City charges: Ahead of PSG, Dias defends celebrations at Liverpool
events.summary: Captain Ruben Dias says that the Manchester City players trust the football club, and that celebrations after the win at Anfield were justified. Manchester City captain Ruben Dias said on Tuesday that “people don’t love us winning and we love to win”, as he robustly defended his football club’s raucous celebrations after beating Liverpool, despite being found guilty of a catalogue of Premier League financial rules breaches. City were jeered throughout by Liverpool fans during a 3-0 win at Anfield last weekend that left them top of the Premier League table, three points clear of reigning champions Arsenal, with six wins from six matches. list 1 of 4 Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa list 2 of 4 Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ NBA Finals jersey sells for record $14m list 3 of 4 Canelo Alvarez ‘will fight in Riyadh’ despite Saudi airport attacks list 4 of 4 Verstappen wins chaotic Singapore GP F1 sprint after Russell crashes It was City’s first game since being found guilty of more than 100 charges relating to breaches of the English top flight’s financial fair-play rules. City have appealed the verdict, with every match featuring the team now played under a huge cloud of uncertainty. Manager Enzo Maresca’s men will be back in European action on Wednesday when they play at home against holders Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in the Champions League. Both clubs are bankrolled by wealthy owners from the Gulf, with City backed by the ruling family of Abu Dhabi while PSG are financed by the Qatari state. “I really feel like I speak for the whole group; we trust the club,” insisted Dias, despite City being found guilty of 34 charges of failing to cooperate with the league’s investigation. The Portugal defender added: “If there’s more or less noise or whatever the reason the noise is, at the end of the day it’s all the same, same as before, because people don’t love us winning and we love to win.” City faced criticism for the exuberant way they celebrated victory over 10-man Liverpool. But an unapologetic Maresca said, “Criticised for what? We won 3-0 at Anfield. What do you want us to do? Even if it was 1-0, it would be exactly the same. “We work every day to win games. It’s the only thing that we can think about and be focused [on].” Dias backed Maresca by saying, “To win at Anfield in whatever circumstance, whether it’s earlier in the season or later in the season, we will enjoy it just as much. “We will celebrate however it feels in the moment, and it will obviously be a show of how much it means to us.” Maresca added that the fallout from the guilty verdicts was more difficult for City supporters to deal with than for his squad. “Probably it has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me,” he said. “It is more complicated because if I was an Arsenal fan or United fan and you are a City fan, I can say ‘My friend, you are a cheat’ or these kinds of things. So probably, it has been more tough for them.” PSG are bidding for a third straight Champions League title, having come from two goals down to beat City 4-2 in stunning fashion during the 2024-25 edition. “The message for tomorrow night is quite easy, in terms of winning the perfect game because they [PSG] are the best team in Europe in this moment,” said Maresca. “They won the last two Champions Leagues, so that shows how good they are. So we need the perfect game, but at the same time doing our best, I think we can beat them and be happy at the end.” Former City manager Pep Guardiola is due to attend Wednesday’s game in what will be his first visit to the Etihad since standing down at the end of last season, with the Spaniard having already publicly backed his old club during the current crisis. “I spoke with Pep after the [Manchester] United game,” said Maresca. “In case he’s coming, it’s a nice feeling – especially for him, because this has been his house for 10 years with what he has done here. It’s exciting for everyone.”
