events.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition. Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood. Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart. Where firing squad is legal The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC . It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer. The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection. Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions. Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios What we know about the execution livestream Few specifics are known about the livestream execution, where it would streamed, or how people would watch it. It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood. It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies. What we're watching: The Army. Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.

events.title: Being chronically online is part of the job description for this top influencer marketer
events.summary: Sophia Sesto is Poppi's VP of culture. Photo Credit: Sophia Sesto If you're lucky, scrolling through TikTok could be part of your job. Sophia Sesto, Poppi's VP of culture, is tasked with keeping the prebiotic soda brand relevant. Poppi's influencer strategy relies on its team of marketers who are deeply fluent in the internet and pop culture. Sophia Sesto has a trick up her sleeve for influencer marketing: staying chronically online. Her role — vice president of culture for the buzzy prebiotic soda brand Poppi — requires her to be tuned in to popular culture. To spot trends and emerging content creators, it's crucial to follow "your own For You Page," Sesto told Business Insider. Sesto was recently featured in Business Insider's 2026 list of most innovative influencer marketers. The search for new, culture-driving creators "is never-ending," said Sesto, who leads Poppi's influencer, partnerships, and social marketing teams. Within Poppi's internal Microsoft Teams , there is a channel called "Seed" where Sesto and other Poppi staff "are constantly dropping" creators and content, accompanied by ideas for how the brand can work with these people in the future. Poppi has a "long-standing" partnership with Alix Earle, Sesto said. Courtesy of Poppi "It is the most manual process," Sesto said, adding that AI tools haven't yet proved useful on this front. "It's all in-house, and we say we get our consumer because we are them." Brands are projected to spend more than $44 billion on influencer marketing in the US this year, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB). As more dollars get pumped into the space, and more creators vie for those checks, standing out and driving conversation carry more weight. Meanwhile, the internet rapidly churns through viral memes and trends. Brands only have a split second to pounce. "A big part of my role is continuously building a model that moves at the speed of culture, while also being able to scale," Sesto said. Poppi's reality TV love affair Poppi's marketing campaigns around the hit reality TV show "Love Island" were right in this sweet spot. While on her honeymoon, Sesto watched "Love Island" and kept up with her colleagues. "We were in the Teams chats like, 'Did you watch last night? What do you think of this? What do you think of that?'" Sesto said. "I promise we get real work done too, but this is when our best work happens." Poppi's team, like many other "Love Island" viewers, grew obsessed with a 2025 cast member, Amaya Espinal . That July, when the plot of the show turned on Espinal, Poppi's staff went on Instagram to show its support with a made-up "Amaya Papaya" flavor. "It's our best-performing Instagram post of all time," Sesto said. What started as a joke turned into a full marketing campaign and flavor launch. By October, Poppi had cast Espinal in a campaign and launched a limited-edition flavor, "Amaya's Island Colada." The drink was sold on Amazon and at Target. Poppi sank its teeth into the "Love Island" fandom even further, working with creators on watch parties and other digital content. According to the company, creator-made content generated more than 212 million views. How Poppi works with pop culture icons Poppi has landed its bright-colored soda cans in the hands of internet celebrities like Alix Earle , Jake Shane, and Charli XCX. Poppi has a "long-standing relationship" with Earle, Sesto said. The brand worked with Earle at Coachella in 2024 and later launched a branded can with her in 2025. Earle's partnership goes deeper than sponsorships, too. She became an investor in the soda brand in 2024. Poppi is a frequent sponsor of Jake Shane's podcast "Therapuss." Courtesy of Poppi The brand has leveraged these faces in some of its highest-budget advertising campaigns, such as its Super Bowl commercials . Poppi recently partnered with actor Shay Mitchell's luggage brand , Béis, on a collection of suitcases. Like many brands, Poppi leveraged an IRL event to coincide with the launch. Poppi isn't only focused on the biggest stars. Sesto said its "always-on influencer program" is a crucial part of the brand's strategy to stay relevant and in front of consumers. When Poppi rolled out its "Shirley Temple" flavor at the end of 2025, it sent cans of the soda to influencers without any context, Sesto said, hoping the creators would post about it. "We gave them the opportunity to launch the flavor for us," Sesto said. Poppi recently partnered with Shay Mitchell's luggage brand Béis. Courtesy of Poppi Big Soda, bigger opportunities After Poppi was acquired by PepsiCo for nearly $2 billion in 2025, a new motto defined the brand's transition: "Let Poppi be Poppi," Sesto said. Poppi's new parent company is "leaning in" to Poppi's cheekiness, Sesto said, and letting Poppi's team "do our thing." The new ownership is also opening up doors. Since the acquisition, Poppi inked a partnership with Starbucks, landing the prebiotic soda on the coffee chain's shelves. Meanwhile, Poppi is also venturing into international markets and launched in the UK this year. "We're working on — spoiler alert — more places where you'll see Poppi," Sesto said. events.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece at White House's request
events.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle said Tuesday that she would resign. New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said earlier that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave her post. President Donald Trump signaled that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., could be on the chopping block. Guilfoyle's tenure was rocked by multiple Wall Street Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarm among ethics experts and former government officials. U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle said Tuesday she would resign, shortly after new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Guilfoyle was being asked to leave her post. "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," Guilfoyle said in an X post. Guilfoyle also broadly denied "recent allegations" against her, apparently referring to multiple critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about her conduct before and after becoming an ambassador, which had prompted questions about her job security. "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle said in the post. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." Asked for comment on Guilfoyle's post, a Wall Street Journal spokesperson told CNBC, "We stand by our reporting." President Donald Trump suggested later Tuesday morning that the reporting on Guilfoyle's conduct prompted the call for her resignation. "She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters outside the White House before boarding Marine One. The president also pushed back when a reporter noted that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. , was almost a member of his family. "No, she wasn't a member of my family," Trump replied. "She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago, but she wasn't." Hours earlier, Zacharia revealed that the White House had urged Guilfoyle to step down. "We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said while taking questions from reporters in the White House briefing room for the first time. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well." Trump had signaled Monday evening that Guilfoyle could be on the chopping block. "Well, we're looking at it," Trump said at the White House when a reporter asked if he was weighing firing the ambassador. Guilfoyle's yearlong tenure in Athens was rocked last month by the first of multiple Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarms among ethics experts and former government officials. A Sept. 25 article alleged Guilfoyle persistently promoted a Greek company and involved a lobbyist for a Greek construction firm in meetings with foreign officials. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal in response to that article that Guilfoyle has "worked with companies across the energy sector" and has not been focused on one company. According to an Oct. 7 report from the Journal, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to quietly pay down her American Express bill before her congressional hearing to become an ambassador. Binnall told the newspaper that Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events prior to being nominated and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." Binnall also disputed the authenticity of messages from Guilfoyle reported in the article, but declined to provide specifics, according to the Journal. On Saturday, the Journal reported that Guilfoyle in January boasted of her close ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invite to a dinner being held for Eric Trump, another of the president's sons.

events.title: The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating
events.summary: Economists expect the consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% on the month and 3.6% year over year. Core CPI is forecast to show a 0.2% gain on the month and 2.5% annual increase. Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, one economist warned. Wednesday's closely watched reading on consumer prices could show intensifying inflationary pressures as energy costs keep climbing. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect the headline consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% for the month and to increase 3.6% compared with a year ago. That 12-month number would signal that the rate of price growth is accelerating and moving further from the Federal Reserve 's goal of 2%. So-called core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is expected to increase 0.2% from August and 2.5% on a 12-month basis. While that would mark a slight slowdown from the prior month, it would be an uptick in year-over-year inflation. Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax firm. Energy costs have been among the biggest drivers of inflation since the U.S. war with Iran began earlier this year. President Donald Trump last week announced loosened diesel restrictions on Russia in a bid to juice the global oil trade, though analysts don't believe it will meaningfully bring down prices. Prices for Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, climbed more than 14% in September, bringing its third-quarter advance to about 42%. Brent prices on Tuesday traded around $105 per barrel. "We've got real upside risk on the September CPI," Brusuelas said. "Typically, when we have these moves in inflation, everyone's models undershoot the actual outcome." Sticky oil prices could also push up costs for items in other, non-energy categories, according to Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. In this scenario, it would become harder for the Fed to write off the energy prices surge as a short-term shock that won't necessitate interest rate increases. After announcing its first increase in three years last month, the Federal Reserve signaled in its minutes from that meeting that it will likely have to hike rates again . Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will next lift rates at its December policy meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "The list of reasons to hike rates in our view is long," Sockin said. "Ultimately, we have low confidence in the timing of the Fed's next move, but more conviction on the direction of travel." Wednesday's release is the last reading on CPI before November's midterm elections , which could determine whether the Republican party will keep total control in Washington. Economic confidence across political affiliation has fallen this year, according to the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment data. Compared with Democrats, Republican and independent voters have posted steeper declines in sentiment since the start of 2026, the data shows. Economists forecast that the producer price index, a gauge of inflation facing wholesalers due on Thursday, will rise 0.6% from August to September and 5.5% on a 12-month basis. Both of those numbers would mark a modest acceleration in growth compared with August's release.

events.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit. There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel .) And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space. Longshot Space Technology , a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission. When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs. The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far. The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says. These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.) “If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.” The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites. “The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes. But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price. It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.

events.title: Greens warn of private school fees loophole in Labor's trust tax
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens concerned private school fees paid out of trusts could escape Labor's 30pc tax Nick McKim has accused Labor of 'watering down' its trust taxation plans. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke/Matt Roberts ) The Greens say a "loophole" for private school fees is a sticking point in Labor's proposed trust laws. Jim Chalmers will introduce legislation for the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts on Wednesday, amid stiff business opposition. Labor requires the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax hike, given that the Coalition is opposed. Parents who pay private school fees from their trust funds could escape Labor's proposed trust tax, in what the Greens say is a "loophole" that must be closed. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will today unveil a bill to impose the 30 per cent minimum tax on some trusts. The budget proposal has enraged the business lobby and unnerved Labor backbenchers anxious about small business hostility. The Greens, whose votes are required in the Senate, have the opposite concern. On Tuesday, the party called for a Senate inquiry into the bill, saying an early draft was "watered down" and the proposal would not get a "free pass". The ABC can reveal the Greens' main concern is an exemption for money paid from trusts to charities, non-profits and other tax-exempt entities, including private schools. "People who are wealthy enough to set up trusts should not get a tax break to pay for private school fees when this option is denied to people who can't afford expensive accountants," Greens economic spokesperson Nick McKim told the ABC. "The treasurer needs to knock this out of the legislation." In a draft proposal last month, the government indicated it would cap the amount of exempt money each year, but that cap has not yet been set. The proposal does not change the tax treatment of private schools, since this avenue already exists. But by carving charitable payments out from the new higher rate of tax, the Greens will argue this makes the avenue more attractive. "There is far too much leniency," Senator McKim said. "Labor is just trying to funnel ever-increasing revenues into the private education system when public schools are being starved of funds." Mr Chalmers says the proposal is a crackdown on those who use trust funds as a vehicle to reduce their tax bills. The 30 per cent minimum tax applies only to so-called "discretionary" trusts, a term the tax office uses to identify trust structures that give their owners the flexibility to shift their money into the names of family members, holding companies, or others. Tax experts say these complicated structures allow a minority of very wealthy, highly motivated people to achieve dramatic reductions in the tax they pay. The government expects to raise $4.5 billion from the tax in its first year of operation. Government offers small businesses a trust tax workaround Those with discretionary trusts can be exempt from the new minimum 30 per cent tax if they agree to hold their trust distributions constant. But business lobbies and the opposition have argued discretionary trusts are used for a range of legitimate purposes, including by small business owners. The government has outlined several exemptions, including for family farms that are placed within trusts, charities that operate as trusts, and trusts that are set up to manage deceased estates. But Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the tax still sent "the wrong message" and targeted business unfairly. "We urge all members of parliament to … listen to the views of those small businesses who will be affected: small and medium-sized home builders, family pharmacies, newsagents, small retailers, restaurants and cafes," he said on Tuesday. The government estimates that 350,000 active small businesses — roughly one in six — used discretionary trusts in 2022-23, the last year of available data. Treasury analysis suggests 140,000 of those would not need to pay the new tax. Others will get government assistance to restructure their affairs, although there remains concern that those who restructure their businesses as companies would have to pay state and territory stamp duties in the process. The concerns have been echoed by some Labor backbenchers, with several questions put to Mr Chalmers about the bill's consequences in a Tuesday Labor caucus meeting. Summarising the angst, one Labor backbencher told the ABC they were "not happy about these compounding attacks on small business".

events.title: Ukraine isn't focused only on making drones and missiles — it's also prioritizing the jet engines inside
events.summary: Ukraine relies heavily on jet engines for drones and missiles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Screengrab via X Ukraine relies heavily on mini turbojet engines for drones and missiles. The country's defense minister said he expects monthly demand for one specific model to rise to 10,000. Local jet engine production has become a priority for Kyiv as its weapons become more advanced. Mini-turbojet engines have become a growing priority for Ukraine's defense industry as the country relies on them to power the next generation of high-speed interceptor drones and long-range strike weapons. Ukraine has long sourced weapons and components from partner nations. But as the country builds more of its own drones and missiles , reducing that dependency and increasing its self-sufficiency has become more important. Yevhenii Khmara, Ukraine's defense minister, told reporters over the weekend that Kyiv views jet engine production as a "critical area" for its local defense industry. For one specific engine model, he said, projected monthly demand could reach 10,000 units. Khmara said that the demand would be spread across just 20 Ukrainian manufacturers. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, said that supporting domestic jet engine production has been a priority for the past year and a half. The 20 active projects include a mix of government and private initiatives. Large-scale mini-turbojet engine production is "crucial for effectively protecting our skies, and we are working hand-in-hand with the Defense Forces to deliver it at pace," Brave1 told Business Insider in a statement on Tuesday. Ukraine puts jet engines in medium-range drones, which it has used to hit Russian logistics and supply routes across occupied regions of southern Ukraine, and deep-strike weapons, including its cruise missiles that can reach military and energy targets hundreds of miles across the border. Jet engines are also essential for Ukraine as it builds a next generation of interceptors to counter a rise in Russian jet-powered attack drones. Earlier Ukrainian interceptor models were designed to counter Russian drones powered by piston engines, which could reach speeds of up to 115 mph. But Moscow is increasingly using jet-powered drones that travel much faster; some variants can reach up to 375 mph and are much harder to intercept. Ukrainian defense firms are now developing faster interceptors , some of which are powered by turbojet engines. The next generation of interceptors has already downed several of Russia's fastest drones. Following a meeting with military leadership in late September on the Russian drone threat, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that "new decisions" had been made concerning domestic jet engine production, according to a statement from his office at the time. He did not elaborate further. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: What it takes to trust AI with real-world fixes
events.summary: Copilot to autopilot: Why no single safeguard is enough We designed a layered model that lets an AI agent resolve production network incidents on its own within defined identity, authorization, tooling, and human-approval boundaries. It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments. We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix. And that is where the demo stops being a demo. Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk. This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack. Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here. An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch. Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it. Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it. Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits. The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls. Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take? A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone. The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence. Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game. The mental model: Four boundaries, layered Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point. Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go. Layer 1: The agent never has more access than you The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access. Layer 2: One tool interface, not a bare shell The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the unbounded one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or a clean audit trail around bash. But a command line invoked as one narrow, declared tool, behind the interface, is fine. This is why the framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy. You want both, chosen by trust level. Put everything behind the tool interface, then pick the implementation per call: a plain function or a sandboxed CLI for low-risk local work inside the trust boundary, and MCP for anything that crosses it, because MCP gives you least privilege, credential isolation, structured audit, human approval hooks, and rate limiting for free. You can secure a CLI, too, but only by paying for per-user sandboxes with tightly limited access, and even then, you can’t match per-tool granularity. Layer 3: Read freely, pause before you write Diagnostics run on their own.

events.title: Photos: French protests over school conditions swell
events.summary: Mass rallies continue across France backing high school protests, piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron. Tens of thousands of people have joined rallies across France in support of protesting high school students, boosting a movement that is posing a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron as his term in office winds down. Some 161,500 people turned out on Tuesday according to the Interior Ministry, more than double the 71,500 it reported for Thursday’s nationwide demonstrations. Unions helping to organise the rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000. Although most of Tuesday’s demonstrations were peaceful, violence broke out on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the Interior Ministry said 41,500 people took part. Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police. The student movement sprang up last month, with students blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions. What many see as a heavy-handed police response to the students prompted more people to join Tuesday’s demonstrations. Police have opened investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators. Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the Education Ministry said. On Monday, Macron urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”.

events.title: The White House is in its Trump-fueled SI era
events.summary: President Donald Trump has said that those who continue to use the term artificial intelligence will be considered an "enemy" of his White House. Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images AI.gov is now fully si.gov. The White House rolled out the new URL on Tuesday. President Donald Trump has said that he wants AI to be called super intelligence now The White House has finally addressed a remnant of the AI era. On Tuesday, the Trump administration rolled out si.gov, giving a new URL to the site that was first launched during the Biden administration. The new site describes President Donald Trump 's artificial intelligence policies, though much of the text itself was changed before Tuesday. "The Super Intelligence era is here. 🇺🇸," Michael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, wrote on X. The new address falls in line with Trump's wishes that artificial intelligence, or AI, now be called super intelligence, or SI. The president formalized his preference in a September 29 executive order. Last week, Trump declared that if others did not go along with his rebrand, they would be considered an "enemy" of his White House. The president has said that using the term "artificial intelligence" makes the technology sound fake. AI and tech leaders have split over how to handle Trump's request. Over the weekend, SpaceXAI followed through on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk 's promise to rebrand the company's AI division as SpaceXSI. On Saturday, days after Trump bestowed an honor on him, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella published a lengthy statement titled: "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era." AI and artificial intelligence were not among the 805 words Nadella wrote. As for OpenAI, whose name contains the very abbreviation Trump wants gone, its CEO, Sam Altman, previously ruled out a rebrand. "No plans to do that," Altman told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot, and we will continue to talk about it." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
events.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting for them to halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. events.title: Cathay Pacific's $19 billion upgrade includes new premium economy and business-class seats. I got a sneak peak — take a look.
events.summary: I tested out Cathay Pacific's business-class Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Cathay Pacific is rolling out new premium economy and business-class seats on Boeing 777-300ERs. The new premium-economy seats feature a winged, cushioned headrest and a footrest. Cathay's business-class Aria Suite comes with storage bins, lie-flat seats, and an art gallery. As Cathay Pacific marks its 80th anniversary, the airline is investing $19 billion into upgrading its fleet, cabins, lounges, and digital products. This includes new-and-improved premium economy and business-class seats, available on select routes aboard its fleet of retrofitted Boeing 777-300ERs. Cathay Pacific's upgraded offerings arrive as airlines increasingly pursue passengers willing to spend more for extra comfort and amenities. Across the industry, carriers are investing in larger premium-economy sections, lie-flat suites , upgraded dining, and lounge access as high-end fares bring in outsize revenue compared to standard economy seats. Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines , for example, recently unveiled new premium-economy cabins and upgraded business-class suites for long-haul flights. At an event in New York City on Thursday, I got to test out Cathay's new premium cabins for a closer look at the enhancements. Cathay Pacific is rolling out the new premium economy and business-class seats on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet. A Cathay Pacific Boeing 777. ADEK BERRY/AFP via Getty Images The upgraded offerings are available Boeing 777-300ERs flights between Hong Kong and Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Vancouver, and will be available on flights between New York-JFK and Hong Kong in 2027. The upgraded seats come with a steep price tag. Mid-November flights from Los Angeles to Hong Kong aboard a retrofitted Boeing 777-300ER range from $1,500 to $2,900 one-way in premium economy and between $3,700 and nearly $5,000 in business class, per Cathay's website. I started in premium economy, where a Cathay Pacific executive told me that "the entire experience is designed from the customer perspective." Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Jason Li, Cathay Pacific's vice president of sales and marketing for the Americas, said that the airline focused on providing "enough differentiation between the premium economy and the economy seat" to make the upgrade worth the higher price. "From the cabin seat perspective, there's more privacy with the little winglet design," Li said of the headrest, elongated on one side to block its neighbor. "The angle of reclining is also much better compared to the economy for our new premium economy class." After I sat down, a flight attendant cheerfully popped the footrest and tilted the seat back to its reclined position for the full premium economy experience. Testing out Cathay Pacific's premium economy seat. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider I felt like I was sitting in an armchair, not an airplane seat. An added bonus is the leather pillow with foldable sides cushioning the headrest, which felt comfortable enough to render a travel neck pillow obsolete. A headrest in Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The longer side of the headrest also featured a built-in reading light. Other amenities include Bluetooth-capable in-flight entertainment on a 15.6-inch 4K screen and numerous charging ports. Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider In- flight WiFi is complimentary for Cathay members traveling in premium economy. Next, I explored Cathay Pacific's business-class offering, the Aria Suite. The Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The Aria Suite, the first version of which debuted in October 2024, comes with a sliding door and divider for maximum privacy. The seat can also recline all the way back for a lie-flat bed on long-haul flights. The Touch Screen Passenger Control Unit, or TSPCU, allows passengers to control their lights and seating positions. The Touch Screen Passenger Control Unit (TSPCU). Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Travelers can choose from three light settings — reading, mode, and console — and three seating positions — taxi, takeoff, and landing (TTL), lounge, and bed. The Aria Suite has several hidden compartments. Hidden compartments and wireless charging in the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider A flight attendant told me these are useful for storing headphones or other items during bathroom breaks or walks to get blood flowing. The Aria Suite also has a wireless charging station indicated by subtle markings in the side console's marble design. There's also a mirror that folds out of a small cabinet that holds the in-flight entertainment remote. A cabinet and mirror in the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider At 24 inches, the Aria Suite's in-flight entertainment screens are the largest ever offered on Cathay Pacific. Aside from the upgraded seats, the Boeing 777-300ER business-class cabins include a new amenity: an in-flight art gallery. A rendering of Cathay Pacific's Gallery in the Skies featuring a painting by Stephen Wong. Cathay Pacific Cathay Pacific partnered with Hong Kong artists to display their original works of art in a "Gallery in the Skies." "It's something that we're very proud of in terms of product differentiation and the experience that we offer in flight, which I think is very unique and also brings us to the next level in terms of customer proposition," Li said. Cathay’s retrofitted 777s aim to win over travelers willing to pay for more space, privacy, and elevated amenities. In the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider For passengers willing to pay a premium, Cathay's new seats could help make long-haul flights a luxurious experience — more than merely bearable. events.title: UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people
events.summary: Retailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget. At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics). Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment . They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets. Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said. Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills. Another attender, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium trade body which represents most big retailers, said: “Retail is a major driver of growth, supporting jobs, investment and communities across the country, and providing vital first jobs and career opportunities for young people. “But after whacking up retailers’ taxes by 20% in two years, including an extra £6.5bn in new employment costs, any new costs will be paid by consumers at the till and make it harder for retailers to create jobs. “The chancellor recognised these pressures, and we had a positive discussion about our shared ambition for growth and tackling youth unemployment. His first budget is the chance to turn that ambition into action by easing costs, making tax fairer and unlocking investment.” Meanwhile it was reported that Healey has rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed. He has come under pressure to increase the rates of capital gains tax (CGT), which is levied on the sale of assets – including second homes and shares – at significantly lower rates than wages. In her first budget in 2024, Reeves increased the rate of CGT from 10% to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers, and from 20% to 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. That compares with a 20% basic rate of income tax, a 40% higher rate and 45% additional rate for top earners. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Economists have suggested an equalisation of the rates could raise £11.3bn a year for the exchequer. However, according to the Financial Times, Healey has dismissed such calls because of fears it could deter inward investment, but may yet opt for a smaller increase in CGT short of equalisation. It comes after senior Labour figures floated CGT increases among options to repair the government finances while funding priorities ranging from public services, support for households and long-term infrastructure projects. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, suggested the idea of equalisation during his ill-fated May pitch to be the party leader as a “wealth tax that works”. And the first secretary, Louise Haigh, a close ally of Andy Burnham, argued in an article in the journal Renewal in May – while on the backbenches before her return to cabinet – that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”. A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

events.title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
events.summary: Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands . With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation. A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated. It is understood the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands . An oil project known as Sea Lion in the North Falkland Basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei , has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors. In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood. Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.” She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.” It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character. Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has told MPs that the UK will protect businesses working in the Falklands from pressure from Argentina through measures under protection of trading interests (PTI) legislation. The legislation allows the UK to issue orders and directions forbidding British individuals and companies from complying with specific foreign laws or trade controls. It also opens up the possibility that those affected by Argentinian legal pressure could claim damages in UK courts. Miliband said: “The UK’s support for the Falkland Islands is steadfast. Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion. “We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development.” The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders. Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against . Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project. A draft national sovereignty bill introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers. The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.

events.title: China sentences three people to death for running Myanmar scam centres
events.summary: Dozens more were imprisoned for their involvement in crimes including telecommunications fraud, trafficking and murder. A court in eastern China has sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death for operating a network of scam centres in Myanmar. In a statement released on Tuesday, Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court, a high court in southeastern Fujian province, said it had sentenced Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”. list 1 of 4 Myanmar military raids online scam hub, arrests nearly 350 on Thai border list 2 of 4 China executes 11 linked to Myanmar scam operations: State media list 3 of 4 More than 5,300 people still held in Myanmar scam centres: rights group list 4 of 4 Online scam centres fuelling human trafficking worldwide, warns UN agency The syndicate was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organised prostitution, illegal casino operations, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese nationals. The court said Wei was one of the group’s leaders and was found guilty of several crimes, including murder. Three other members were jailed for life, while 55 others were handed sentences ranging from three years and three months to 24 years in prison. The court said the gang’s operations netted more than $1.8bn. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” compounds and having lured “thousands” of Chinese nationals with promises of high wages to Myanmar. The verdict comes as Beijing intensified its crackdown on cross-border scam networks operating in southeast Asia, where scam parks have become an industrial-scale business. The International Organization for Migration in July warned that scam centres in southeast Asia employ as many as 300,000 workers and use online schemes to defraud people in the West, many of them elderly. Many of those conducting the online scams are trafficked foreign nationals forced to work in prison-like compounds.

events.title: After traveling to all 50 states, I think these 6 state parks are some of the country's most incredible hidden gems
events.summary: In my opinion, Devil's Lake State Park in Wisconsin is one of the best lesser-known US state parks. Emily Hart I've traveled to all 50 states and love exploring the country's lesser-known state parks . Letchworth State Park in New York and Matthiessen State Park in Illinois have gorgeous waterfalls. Utah's Kodachrome Basin State Park feels like stepping into another world. The US national parks are incredible, and I understand why so many people flock to these iconic landscapes to see some of the most breathtaking scenery in the country. However, after traveling solo to all 63 US national parks and all 50 states, I've discovered that some of the most stunning and underrated places aren't part of the national park system — they're state parks. These hidden gems offer the same beauty, adventure, and solitude, often without the crowds, reservations, or permit hassles that come with national park visits. Here are some of my favorites. Devil's Lake State Park in Wisconsin has something for everyone. Emily Hart Despite being Wisconsin's most-visited state park, I find that many people I talk to don't know about Devil's Lake in Baraboo. However, it's my favorite of Wisconsin's 50 state parks. In my opinion, the park's East and West Bluff trails offer some of the best panoramic views in the Midwest. Additionally, the massive rock formations — like Balanced Rock and Devil's Doorway — make it a favorite for hikers and rock climbers alike. Beyond the cliffs, the park offers kayaking, swimming, and peaceful lakeside picnic areas, making it a perfect year-round destination. Coopers Rock State Forest in West Virginia is the perfect place to watch the sunset. Emily Hart West Virginia is another one of my favorite states for outdoor recreation. Its state park system is full of gems, but I always recommend visiting Coopers Rock State Forest. I love hiking in this park or simply enjoying a sunset at Coopers Rock Overlook, which offers a panoramic view of the Cheat River Gorge. The park also has many unique rock formations scattered throughout the forest along the miles of scenic trails. Letchworth State Park in New York is home to stunning waterfalls. Jim Vallee/Shutterstock Often nicknamed the "Grand Canyon of the East," Letchworth State Park is a natural wonder where the Genesee River carves through a deep gorge, creating three stunning waterfalls framed by towering cliffs. With 66 miles of hiking trails, scenic overlooks, and endless opportunities for outdoor recreation, Letchworth is a paradise for nature lovers. The park is especially magical in the fall, with its vibrant autumn foliage, making it one of the most spectacular leaf-peeping destinations in the Northeast. Visiting Utah's Kodachrome Basin State Park feels like stepping into another world. Emily Hart When visiting Utah, many travelers aim to see one (or all) of the state's "Mighty Five" national parks . However, Utah is also home to 46 state parks — my favorite being Kodachrome Basin. Just over 20 miles from Bryce Canyon National Park, Kodachrome Basin feels like stepping into another world entirely. The less-crowded landscape is a stunning mix of red, orange, and yellow hues, and striking "sand pipes" — tall, thin spires of rock that the park is known for. Hike, camp, or drive through the rock formations of this hidden gem park for a peaceful adventure. Matthiessen State Park in Illinois feels magical. Joseph Hendrickson/Shutterstock Matthiessen State Park is a hidden gem known for its dramatic canyons, cascading waterfalls, and towering forests, creating a stunning, almost magical landscape. With peaceful trails and fewer crowds than nearby Starved Rock State Park, Matthiessen is a must-visit for nature lovers in the Midwest. I especially love visiting in the fall to enjoy the changing foliage. Eldorado Canyon is one of my favorite state parks in Colorado. Emily Hart With four major national parks and over 40 state parks, Colorado is known for outdoor recreation. However, I've found that, outside of the locals, many people don't know about one of my favorite places to visit — Eldorado Canyon State Park. Just 9 miles outside Boulder, the park is known for its dramatic canyon views, rock climbing, and scenic hiking trails. Its towering golden sandstone cliffs make it one of the top climbing destinations in the US, with over 500 routes. Visitors can also choose to cross-country ski or snowshoe in the winter months. events.title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: overdue, but proceed with care | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambition The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards T he German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision. Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off. A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin. That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk. Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield. For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold. As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat. It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country. events.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said. Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13. Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision. “We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. “It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.” While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. “They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said. Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. “There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.

events.title: Only 13 albums have spent at least 10 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 this century — here they all are
events.summary: Adele, Taylor Swift, and Morgan Wallen. Kevin Mazur/Kate Green/Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images The Billboard 200 tracks the most popular albums every week in the US. Only 13 albums have spent 10 or more weeks at No. 1 on the chart so far this century. Taylor Swift, Morgan Wallen, and Adele all have multiple albums on the list. Since 2000, only 13 albums have spent double-digit weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart, widely considered the definitive weekly ranking of best-selling albums in the US. Taylor Swift is the only woman to have four albums spend at least 10 weeks atop the Billboard 200, joining The Beatles and Elvis as the only artists in history to achieve this feat. Keep reading to see a complete list of the chart's longest leaders in chronological order. 1. "Fearless" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's sophomore album, "Fearless," was released in 2008. Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's sophomore album spent 11 weeks at No. 1 and was certified diamond by the RIAA . It's still known as the most-awarded country album of all time. Prior to "Fearless," the top-charting album of the millennium was Usher's "Confessions," which spent nine weeks at No. 1. 2. "21" by Adele Columbia Records Adele's sophomore LP spent a whopping 24 weeks at No. 1, the biggest nonconsecutive sum for any album by a woman. "21" won album of the year at the Grammys and was later crowned the top-performing album in the history of the Billboard 200. 3. "Frozen (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)" by Various Artists Walt Disney "Frozen" spent 13 weeks at No. 1, the most for any film soundtrack since "Titanic" in 1998. 4. "1989" by Taylor Swift "1989" was released on October 27, 2014. Taylor Swift Swift's fifth studio album spent 11 weeks at No. 1 and went on to win album of the year at the Grammys, becoming Swift's second win after "Fearless." (She has since won four times, more than anyone else in history.) 5. "25" by Adele "25" was released in 2015. Columbia Adele's third album spent 10 weeks at No. 1 . It also won album of the year at the Grammys, beating Beyoncé's "Lemonade." 6. "Views" by Drake Young Money Drake's fourth studio album, "Views," spent 13 weeks at No. 1, besting Adele's "25" for the top-charting album of 2016 . 7. "Dangerous: The Double Album" by Morgan Wallen Big Loud/Republic Morgan Wallen's second studio album spent 10 consecutive weeks at No. 1, becoming just the third album in history to spend its first 10 weeks atop the chart, joining Whitney Houston's "Whitney" (1987) and Stevie Wonder's "Songs in the Key of Life" (1976). 8. "Un Verano Sin Ti" by Bad Bunny "Un Verano Sin Ti" was released on May 6, 2022. Rimas Entertainment Bad Bunny's fourth studio album spent 13 weeks at No. 1 . "Un Verano Sin Ti" was ranked among Business Insider's best albums of 2022 and nominated for album of the year at the Grammys, but lost to "Harry's House" by Harry Styles . 9. "SOS" by SZA "SOS" was released on December 9, 2022. Daniel Sannwald/RCA SZA's sophomore album, "SOS," was the first R&B album by a woman to spend 10 weeks at No. 1 since Mariah Carey's self-titled debut in 1991. It later returned to the top for a total of 13 weeks . 10. "One Thing at a Time" by Morgan Wallen Big Loud/Republic Morgan Wallen's third studio album spent 19 nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1, surpassing "Un Verano Sin Ti" for the most weeks atop the chart this decade. It's also the biggest country album in the history of the Billboard 200; Garth Brooks previously held the record with "Ropin' the Wind," which reigned for 18 weeks in the early '90s. Wallen's commercial success has come despite a string of controversies , including canceling concerts at the last minute, using a racial slur , and partying without a mask during the pandemic. 11. "The Tortured Poets Department" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's 11th album, "The Tortured Poets Department," was released in 2024. Taylor Swift Swift's 11th studio album spent its first 12 weeks at No. 1, the longest post-release run by a female artist since Houston's "Whitney." " The Tortured Poets Department " joined Wallen's "One Thing at a Time" and Wonder's "Songs in the Key of Life" as the only three albums to spend their first 12 weeks in the chart's top position. (Wonder holds the record with a 13-week streak.) "Poets" later returned for five more weeks atop the Billboard 200 for a grand total of 17, the longest reign of Swift's career . 12. "I'm the Problem" by Morgan Wallen "I'm the Problem" was released in 2025. Big Loud Wallen's "I'm the Problem," his fourth studio album, spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. 13. "The Life of a Showgirl" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's 12th album, "The Life of a Showgirl," was released on October 3, 2025. TAS Rights Management Swift's 12th studio album, " The Life of a Showgirl ," has spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Read the original article on Business Insider
