events.title: Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' is one of her biggest albums on the Billboard 200. Here's how her others rank.
events.summary: Taylor Swift performs during The Eras Tour in Dublin. Charles McQuillan/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl" has spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. It's her second-longest reign atop the chart, surpassing "Fearless" and "1989." "The Tortured Poets Department" holds the record in Swift's catalog with 17 weeks at No. 1. Taylor Swift gave us fair warning in her newest album: "I'm married to the hustle." Swift's 12th studio album, " The Life of a Showgirl ," not only broke the record for the biggest debut sales week ever , but it continued to amass sales and streams in the US for a year after its release. With 14 nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 , "Showgirl" has surpassed "Fearless" and "1989" as Swift's second-longest reign on the all-genre album chart. The impressive tally comes shortly after Swift set a personal-best chart record with " The Tortured Poets Department ." Keep reading for a ranking of her 16 studio albums (including both originals and rerecords) based on their Billboard 200 performances. 10. "Taylor Swift" Taylor Swift's debut album, "Taylor Swift," was released in 2006. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 5 Swift's self-titled debut is the only studio album in her catalog that hasn't reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200. "Taylor Swift" debuted at No. 19 and scaled the chart for more than a year, peaking at No. 5 in 2008. 9 (tie). "Lover" Taylor Swift's seventh album, "Lover," was released in 2019. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week Swift's seventh studio album was the first one that she owned outright, thanks to her new label contract with UMG. "Lover" was promoted by several singles, including "You Need to Calm Down," " The Archer ," and " The Man ." Four years later, after Swift kicked off the Eras Tour with "Cruel Summer" near the top of the set list, the fan-favorite song climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and remained there for four weeks, becoming the album's biggest hit. 9 (tie). "Red (Taylor's Version)" The cover art for "Red (Taylor's Version)" was photographed by Beth Garrabrant. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week The extended tracklist for " Red (Taylor's Version) " included the storied extended cut of "All Too Well," a longtime fan-favorite song in Swift's catalog. "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" was released alongside a short film directed by Swift and promoted by a convention-breaking performance on "Saturday Night Live." It became the longest song to reach No. 1 in the history of the Hot 100. 8 (tie). "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2021. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks "Fearless" was the first rerecorded album that Swift ever released. The "Taylor's Version" series was inspired by the sale of Swift's masters to Scooter Braun in 2019, which she described as her "worst case scenario" in a passionate open letter. Swift decided to remake and rerelease her first six albums in a bid to reclaim ownership of her life's work. Braun later sold Swift's masters to a private equity firm. In addition to faithfully recreating each tracklist , Swift decided to add never-before-heard songs "from the vault" that were written during the album's original creative process but cut from the final product. "I've spoken a lot about why I'm remaking my first six albums, but the way I've chosen to do this will hopefully help illuminate where I'm coming from," Swift explained. "Artists should own their own work for so many reasons, but the most screamingly obvious one is that the artist is the only one who really knows that body of work." "For example, only I know which songs I wrote that almost made the 'Fearless' album," she continued. "Songs I absolutely adored, but were held back for different reasons." Many were skeptical that the "Taylor's Version" project would be embraced by fans, let alone achieve commercial success . Those skeptics were forced to eat their words when "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" began to outpace the original on streaming platforms. According to Billboard , "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" earned more equivalent album sales in its first week of release than "Fearless" earned over the entire next year. Four years later, in May 2025, Swift announced that she bought back her masters from Shamrock Capital, giving her complete control over her musical catalog and rendering her "Taylor's Version" project moot. 8 (tie). "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2023. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks The rerecorded version of Swift's third album featured six songs from the vault , including two duets with Fall Out Boy and Hayley Williams. 7 (tie). "Reputation" The album cover for "Reputation." Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Reputation" arrived after an extended period of silence. Swift's longtime feud with Kim Kardashian and Ye (then known as Kanye West) had reached a fever pitch; in response to a massive social media hate campaign, Swift decamped to London and withdrew from the public eye. She returned with a new snake-infested aesthetic and "Look What You Made Me Do," a cheeky lead single that poked fun at her own persona — and quickly rose to No. 1 on the Hot 100. Swift also declined to participate in interviews or media appearances while promoting her sixth album. Instead, she relied on a simple tagline: "There will be no further explanation. There will just be reputation." 7 (tie). "Evermore" Taylor Swift's ninth album, "Evermore," was released in 2020. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Evermore" was surprise-released just five months after Swift's previous album, "Folklore." The two were billed as "sister albums," created under near-identical conditions with the same team of collaborators. "To put it plainly, we just couldn't stop writing songs," Swift explained on social media. "Evermore" was nominated for album of the year at the 2022 Grammys, but lost to Jon Batiste's "We Are." 6 (tie). "Speak Now" Taylor Swift's third album, "Speak Now," was released in 2010. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for six weeks Swift's third album had a lot to live up to, following the blockbuster success of "Fearless." In response to skeptics — who questioned whether the teen phenom was relying too heavily on her collaborators — she decided to write "Speak Now" entirely by herself. Swift is the only songwriter credited on the standard tracklist. 6 (tie). "Midnights" Taylor Swift's 10th album, "Midnights," was released in 2022. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for six weeks Swift's 10th studio album sold over 1 million copies in its debut

events.title: Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' is her newest No. 1 hit. Here are all 16 of her songs that topped the chart.
events.summary: Taylor Swift onstage at the Eras Tour. Shirlaine Forrest/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's newest single, "Patient Zero," debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Swift has the fourth-most No. 1 hits in history, trailing Elvis, Mariah Carey, and The Beatles. Swift's biggest hits also include "Blank Space," "Anti-Hero," and "The Fate of Ophelia." Since releasing her first No. 1 album in 2008, Taylor Swift has enjoyed a historic run on the charts, topping the Billboard 200 and Billboard Hot 100 over a dozen times each. Swift's collection of chart-toppers includes both radio-friendly pop singles and understated gems pushed to the top of the chart by passionate fans. Most recently, "Patient Zero" joined the ranks of Swift's biggest songs. On the all-time ranking of most No. 1 hits , Swift only trails Elvis, Mariah Carey, and The Beatles. All of Swift's No. 1 songs on the Hot 100 are listed below in chronological order of their peak dates. 1. "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" was released as a single in 2012. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Three Despite writing ubiquitous hits like "You Belong With Me" and "Love Story" earlier in her career (which peaked at No. 2 and No. 4, respectively), "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" was Swift's first-ever song to top the Hot 100. The country-pop crossover smash was released as the lead single from Swift's fourth album, "Red." It rose from No. 72 to No. 1 in its second week of tracking and remained atop the chart for two more weeks. 2. "Shake It Off" "Shake It Off" was released as a single in 2014. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Four "Shake It Off" was released as the lead single from Swift's fifth album, "1989." It became her first No. 1 debut on the Hot 100. 3. "Blank Space" "Blank Space" was released as a single in 2014. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Seven "Blank Space," the second single from "1989," debuted at No. 18 on the Hot 100. It rose to No. 13 before soaring to No. 1 in its third week — dethroning "Shake It Off" and making Swift the first woman in history to replace herself in the chart's top spot. "Blank Space" went on to become one of Swift's biggest hits, reigning atop the chart for nearly two months. 4. "Bad Blood" featuring Kendrick Lamar "Bad Blood" was released as a single in 2015. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One In May 2015, a remix of "Bad Blood" featuring Kendrick Lamar was released as the fourth single from "1989." It rose from No. 53 to the chart's top spot after the music video premiered at the 2015 Billboard Music Awards and broke the Vevo record for most views in 24 hours. 5. "Look What You Made Me Do" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Three Despite mixed reactions from critics, Swift's lead single from "Reputation" rose to No. 1 after its first full week of tracking, breaking the weekly streaming record for a song by a woman. Once again, Swift's music video broke the record for most views within 24 hours , racking up 43.2 million views in its first day. 6. "Cardigan" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One Swift announced the arrival of her eighth album, "Folklore," just one day in advance. The second track, "Cardigan," was released alongside the album and promoted with a whimsical music video. "Folklore" debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 while "Cardigan" simultaneously debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, making Swift the first artist in history to open atop both charts in the same week. 7. "Willow" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One Just five months after "Folklore," Swift repeated her pandemic-era strategy and surprise-released her ninth album, "Evermore," alongside its lead single. Again, "Willow" debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 while "Evermore" simultaneously debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. 8. "All Too Well (Taylor's Version)" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One " Red (Taylor's Version) " was the second rerecorded album Swift released. It was accompanied by the long-awaited 10-minute version of " All Too Well ," a fan-favorite track from the original album. "All Too Well (10 Minute Version) (Taylor's Version)" was promoted with a self-directed short film starring Sadie Sink and Dylan O'Brien, a convention-breaking performance on "Saturday Night Live," and plenty of theories about the song's muse . It debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, becoming the longest song in history to top the chart. The record was previously held by Don McLean's "American Pie (Parts I & II)" at 8 minutes and 37 seconds. 9. "Anti-Hero" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Eight "Anti-Hero" was released alongside Swift's 10th album, "Midnights," and promoted as the lead single. It dominated the Hot 100 for eight weeks, surpassing the high-water mark set by "Blank Space." The same week that "Anti-Hero" debuted at No. 1, Swift became the first and only artist in history to occupy the entire top 10 on the Hot 100. The hit single was flanked by "Lavender Haze" (No. 2), "Maroon" (No. 3), "Snow on the Beach" (No. 4), "Midnight Rain" (No. 5), "Bejeweled" (No. 6), "Question...?" (No. 7), "You're On Your Own, Kid" (No. 8), "Karma" (No. 9), and "Vigilante Shit" (No. 10). 10. "Cruel Summer" John Shearer/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Weeks at No. 1: Four "Cruel Summer" was originally released as the second track on Swift's 2019 album "Lover." Although it was identified early as a fan favorite, the song was never promoted as a single and debuted modestly at No. 29 on the Hot 100. Four years later, Swift transformed "Cruel Summer" into a showstopping spectacle on the Eras Tour . Streams of the song began to surge, and it reigned atop Billboard's Pop Airplay chart for two months. Swift's label sent the song to pop radio in June 2023. Finally, following the release of "The Cruelest Summer" EP — which includes a live version of the song and a remix by LP Giobbi — the song reached No. 1 on the Hot 100, marking Swift's milestone 10th chart-topper. 11. "Is It Over Now?" Kevin Winter/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Weeks at No. 1: One "Is It Over Now?" was released as the final vault track on " 1989 (Taylor's Version) ," a rerecording of her beloved fifth album. Although it wasn't initially slated as a single, its enthusiastic reception from fans pushed Swift's team to serve the song to pop radio. "Is It Over Now?" debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, dethroning "Cruel Summer." Swift remains the only woman in history to replace herself in the top spot, a feat she's now achieved twice. 12. events.title: The Xteink X4 Pro is a great, tiny e-reader, and it’s cheaper than ever
events.summary: The Xteink X4 Pro is still matching its Prime Day price. | Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge ﻿ If you’re looking for an e-reader that can easily fit in your pocket (or snap onto your magnet-equipped phone), the tiny Xteink X4 Pro might be worth a look. It features a 4.26-inch, 800 x 480 E Ink display, making it significantly smaller and thinner than Amazon’s smallest six-inch Kindle . It’s also quite a bit cheaper. Right now, you can pick it up for $84.15 ($25 off) at Amazon , which is its best price to date. Xteink X4 Pro Where to Buy: $109 $84.15 at Amazon $109 at Xteink The X4 Pro brings several welcome upgrades over its predecessors, including a touchscreen that gives readers another way to interact with it. It still has physical page-turning buttons, though. There’s also a new touch-sensitive button below the display for quickly returning to the home screen, along with a built-in light with adjustable brightness and color temperature, so you can read in the dark. It ships with the excellent CrossPoint Reader software , which makes navigating your library and reading books a much better experience than on previous Xteink models we’ve tested, though it’s still not quite as polished as Amazon’s software. Understandably, not everyone is a fan of Xteink’s decision to swap the X4 Pro’s USB-C port for a proprietary charging connector. If you can look past that, the X4 Pro is a great, little e-reader that features magnets that let you attach it to compatible smartphones, just like previous models. The magnetic connection is stronger this time around, though we still wish it were a little more secure. All the same, my colleague Andrew Liszewski still considers the X4 Pro the best tiny e-reader you can buy , calling it a device he “won’t leave the house without.” Read our hands-on impressions.

events.title: My friend and I live thousands of miles apart. We take cruises together every year to maintain our relationship.
events.summary: My friend and I book cruises around the world together that help us stay in touch and make new memories. Jenna DeLaurentis My friend and I live in different countries, but we take cruises to meet up and spend time together. They're often fairly easy to plan, and we get to see a bunch of new places, too. Making new memories together helps us maintain our friendship across distances. Maintaining friendships as an adult can be challenging, but my middle-school bestie and I found a solution that works for us — booking a cruise. Samantha and I have been friends for nearly two decades, but when she moved from the US to the UK after college, we went years without seeing each other. Our lives were becoming increasingly busy. Despite frequent phone calls to catch up, it took a lot of effort to stay connected. Without proper planning, the chances were slim we'd ever be in the same place at the same time. So, when a travel writing assignment took me on a cruise, Samantha joined me on board. The trip proved to be an ideal way to reconnect, explore new places, and make new memories together. We quickly realized that a cruise was the cheat code to maintaining our long-distance friendship in a fairly low-effort but exciting way, and we've been booking cruises together ever since. Right away, I appreciated the ease of logistics when planning our cruise Our first cruise visited ports in northern Spain and France. Jenna DeLaurentis Our first cruise together left from Southampton, England. Conveniently, the port was just a short train ride from Samantha's apartment in London. It seemed like all the cards were in our favor, and we couldn't wait to board the ship for a weeklong cruise to Spain and France. I felt confident that a cruise would be a stress-free way to travel together. Unlike many land-based trips, where you need to plan everything yourself, we simply had to get to the embarkation port. After that, the cruise line would take care of the rest, from meals to itinerary. This meant the two of us didn't need to figure out a bunch of logistics and coordinate bookings while being thousands of miles apart in different time zones. Although we still planned our port days, much of the legwork was done by the cruise line. The cruise was the ultimate girls' trip, and it made us want to plan more We've been able to visit some incredible places around the world together. Jenna DeLaurentis As soon as we got on board, Samantha and I checked out our windowless, closet-sized inside cabin. We couldn't help but laugh — our long-distance friendship was now in extremely close quarters. One of the most challenging parts of maintaining old friendships is finding opportunities to make new memories together. All too often, hangouts become nothing more than a dinner to catch up rather than an experience you'll remember for years to come. Cruising, though, was an excellent way to have new experiences. Whether sipping rosé in France or watching a sunset from the ship, every day led to something we'd look back on. We also appreciated the structure of a cruise vacation . It gave us a lot of freedom to do things together or on our own. If I wanted to see a show but Samantha wanted to spend time reading, we simply planned a spot to meet up later. Our first cruise let us slow down from our busy lives and focus on our friendship. It was a rare chance to make new memories together — something that's nearly impossible to do over a phone call. We've been booking cruises together ever since, and it's the best way to maintain our friendship Cruising to the South Pacific has been our favorite itinerary yet. Jenna DeLaurentis After returning from our first cruise, we couldn't wait to book another. So, the next year, we set sail once more, visiting ports in the Mediterranean like Naples, Italy, and Valletta, Malta. After that, we cruised from Sydney, Australia, to five islands in the South Pacific. Currently, we're planning our next cruise, a short-and-sweet trip to The Bahamas . Samantha and I still live in different countries, but cruising has become our tried-and-true method of seeing each other in person. If we realize it's been too long since a proper hangout, the solution is simple — book a cruise . It may not be a conventional way to maintain a friendship, but it works for us. Spending uninterrupted quality time together while exploring new places is a great way to stay connected. I can't wait to see where our future sailings take us. events.title: Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
events.summary: Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of cases from the last four weeks. Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in the past three weeks, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns, as civilians continue to escape renewed fighting and seek safety in unsanitary camps. Ramped up combat, which has pushed more than 200,000 people to flee their homes, the WHO said in a report on Tuesday, driving suspected cases from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of September 27 to October 3. list 1 of 3 At least 139 dead as migrant boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes list 2 of 3 The escalation in Yemen is a turning point list 3 of 3 Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting “Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated,” said Annette Heinzelmann, the UN agency’s emergency director for the region. “Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities.” This year, the global health watchdog said, Yemen had reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths, with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks. Five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people in the southwest – Abyan, Lahij, al-Dhalea, Taiz and Aden – account for 92 percent of reported cases, they reported. The disease has also reached remote displacement camps in Hadramout in the country’s east that are particularly difficult for medical teams to access. Cholera has ebbed and flowed for years as the conflict in Yemen has continued. In 2024, the WHO warned that the country was facing the “highest burden” of a global cholera outbreak. In 2017, a wave of the disease infected hundreds of thousands and killed at least 2,000. Yemen was already suffering one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises ” and has seen an escalation of food insecurity and disease since fighting reignited between the Houthis and the government in July, shattering four years of fragile calm. Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, often from faeces. It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps. Contracting the illness can be deadly when not treated with oral rehydration or antibiotics for more severe cases. The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78m of the $31m needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen. The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

events.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.

events.title: AI agent company Decagon is holding early M&A talks with ServiceNow, others
events.summary: Lisbon , Portugal - 12 November 2025; Jesse Zhang, Co-founder & CEO, Decagon AI on Centre Stage during day two of Web Summit 2025 at the MEO Arena in Lisbon, Portugal. (Photo By Shauna Clinton/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images) Shauna Clinton/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images AI startup Decagon builds AI agents to automate customer support for enterprise customers. The company has hired an investment bank to evaluate M&A interest. The discussions with potential buyers, including software company ServiceNow, are in the early stages. Buzzy AI agent startup Decagon could be the latest company swept up in a growing wave of AI dealmaking. The company, which was last valued at $4.5 billion earlier this year, has hired a bank to evaluate acquisition interest, according to people familiar with the matter. Decagon has held early discussions with cloud software giant ServiceNow and additional companies, the people said. If a deal does not materialize, Decagon could instead raise a new funding round. The interest in Decagon represents a new shift in the AI boom: after years of huge venture rounds and soaring valuations, tech companies are increasingly looking to buy their way into promising AI markets. Hugging Face was recently acquired by Nvidia for 12.9 billion, and OpenRouter was snapped up by Stripe for around $8 billion. Growing AI-related businesses are often getting offers at a significant premium to their last valuation, so if Decagon were to accept an offer, it could be considerably higher than its previous $4.5 billion value. Founded in July 2023 by Jesse Zhang and Ashwin Sreenivas, Decagon uses generative AI to automate customer support for enterprise customers , including Delta, Snapchat, and Ticketmaster. The company has raised over $400 million from a roster of well-known Silicon Valley investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Index Ventures, Bain Capital Ventures, and Accel. It competes with industry veteran Bret Taylor's Sierra, which was valued at $15.8 billion earlier this year. A deal would also come as ServiceNow looks to reassure investors that it can adapt to AI’s threat to traditional software businesses. Its shares tumbled earlier this year during the so-called SaaS-pocalypse , when investors feared AI could erode software companies’ profit margins. It was also punished for making a $7 billion acquisition of the security business Armis, a deal announced late last year. The stock has since rebounded as ServiceNow continues to invest heavily in AI and reshape parts of its business. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jamie Dimon says JPMorgan Chase is putting up gates to protect against 'rogue agents'
events.summary: Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JPMorgan Chase. Bloomberg/Getty Images The biggest concern for clients adopting AI agents is security, said JPMorgan executives. Jamie Dimon said that the bank will protect against "rogue agents" by keeping most out. AI agents that access banks using their credentials and screen sharing are especially dangerous. JPMorgan Chase customers shouldn't expect their personal AI agents to have access to their accounts anytime soon. The typical security concerns around any new adaptation of technology are "heightened" with AI agents, "because you don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them," JPMorgan Chase CEO Dimon said during an earnings call Tuesday. Unlike chatbots, which primarily answer questions, AI agents are designed to take action on behalf of a user and have increased in popularity after the introduction of Meta's personal AI assistant, Muse. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said, saying there's a "liability transfer" away from the bank, as well as risks that their data is "misused." The company is building its own agentic tools for clients, Dimon said, but for now, it plans to closely guard the bank from the onslaught of outside AI agents. "In the meantime, we're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon said. The bank is already blocking access to "to the extent that we're able to block those," Jeremy Barnum, the bank's chief financial officer, said. "I think right now, some of the services that offer that do it through credential sharing, and we have a long record of being against that way of doing things, screen scraping, et cetera," he said. "It's not secure." If a customer gives an AI agent their credentials, they could be responsible for any unwanted actions the agent takes. "It's not an ideal state of things," Barnum said. JPMorgan has also tightened controls on AI agents used by its own employees. Business Insider previously reported that the bank rolled out new security measures for some engineers who use Anthropic's Claude, restricting AI's access to employees' internal systems. Dimon and Barnum's comments were contrasted with concerns that AI agents could cause a bank run from low-yield into high-yield savings accounts, a theory raised by Apollo chief economist Torsten Sløk in late September. Bank stocks, already declining following bond market turmoil, have fallen further since the launch of Meta's Muse on September 22 , and Barnum said they saw "a little bit of a response in bank stocks around those releases." Barnum suggested this concern is a continuation of two trends the bank has felt: "yield-seeking flows" and competition from fintechs. As for yields in high-interest savings accounts, Barnum said the bank is focused on "primary bank share" rather than yield chasers. The bank's standard Chase Savings account earns a 0.01% annual percentage yield, while others in the market earn 4% (though it does offer higher-yield cash products to its private wealth clients). And while Barnum said the bank works to "have parity" with f intech companies , he also thinks the bank's traditional brick-and-mortar footprint provides its own defense against encroachment. "Our perspective is that, on the one hand, it's nothing new, but that doesn't mean that we're complacent about it," Barnum said about fintech competition. Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, left the role to spend more time with her two young children. "Though my work will be demanding, they will always be a priority," Zacharia said of her children. At her first briefing as White House press secretary on Tuesday, Katie Zacharia fielded a personal question. Elina Shirazi, senior political correspondent at The Daily Mail, asked Zacharia how she planned to manage work and family in her new White House role, citing Karoline Leavitt 's decision to leave the job in August to spend more time with her two young children. Leavitt has previously spoken about the toll that serving as White House press secretary took on her family, telling Tucker Carlson in a September podcast interview that "being a working mom was the hardest thing I've ever had to do in my life." Zacharia, who has four children ranging in age from 6 to 12, said that Leavitt had been "an incredible support" who gave "great and wonderful feedback" on balancing career and family as a working mother. She also acknowledged the demanding nature of the role. "I think this job is not one you necessarily balance," Zacharia said. 'They will always be a priority' White House press secretary Katie Zacharia with President Donald Trump on the South Lawn of the White House. Win McNamee/Getty Images Zacharia, who previously worked as a senior communications advisor for Trump Media, said that her family will move from California to join her in Washington, DC. "They are my priority. I love being with my kids," she said. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable." Zacharia also shared that she stayed home with her children from 2014 to 2020 and would often bring them to the Fox News bureau where she worked as a political commentator when she returned to work. "I intend to, to the extent possible, include my family, include my kids in my work," she said. "Though my work will be demanding, they will always be a priority." Zacharia concluded the briefing by calling Trump "the most family-friendly president we've ever had" and touted the hiring of other women with children in his administration. "The fact that he knew I had four kids, and he knew that this job would be demanding, and still placed his trust in me, shows that I know I'm capable of being able to step up to that," she said. 'A fabulous and wonderful addition' White House communications director Steven Cheung told Business Insider on Tuesday that Zacharia is "a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team." "She is uniquely qualified and whip-smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary," he said. Zacharia also told Business Insider, "I am grateful to serve President Trump as press secretary, and I will diligently and effectively amplify his successful agenda." events.title: Elon Musk becomes biggest donor of US midterms cycle with $366m spent
events.summary: Musk’s midterm donations, mostly for rightwing candidates and causes, surpass his contributions to Trump in 2024 Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections Elon Musk has become the biggest political donor of the 2026 US midterm elections cycle, funneling about $366m into political groups and campaigns as he backs conservative candidates and rightwing causes. The world’s richest person has poured more than $276m into politics since July alone, some of the most rapid political spending in US history. He’s targeting key races that will determine which party controls the US Senate . The New York Times first reported the spending numbers, which will be released in a federal filing on Thursday. Musk’s spending outpaces his 2024 presidential election contributions, in which he sunk nearly $300m into Donald Trump’s re-election campaign. Musk’s political spending reasserts the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as the top Republican mega-donor and furthers his rightwing political influence. Musk, who led the Trump administration’s efforts to gut federal agencies last year, has become an international linchpin for far-right political movements in recent years as he aligns himself with anti-immigrant, conservative leaders. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives The tech mogul’s spending spree is also a reversal from a period in the middle of last year when Musk claimed he would step back from making such large-scale political donations. The failures of his so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) and costly public backlash to his political influence, as well as a dramatic falling out with Trump, appeared to have dampened his interest in Washington politics. Musk’s spending is spread throughout a series of political action committees, according to Reuters and the New York Times, including his own America Pac. His largest single spend was a $158m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund, a Super Pac working to help Republicans retain control of the Senate. Musk has also given $10m to a Pac supporting Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican Senate candidate who is facing Democratic nominee James Talarico in a closely watched and intense race. Other blockbuster Musk contributions include $76m for America Pac, $20m for the Congressional Leadership Fund Republican Super Pac and $10m for the Republican Governors Association. Musk also gave $10m in January to Nate Morris, a Kentucky Republican Senate candidate who withdrew from the race in May after accepting an offer to become the US ambassador to Colombia. Some of Musk’s money is going to advertising and messaging campaigns that focus on anti-transgender rhetoric and accuse Democratic candidates of being radical socialists. Musk has long used X, the social media platform he owns, to target his political opponents , push election misinformation and attack trans rights. Over the weekend, he reposted a video from America Pac that showed Talarico’s previous statements on gender, calling it “madness”. Musk’s immense spending involves some of the largest political donations in US history, but is still only a tiny fraction of his nearly $1tn wealth. The $366m in midterms spending represents about less than 0.04% of his net worth.

events.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
events.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. events.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout. For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies . LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.) Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly. LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck. “A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.” Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors. The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.” Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck. The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said. events.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. events.title: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people | Letters
events.summary: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people Terry Peach responds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, while Penelope Turton writes on her promise to cut inheritance tax Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech rehearsed the argument that Andy Burnham’s economic policies were warped by his “nostalgia” for the 1970s, unlike her own forward-looking programme for “a better tomorrow” ( Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan, 7 October ). She appears not to see that her preference for a lesser-regulated capitalist market economy, with lower public expenditure, taxes and national debt, coupled with “tough love” welfare policies, is itself harking back to arguments that have circulated for centuries. Admittedly, her position is not as extreme as the one espoused at the beginning of the 19th century by the leading political economist David Ricardo, who argued that Great Britain would be happy and prosperous if the “evil” of the national debt was extinguished completely, and the country embraced a system in which trade is left “perfectly free” and taxation reduced to a bare minimum. His own “tough love” proposal was to scrap the Poor Laws, as they encouraged overbreeding by the working class, thereby depressing market-determined wages. Terry Peach Chester Kemi Badenoch says “people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort” and regards inheritance tax (IHT) as unfair double taxation on people who have already paid tax on their earnings. In fact, most IHT revenue is driven by inherited and asset-derived wealth, which expands through unearned capital appreciation and is untaxed during a person’s lifetime. Badenoch has elsewhere called IHT immoral . The real moral injury is borne by all those low-paid, hard-working people who face a choice between heating or eating, and for whom acquiring sufficient wealth in a lifetime to leave money to their children is an unimaginable dream. events.title: US home sales rose in September, but slowed from a year earlier
events.summary: Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers. Existing home sales rose 1.5% last month from August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday. One of the factors in the monthly increase is that sales in August were revised lower. Sales fell 2.2% compared with September last year. The latest sales tally is slightly above the 3.98 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2-million. September is the second month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million. Home prices continued to rise nationally last month. The U.S. median sales price increased 1.3% in September from a year earlier to $417,500, an all-time high for the month of September based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 39 months in a row. “This is a very tough market out there, especially with mortgage rates rising,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This year, sales have been in a rut in large part due to rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the U.S. and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher. The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 7.4% last week , its highest level in nearly three years. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started. Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in August and July, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.69%, according to Freddie Mac. Mortgage rates are not likely to drop meaningfully any time soon, given the ongoing uncertainty over oil prices, geopolitical tensions, the exploding U.S. government debt and other factors that have been driving rates on home loans higher, Yun said. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Homebuyers should consider mortgage rates at 7%, or slightly above 7%, “the new normal,” he said. The sharp rise in mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, has led many would-be home shoppers to put their home shopping plans on hold. However, those who can afford to buy at current rates, or pay all cash, have a much wider selection of homes to choose from than they've had in years as properties sit on the market longer. Although home inventory levels remain below historical norms, there were 1.6 million unsold homes at the end of last month — the highest level of unsold inventory on the market since November 2019, NAR said. All told, unsold home inventory rose 1.9% last month from August and climbed 4.6% from September last year, NAR said. September’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.8-months’ supply at the current sales pace. Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers. The more balanced market gives home shoppers potentially more leverage in negotiating better terms with sellers, especially if a property has not fetched offers in weeks or months. Consider, in September, the national median home listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250 as about 21% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com. “The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate for better prices,” Yun said. Global life expectancy is rising, meaning a greater percentage of the world's population is older adults . However, not every country has experienced this elder boom equally. The World Bank Group compiled data on the percentage of the population aged 65 or older for each country in 2025, using data from the United Nations. Business Insider rounded each percentage to one decimal place and excluded non-countries. The data, for example, showed sizable older populations in territories such as Puerto Rico and special administrative regions such as Hong Kong. We also included data on the percentages of the male and female populations aged 65 and older — also compiled from the World Bank Group. The data overwhelmingly indicates that European countries have the highest numbers of older adults per capita. Japan is the only non-European entry in the top 25. A 2025 study by Brown University found that Europeans are more likely to live longer than Americans, regardless of wealth level. The study's author, health economist Irene Papanicolas, said systemic issues in the US, such as "economic inequality or risk factors like stress, diet, or environmental hazards," contribute to lower life expectancy. events.title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle case over opioid prescriptions
events.summary: CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids WASHINGTON -- CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of prescribing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.” It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.” The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids. The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart. events.title: Cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems hits 700 supermarkets
events.summary: Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France PARIS -- Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France’s food supplies but acknowledged that the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” ″It was a wake-up call for everyone,” he said. The Paris prosecutor’s office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack, including the extent of damage caused by spoiled food and possible fires. Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Cooperative U, said 80 of the company’s 2,000 stores were affected. Most managed to prevent disruptions to refrigeration, but some had to discard food, he said in a post on X. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products is an attack on the French food supply chain. It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable,” Schelcher said. Danish technology company Danfoss, which supplied the refrigeration management software, said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates. “Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall,” the company said. events.title: The AI trade is cracking. Here's how to profit
events.summary: Concerns over OpenAI's revenue growth have hit neocloud stocks, and chips are selling off Tuesday on concerns about Chinese competition. Add the Fed's first rate hike since 2023 in September, with another expected right behind it, and the tech-heavy index has plenty working against it. The opportunity: When the market dips but moves less than options expect, selling premium into the weakness lets traders collect elevated prices while setting strikes below a market that's already come in. Despite the Magnificent Seven making record highs, the AI trade is showing signs of cracks. Concerns over OpenAI's revenue growth have hit neocloud stocks, and chips are selling off Tuesday on concerns about Chinese competition. Those pressures are real, but options traders have been bracing for bigger swings than the Nasdaq has delivered in recent weeks. QQQ's implied volatility index (IVx), a measure of how much movement options traders are pricing in, closed Monday near 20.7%. That puts Nasdaq-100 volatility on par with small caps. The Russell 2000 typically carries a higher IVx than the Nasdaq-100, but right now QQQ and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) are essentially tied near 20.7%, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) sits at 15%. And for 29 straight sessions, QQQ's IVx has sat at least three points above the volatility the index actually delivered. In other words, every day since the start of September, options have priced in bigger moves than QQQ ended up making. This week's selling has yet to close that gap. When the market dips but moves less than options expect, selling premium into the weakness lets traders collect elevated prices while setting strikes below a market that's already come in. Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the November 13 720/710 put spread for a credit of roughly $1.81. This is a bullish-to-neutral trade, in line with how QQQ has traded this fall. Even after this week's dip, QQQ is up about 5% since the start of September and hit a record just a week ago. The trade doesn't need the pullback to reverse, just to stay contained through November 13, or until it's managed. It reaches its maximum profit of $181 as long as QQQ stays above $720 through November 13. The $720 short put sits below the 50-day moving average, near $726, and the $710 long put sits just below the market's expected move, near $713. With a breakeven of $718.19, about 3.7% below Monday's close, the trade leaves room for a further pullback through earnings season. The choice for the November 13 weekly was made to avoid Nvidia's earnings report, expected around November 18. QQQ's options are liquid enough that its weeklies can be considered for this trade. The maximum loss of $819 is reached if QQQ closes below $710, roughly 4.8% lower, by expiration. The credit is a bit light, but that's the trade-off for a wider cushion: the trade carries a 70% theoretical probability of profit and an 80% theoretical chance of collecting half the max profit. If QQQ finishes between $710 and $720 at expiration, the short put can be assigned and result in an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $720. After the credit, the effective cost basis is $718.19, about 5.5% below the record high. QQQ last closed below $720 on September 17. Because of that exposure, consider closing or rolling the trade before expiration rather than holding it into settlement. The biggest risks are on the calendar: CPI on Wednesday, bank and Taiwan Semiconductor earnings this week, and Microsoft and Alphabet reporting alongside the Fed decision on Oct. 28. The Nasdaq is under pressure, but it has yet to outrun what options are pricing. This trade sells into that weakness and leaves room for it to run a little further. events.title: UK's Burnham weighs approval for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces a crucial decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing a key test of his environmental policies as he decides on whether oil and gas companies should be allowed to drill in the North Sea. Burnham's government has been under heavy pressure from climate campaigners and businesses over whether to approve two oil and gas fields in waters north of Scotland, including one said to be the U.K.'s largest untapped oil resource. Environmental groups have urged Burnham to refuse permission for the projects, known as Rosebank and Jackdaw, saying they would accelerate climate change at a time when the U.K., like the rest of Europe, faces record extreme heat linked to human actions including burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. But opposition politicians, the oil and gas industry and U.S. President Donald Trump have piled pressure on Burnham to give the green light, arguing it would protect jobs, cut household bills and boost Britain’s energy security. British officials have been expected to make a decision since August, when public consultations on the two projects closed. Rosebank is an oil field that also will produce gas. Located 80 miles (130 kilometers) north of Scotland's Shetland Islands, it is estimated to be the largest undeveloped oil and gas field in the U.K., reportedly with capacity to produce 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil within about 25 years. Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles east of Aberdeen on Scotland's northeast coast. Production there was expected to last under a decade. The Shell Group, one of the project's co-developers, predicts the field can produce around 6.5% of the U.K.’s gas production at its peak. The opposition Conservative Party, which has pushed for the developments to go ahead, said the Jackdaw field could start heating 1.4 million homes in the U.K. this winter if approved. The former Conservative government previously approved production at both sites, which were scheduled to start operations later this year. But a court in Edinburgh ruled last year that the approvals were unlawful, after considering a legal challenge from Greenpeace and another nonprofit. “The public interest in authorities acting lawfully and the private interest of members of the public in climate change outweigh the private interest of the developers,” judge Andrew Stewart ruled at the time. Critics have argued that the oil and gas reserves in Britain's North Sea holdings are small and would make little difference to energy bills because prices are decided by international markets. They contend that new developments would increase carbon emissions while failing to contribute to Britain's energy security. Analysts at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a London-based nonprofit, estimated that more than 90% of the oil and gas likely to be produced from the North Sea has already been extracted. “We’ve just had record-breaking heat waves this summer, wildfires, half of the country’s still in drought. We’re facing potential crop failures and food shortages this winter from a super El Niño ,” said Victoria Smith, a Fossil Free London activist protesting on Tuesday. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer “Drilling for new oil and gas now ... would just be a wild decision, completely reckless by this government," she said. Almost 600 climate and health experts wrote a joint letter to the government last month arguing that approving the projects would breach the U.K.'s national and international climate commitments. Separately, critics also have raised concerns about Rosebank's links to Israeli company Delek Group, which activists say profited from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Green Party leader Zach Polanski is among critics who have asked how the U.K. can ensure revenue from any oil and gas production did not finance the settlements. Supporters of further drilling say it will not make a significant difference to emissions and is vital for protecting jobs. Some also argue that domestic production will result in less carbon emissions than importing oil and gas. The governing Labour Party is split on the issue. Some warned that going ahead will renege on the party's pledge in its 2024 manifesto not to issue new licenses for oil and gas exploration in the North Sea. Others disagree. “If we do not proceed with Jackdaw and Rosebank, investment will leave the UK, jobs will disappear and expertise will be lost,” lawmaker Graeme Downie said. The issue became more politicized after Trump waded in. The U.S. president, who criticized former Prime Minister Keir Starmer's energy policies, claimed in August that people in Aberdeen were “dancing in the streets” following reports that Burnham would approve new drilling.

events.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming. The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space. “When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch. So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt , a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch. The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher. Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure. “The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites. Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground. Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year. A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software. Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders. The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said. Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business. One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.” Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites. “If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says. This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco.
