events.title: Apple unveils new smart home devices that showcase upgraded Siri AI
events.summary: New products from Apple include the HomeView, an iPad-like device that acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets Apple on Tuesday began showing off a ⁠new round of smart home products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops ⁠and act as a hub for other smart home devices. The HomeView device starts at $299 and will begin shipping next month. It will feature a 7in screen and face recognition, will help users ⁠control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. The device will also showcase Apple’s AI-upgraded Siri virtual ​assistant. Preorders begin today and the devices are expected to be available starting 13 November. Apple is launching these products as it ⁠tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon – which has invested heavily in ​its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and ‌last week launched premium tablets – as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own. Apple’s HomeView launch was accompanied by updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of ‌accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple. The new line of devices are accessible and managed in the Apple home app. The accessories include a Schneider smart thermostat and LG home security devices including indoor and various outdoor cameras including a doorbell camera and floodlight camera as well as a smart lock. The lock can be unlocked using the Apple home app. The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said. Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, ⁠with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with ​Alphabet’s Google Home speakers and ​Amazon’s Echo line. Analysts said ​two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a ​variety of third-party gadgets and ‌the limited ability ​of Siri to ​give useful answers. The HomeView device includes a revamped version of Siri AI, the company announced. An Apple press release described the new version of Siri as more capable and conversational, using information from personal apps like Messages and Calendar to provide more relevant answers. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives “It’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure,” the release said.

events.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
events.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday that she was asked to resign during her first press briefing. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America." Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath. events.title: Celebrity deaths in 2026: Remembering the famous people we lost this year
events.summary: Mike Ditka. George Gojkovich/Getty Images Actors James Van Der Beek, Hayden Panettiere, Robert Duvall, Chuck Norris, and Eva Marie Saint died in 2026. So did musicians Dolly Parton and Duncan Sheik. Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, activist Gloria Steinem, and NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka also died this year. Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Scott Adams, 68 Scott Adams. Michael Macor/Getty Images Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert." By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips. At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons. Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams. Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer . Brad Arnold, 47 Brad Arnold. Scott Gries/ImageDirect/Getty Images The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year. The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom. Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer. Afrika Bambaataa, 68 Afrika Bambaataa. Paul Natkin/WireImage/Getty A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx. He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career. Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse . Bambaataa denied all claims. He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer . Rob Bass, 59 Rob Bass. Al Pereira/Michael Osche Archives/Getty Images One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstream, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock. The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine. Bass died on May 22 following cancer . Nicholas Brendon, 54 Nicholas Brendon. Getty Images Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential." Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement. In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries. "While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart." Peabo Bryson, 75 Peabo Bryson. ABC Photo Archives/Getty Images Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads. Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain." Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin." Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given. James Burrows, 85 James Burrows. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier." Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes. Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given. Kyle Busch, 41 Kyle Busch. Sean Gardner/Getty Images Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time. Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead. Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis. Robert Carradine, 71 Robert Carradine. Bobby Bank/WireImage/Getty Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds." As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career. He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series. Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness. "We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness." Carradine died by suicide on February 23. If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline . Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US. events.title: Football regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester City
events.summary: Kogan says he has faced ‘absolutely no political pressure’ Regulator wants deal on redistribution through leagues The chair of the Independent ­Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, has said he will resign if he faces any political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, insisting “my independence is absolute”. Kogan could remove City’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) should the damning verdict of an independent commission be upheld at the end of an ongoing appeal process. ­Concern had been raised, however, that the proximity of City’s ­ownership to Abu Dhabi’s rulers could trigger a political intervention by the UK ­government and an immediate test of the new regulator’s powers. Those concerns have been rebuffed by Kogan. “Our independence is absolute and my independence personally is absolute,” he said. “I [have] made it very clear … any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. And, just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic.” Kogan was speaking on Tuesday at the launch of the long-awaited State of the Game report, a document that lays out the financial challenges facing the English football pyramid. The City case has cast a huge shadow as the regulator prepares to introduce a new licensing regime for clubs later this season. “We have powers within the legislation that allow us to review not only owners and directors and senior executives, but also whether those owners are fit and proper ­people to run clubs going forward,” said Kogan, describing the process by which the regulator might intervene. “That process is reliant on us ­having very detailed knowledge and information, which requires a ­certain amount of investigation. Then we would take judgments based on the legal advice that we then receive.” Should a club owner ultimately be found to have failed a “fitness” test related to “integrity, honesty and financial soundness”, the regulator could force the club to be sold. “We deal with issues of this type much more frequently than you might realise because we are constantly looking at clubs,” Kogan said, stating if any decision by the regulator became the subject of legal action then clubs would be asked to foot the bill through a funding levy. The acceleration of revenues among the Premier League’s biggest clubs is one of the key findings in the State of the Game report. The highest earning top-flight club currently earns 605 times the revenue of the lowest earning National League club. At the same time, spending has increased at all levels of the game, with 94% of the 116 clubs under the regulator’s regime posting a financial loss in 2025-26. In one particularly eye-catching statistic, the report found 11 Football League clubs recorded costs that exceeded their income even once player wages had been stripped out. Kogan argued that a number of external factors that fall outside the regulator’s purview are affecting the game, including the expansion of the club calendar, the regulation of ­players’ agents and the recent rise in interest rates. However, he argued that one key measure – the agreement of a redistribution deal between the Premier League and EFL – could unlock change immediately. While Kogan accepts the Premier League’s argument regarding the need for parachute payments due to “colossal” drops in revenue caused by relegation, he believes they have had a “distortive effect that’s grown over the years”. Kogan said that if a deal was done that reduced parachute payments but increased the amount going to all clubs then “that will go some way towards looking at the ­distorted effect”. Once that money was distributed, he said, “you’re going to see a softening effect going through down the 116 clubs”. The Premier League welcomed the publication of the report, arguing: “It recognises what English football has built – the world’s most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth.” The league argued that a recent offer of financial redistribution to the EFL – understood to amount to £320m per season – “meets the ­objectives the IFR has set out in its report” and said it “remains ­committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and ­balances the interests of all clubs”. The EFL said the report’s findings “reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid” and it remained “committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game”.

events.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
events.summary: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios. Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity. "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says. By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024. New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%. What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom. Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall. "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X . The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

events.title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 02:36 BST Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity". Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule. Bumble ditched the rule in August this year. Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago. While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners. Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI". They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity." This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity . Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021 . Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023. In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app. Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles. This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. events.title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
events.summary: Iran is fortifying sensitive sites, including nuclear facilities, and rallying supporters as it prepares for possible renewed U.S. attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported. U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The Journal reported Iran was strengthening defenses at nuclear sites and vowing wider retaliation in response to any U.S. strikes. Iran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East. The Journal's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3. The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Journal report. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reuters reported . The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attack resulted in multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia. The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday. On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration urged airlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard." Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil." British police arrested five men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites. Trump later said the U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat." events.title: In charts: How one of the world's biggest economies got trapped by debt
events.summary: France's National Assembly begins debate on the revenue side of the 2027 budget on Oct. 13 as lawmakers confront a difficult fiscal outlook. France posted a 5.1% budget deficit and debt of 115.6% of GDP in 2025, leaving the country under pressure to consolidate its public finances. Student protests over education resources are adding pressure as lawmakers weigh spending choices ahead of the 2027 presidential election. France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation. The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit, according to many market watchers. Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron. Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate. With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty is weighing on the euro . French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation. The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take the expensive and politically controversial step of intervening to stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France. "The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email. events.title: Paul Tudor Jones is bullish on oil, says it could rally another $20-$25 because of Iran conflict
events.summary: Paul Tudor Jones said that oil could rally as much as $20 to $25 higher in the near-term. He comes to that belief with a lack of resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict likely ahead of the midterm elections in November. If that oil rally were come to pass, he said the equity market would "absolutely, totally hate it." Hedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones says oil is set to take another leg higher because of the U.S.-Iran conflict . "I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said Tudor Jones, founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment, on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms." A rally of that size in U.S. oil prices from current levels would send them above their previous closing high for 2026 of just under $113 per barrel. Western Texas Intermediate crude futures were trading at around $92.50 Tuesday morning. Tudor Jones said if the rally were to happen, the equity market would "absolutely totally hate it," though equities were able to relatively manage higher oil prices earlier in the year. The S&P 500 only fell just over 7% at its trough in late March after the start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28, which was lower than analysts estimated would happen based off of oil's surge. U.S. oil prices jumped in March after the start of the war, and hit their peak in early April. Prices then fell in June, falling below $70 per barrel that month . However, they started rising again in July, as the conflict in the Middle East heated up again and the status of the Strait of Hormuz — a critical passageway for oil — remained unclear. Prices hit a recent high of almost $106 per barrel in September, though have traded off those levels since. Oil prices are just one headwind that Tudor Jones thinks the equity market needs to handle at the moment. He said 2027 in particular may be difficult for the stock market as investors digest increased equity supply from megacap tech IPOs, like that of Anthropic and OpenAI . While Tudor Jones thinks it's too late before the U.S. midterm elections for a resolution to the conflict, he believes that President Donald Trump will seek to seek peace after voters cast their ballots. "I assume the president has a plan post-election," he said. "I assume he has a plan because, clearly, what's going on is untenable. It's not sustainable, I don't think, in the long-run."

events.title: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’
events.summary: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount. Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%. In Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15%, while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%. On Wall Street the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 100 points, or 0.35%, to 30,556 after the open. Micron Technology slid 4.8%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 1.4%, while Nvidia lost 0.8% and Broadcom slipped 0.2%. However, the Dow Jones industrial average, which tracks 30 large US companies, rose nearly 0.4% in early trading, while the FTSE 100 index in London hit a three-week high on the back of gains in ‌financial stocks, retreating oil prices and easing bond yields. The UK’s leading share index rose 0.73% to 10,762. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $105.36 a barrel. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt. The latest sell-off came after CXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density, with plans for a product rollout. Investors are worried that the company could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers. CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July, makes Dram chips , which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations. “The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG. “CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “While great for customers who can enjoy the white heat of technological improvement and get falling margins into the bargain, it is dangerous for high-flying tech stocks who have promised so much, and on whom the entire stock market rally seems to rest.” Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chip maker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors who did not really understand what they were betting on. “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said at a conference in Singapore, in comments reported by Bloomberg . They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”. AI companies such as the ChatGPT maker OpenAI are still lossmaking. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenues of $50bn (£38bn) at the end of September suggested a viable business model but offered little guarantee on long-term profitability. “For now it’s still losing money because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.” He noted that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue came from pilot projects. “When you are a kid you go to a video arcade, you play,” he said. “Your parents give you $10 of tokens, you finish it in 10 minutes and you haven’t learned anything.”

events.title: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim
events.summary: The Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt. The FTC and the states allege that Shkreli "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry. The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. The Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge in New York on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt, alleging he "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 civil court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry. The FTC and the states allege that Shkreli, since being released from prison in May 2022 for unrelated financial crimes, violated that court order by publicly trading in at least 60 pharmaceutical industry stocks and "publicly broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of many Pharmaceutical Companies through livestreaming and posting on numerous social media platforms, including YouTube, X, and Reddit," a court filing says. The contempt filing asks a judge to order Shkreli to "divest any pharmaceutical company stocks he currently owns" and "pay a fine equal to his profits from any pharmaceutical company stock trading (plus prejudgment interest) without the ability to account for offsetting losses." The filing in U.S. District Court in Manhattan also asks that a judge make Shkreli "face clear and escalating consequences for any future violations, including financial penalties and potential incarceration." FTC Commissioner Mark Meador said in a statement, "A lifetime industry ban is only effective if breaches are met with consequences commensurate with the seriousness of the order." The court order stems from a finding that Shkreli organized an anti-competitive scheme to perpetuate his company Vyera Pharmaceuticals' monopoly in the anti-parasitic drug Daraprim. Shkreli had hiked the price of Daraprim from $17.50 per tablet to a whopping $750 per pill. In addition to banning him from the drug industry for life, a judge ordered Shkreli to disgorge more than $64 million. The 2nd Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals upheld the permanent injunction against Shkreli in January 2024, and the Supreme Court declined to take his appeal of the order in October 2024. CNBC has requested comment from an attorney for Shkreli. In addition to the FTC, the states that joined Tuesday's court filing are New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia. The filing asks the judge to order Shkreli's sister, Leonora Izerne, and his "significant other, Chelsea Voss," to preserve all evidence relating to potential violations of the injunction against Shkreli because both women "appear to have assisted or be assisting Shkreli in violating the Permanent Injunction." The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. Shkreli was sentenced to seven years in federal prison in 2018, and was released in 2022 with credit for time locked up before he was sentenced and other factors. "When judgment is entered by a court, whether it's a settlement or an order following a trial, defendants must fulfill their obligations," Guarnera said. "Today's action should serve as notice that the FTC will not hesitate to enforce violations of court orders."

events.title: ‘Brutal session’ for chip stocks shows AI trade is turning
events.summary: In Asia, selling of South Korean chipmaker shares extended into a fifth straight day on Oct 13, with the KOSPI index falling more than 6%, while in Tokyo memory-maker Kioxia, down 13%, led AI-related losses. AI chip shares sold off sharply as rising bond yields and volatility raised fears that expensive AI spending could slow. Asian and US chip markets fell hard, with South Korean stocks, Kioxia, Micron and the KOSPI all hit, while the IMF warned the AI correction could be global. Investors are now focusing on capital costs and returns, with some deals delayed and analysts saying this may be a new phase of the AI cycle, not its end. SINGAPORE – A sell-off in AI supplier shares on Oct 13 is the strongest sign to date that the mood on the trade of the decade is shifting, with worries that rising interest rates could scupper a spending spree bigger than America’s historic railroad boom. Nearly four years since the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, cash has streamed into semiconductor companies, data centre owners, cable companies and anyone reaping revenues from an unprecedented race to build computing infrastructure. Cracks in those bets began in June and are now widening across markets, with a data centre IPO collapsing last week in Australia and credit investors becoming picky on AI debt. In Asia, selling of South Korean chipmaker shares extended into a fifth straight day on Oct 13 , with the KOSPI index falling more than 6%, while in Tokyo, memory-maker Kioxia, down 13%, led AI-related losses. In the US, the chip stock selling continued into a fourth day on Oct 13 , with the Philadelphia semiconductor index down 1.7% and Micron Technology off 4%. The SOX remains up 68% for the year, and Micron stock has tripled. The falls are the heaviest since the same sort of stocks collapsed at the end of July. The KOSPI is on its longest losing streak for more than two years, down a quarter from July highs, while Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR Market has lost more than a third from July peaks. “The most important development has been not just bond yields going up, but the volatility for bonds... and that’s starting to work its way out through asset pricing across the board,” said Damien Boey, portfolio strategist at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney. “It’s a very uncomfortable situation on many fronts... Maybe AI capex just comes off the boil a little bit, and maybe a few players are casualties in that.” The SOX dropped 2.7% on Oct 12 and even heavier selling drove Seoul-listed chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down by 10% and 8%, respectively. On Oct 12 , the research arm of BlackRock, the world’s biggest asset manager, downgraded its US stocks outlook to neutral, citing “potential volatility around the AI build-out” and turned bullish on short-term Treasuries. “The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the International Monetary Fund warned on Oct 13 in its latest financial stability report. The International Monetary Fund called out AI’s contribution to growth but said there was growing evidence that capability investments and economic gains may not be as big as expected. Caution is also coursing through primary markets. Last week, Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia, shelved a US$5 billion (S$6.4 billion) initial public offering in Australia as investor interest shrivelled, underscoring how suddenly risks are becoming the chief focus in allocating capital to the sector. Oct 13’ s dollar and dim sum bond sale by Tencent Holdings in Hong Kong was the latest deal in debt markets’ sights, with guidance for 10-year dollar notes about 1.15 percentage points on top of Treasury yields, which sit at 5.2%. Japan’s tech investor SoftBank in September sold the biggest high-yield debt pile ever and promised to pay as much as 9.75% on US$4.5 billion it raised at a 7½-year tenor. The mood shift was front of mind at a slew of top financial conferences in Singapore, most recently on Oct 12, when Broadcom’s chief executive said capital was the biggest constraint on growth. To be sure, few are calling time on the AI trade altogether, and on Oct 12, Meta shares jumped 3.4% on the release of a new AI model, but many see semiconductors as a warning sign. Marc Velan, head of investments at Lucerne Asset Management in Singapore, believes the “brutal session” in South Korea says more about positioning and the cost of capital than about any fundamental deterioration in AI demand. “I suspect we’re entering the next phase of the AI cycle, where markets increasingly focus on monetisation and returns on invested capital – I wouldn’t call this the end of the AI trade,” Velan said. “But Korea could be an early warning of a broader shakeout.” Reuters

events.title: Kroger to lay off 3K corporate employees over 3 years as it leans into AI
events.summary: Grocery store chain Kroger says it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations. “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.” Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.” Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer. Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO . Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities. Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Iran live updates: At least 20 killed in week of attacks on Saudi airports PepsiCo sees strong overseas demand but lackluster North American performance in Q3 Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon. Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed. A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value. Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee. Kroger shares fell 1.6% in morning trading Tuesday, to $61.66. events.title: Britons travelling to EU countries told not to apply for delayed Etias visa waiver
events.summary: Abta advice comes as more than more than 150 websites offer service of securing entry to Schengen zone Britons travelling to EU countries have been told not to apply for an Etias visa waiver, with more than 150 websites touting the service despite its introduction being delayed. Non-EU citizens, including UK travellers and those from other visa-exempt countries including the US, Australia and Canada, will soon need to pay €20 (£17) for an electronic waiver to enter the Schengen zone under the European travel information and authorisation system (Etias). The system was scheduled to be come into effect soon after the rollout of the EU’s parallel border scheme, the entry-exit system (EES). Both, however, have been repeatedly postponed , and the persistent problems after the introduction of EES, including the software at French entry points , have meant Etias remains suspended. The director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, Luke Petherbridge, said: “While Etias was due to come into force this year, it is now back on hold. Abta believes it shouldn’t be brought in until EES is fully operational and working properly. “This is particularly important when you consider that European authorities believe over 150 websites offering Etias already exist, but there is only one official site people should apply through when live.” Abta research found awareness was growing of the impending border requirements – up from 41% in 2024 to 56% now. The price to apply has risen from €7 to €20 – over-70s and under-18s do not need to pay – but no date has been set for launch. The pan-European border agency, Frontex, warned about the existence of scam websites long before Etias was to have been introduced. Commercial sites can legitimately apply for the waivers on behalf of clients, but the agency said the risk posed by third parties ranged from data protection and identity theft to extortionate fees. It found that some unofficial websites were also providing inaccurate information over who needed an Etias while mimicking the layout of the official website and using convincing domain names. “If you use one of these sites, not only will you lose money, you are also putting your personal data at risk as well,” Petherbridge said. “What I can’t stress is enough that you can’t – and shouldn’t - apply for an Etias now.” EES is in full operation, but border authorities have been told the EU will not enforce penalties if they continue to suspend the system at entry points when queues escalate. That flexibility has meant the worst fears of the travel industry have largely been avoided this summer. Abta surveys found only 46% of visitors to Europe reporting having full checks, with half of those people waiting less than 30 minutes, and only 13% queuing for an hour. * Gwyn Topham attended Abta’s convention in Maderia. His travel was provided by Abta

events.title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip which helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
events.summary: Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral Published 13 October 2026, 00:01 BST Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree.

Time: 10am – 11.30am | Location: Bank of England, 20 Moorgate, London, EC2R 6DA The Chair thanked members for attending and confirmed that the Minutes of the Money Markets Committee (MMC) June 2026 meeting had been published on the Bank’s website. footnote [1] The Chair updated on recent usage of the Bank’s market-wide repo facilities. Members were reminded that use of the Bank’s facilities, including against a broad range of eligible collateral, was consistent with the intended transition to a repo-led operating framework. The Chair provided a brief update on the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC’s) September decision on Quantitative Tightening footnote [2] , including the exchange of letters between the Governor and the Chancellor regarding QT and the APF. footnote [3] The Chair also noted the related announcements made by the Bank and HM Treasury that came out at the same time. footnote [4] Item 2 – Discussion on market conditions Members noted that money markets continued to function smoothly and that funding conditions remained stable, even during recent increased bond market volatility. Liquidity was reported to be ample, with limited signs of stress. Members also reported stable cross-currency funding conditions despite recent geopolitical developments and broader market volatility, with quarter-end and year-end conditions expected to remain orderly. While some highlighted the potential for volatility in outright asset markets to transmit into funding conditions through reduced risk appetite or position unwinds, the overall assessment was that money market functioning remained robust. Some nevertheless noted emerging funding pressures further out the euro curve as Eurosystem liquidity continued to decline. Members also discussed developments in European Commercial Paper (ECP) markets, noting increased issuance activity and growing use of these funding channels. Members also discussed the Financial Policy Committee’s proposed changes to the leverage ratio framework footnote [5] . Members generally welcomed the direction of the proposals but considered that leverage requirements are just one of a number of constraints on their activity including stress-testing assumptions, investor expectations and risk-weighted capital requirements. As a result, members considered that it was difficult to predict the extent to which the proposals would lead to a material increase in leverage or balance-sheet deployment in UK money markets in the near-term. Some noted that greater releasability of constraints in stress could support increased use of gilts and reverse repo within buffers. Members noted increasing competition for retail and corporate deposits. While this had not materially affected funding plans, some observed that sustained competition for deposits could increase wholesale funding requirements and funding costs over time. Members agreed this would remain an area to monitor. From a market infrastructure perspective, strong trading activity across gilt and international markets was reported, with no material change in cleared repo conditions. Members also welcomed the predictability provided by the MPC and Bank's recent balance sheet announcements and noted that the Bank's liquidity facilities continued to support confidence in firms' ability to manage reserves and liquidity needs.

events.title: The 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20: From organs to orbit and everything in between
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Twenty founders just earned their shot at Disrupt glory. They’re headed to the Disrupt Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to compete for the $100,000 prize and the coveted Disrupt Cup. Every year, thousands of founders from around the world pitch us on what they believe the future should look like. This year’s Top 20 are building it from organs to orbit and everywhere in between. Across this cohort, one theme kept emerging: Making the previously invisible measurable. These founders are finding ways to understand signals we couldn’t previously capture, model systems too complex to predict, and turn the physical world into data that machines can actually act on. They’re measuring the biological clocks inside our bodies and growing miniature human organs in labs. They’re teaching robots to take on increasingly complex physical work and modeling the real world closely enough to predict what might happen next — even the behavior of wild animals. They’re extracting intelligence from scam calls and finding new ways to use the computing power already orbiting above our heads. And then, of course, there’s the company trying to launch cargo into space with a giant hydrogen-powered cannon. What connects these 20 companies isn’t a single technology or industry. It’s an ambition to understand more of the world around us — biological, physical, industrial, and digital — and use that understanding to make better decisions, automate what once required human intervention, and tackle problems that previously seemed too complex to solve. Now they have six minutes on the Disrupt Stage to prove it. Here are the 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20. Startup Battlefield Semifinals Session 1 (10:00 a.m. – 11:15 a.m.) Longshot Space : Reinventing the economics of space by launching cargo to orbit at $50/kg using hydrogen-powered kinetic launchers. Veritas : Protecting luxury brands with custom microchips that verify authenticity and enable connected post-purchase experiences. Laplace Intelligence : Building agentic world models that help cities, ports, and airports roll out counterfactual futures of the real world before they act. Flox Intelligence : Preventing deadly wildlife collisions at airports and railways with real-time AI that detects animal behavior and safely redirects them. Satlyt : Helping satellite operators unlock and monetize idle compute by transforming their spacecraft into virtual AI data centers with a single line of code. Battlefield Semifinal Session 2 (1:00 p.m. – 2:15 p.m.) LNK Energies : Delivering clean hydrogen power cheaper than diesel through breakthrough compact reactor technology compatible with existing diesel infrastructure. Helix Carbon : Helping steelmakers cut emissions and fuel costs by electrochemically upcycling blast furnace waste gas into replacement fossil fuels on-site. IndustrialNext : Automating high-precision, contact-rich assembly tasks by deploying AI-driven robotic systems that learn from production data and adapt to new products. Niobia AI : Helping process and materials engineers compress weeks of root-cause analysis into minutes with domain-expert AI reasoning. Licube : Producing ultra-high purity lithium and lithium isotopes (Li-6/Li-7), the critical inputs for nuclear fusion and advanced materials. Battlefield Semifinal Session 3 (10:00 a.m. – 11:15 a.m.) Mosqitter : Detecting and preventing mosquito-borne disease spread with real-time disease intelligence platforms that turn sensor networks into early warning systems for national health agencies. Hiyd AI : Delivering proactive health insights by combining sleep, movement, and nutrition data through an ultra-slim, discreet wearable tracker and AI app. TimeTeller GmbH : Measuring people’s biological clocks to determine optimal treatment timing through molecular diagnostics and AI, improving efficacy and reducing side effects. NTangible : Helping coaches and front offices make smarter recruiting decisions by quantifying how athletes perform under pressure with a validated cognitive score. Intero Biosystems : Accelerating drug development by producing miniature human organs that enable pharma companies to identify safer, more effective medications while reducing clinical trial costs. Battlefield Semifinal Session 4 (1:30 p.m. – 2:45 p.m.) Apate.ai : Dismantling scam operations by deploying conversational AI bots that engage scammers and turn their interactions into real-time intelligence for banks, telcos, and governments. CedarDB : Delivering the data layer for the AI age — real-time transactions and analytics in one engine with guardrails inside the database system that AI agents can’t bypass.

events.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
events.summary: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”. Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported . Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts. C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.” Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper . And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions. Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment. “We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.” AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”. Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added. Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said. Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity. One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. “This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif.

events.title: Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K: What to know about smart hub and updated console
events.summary: Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home. A video posted to Apple 's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen one morning using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders. “Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple 's AirTag. In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”. The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall. Before Apple's HomeView announcement, Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint , said that such a device would help the US technology giant strengthen its consumer product offerings. “The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. Apple also seems prepared to allow devices made by other companies to work with HomeView. “Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories – including smart cameras, thermostats and a door lock – are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home,” the company posted to its site. It added that the collection of devices would arrive at a later date. Mohit Agrawal, research director with Counterpoint, said that this aspect was intriguing. “Rather than buying its way in, as Amazon did with Ring and Google with Nest, Apple is partnering with LG and Schneider Electric,” he explained. “This lets it fill out the home quickly, from the front door to the thermostat, while keeping control of the experience through Siri and the Home app.” Apple seems to be positioning the forthcoming HomeView product as a device that is used passively in day-to-day life. “HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house,” a description reads. “And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos and calls look and sound amazing … meet the new heart of your home.” According to technology news outlet, The Verge , HomeView will be initially available in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and India. HomePod mini 2 Also on Tuesday, Apple announced its HomePod mini speaker devices would be getting an upgrade. “Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the centre of your home,” the company said. “Once set up with your iPhone or iPad , Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.” The HomePod 2 will be available on October 30, with prices starting at $149. Apple touts improved sound, touch controls, a mesh design and a woven power cord among the HomePod's improvements. “With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. “Still, shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year over year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles.” Apple TV Apple's TV console has gone several years without an update, but that changed on Tuesday with the unveiling of Apple TV 4K. The company says the updated console has an A19 processor that assists in delivering 4K video quality, and it will also have a Siri remote. Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13, with prices starting at $299. “Apple TV 4K delivers the ultimate cinematic experience, from shows and movies to games and workouts,” the company said. “With the new, more powerful Siri AI and built-in microphones, enjoying what you love is as easy as using your voice.”

Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. It’s now easier to use Spotify by talking to Siri on iPhones updated to iOS 27, Spotify said on Tuesday. Users will no longer need to specify “on Spotify” when they’re asking Siri to play music or other content using the streaming service’s apps. Instead, users can just say whatever it is they want to hear, and Spotify will play the content, whether that’s a specific track, album, podcast, audiobook, or a broader query, like “play workout music,” or a request for one of Spotify’s features, like “play my DJ.” Siri’s voice control can also be used to do things like request personalized recommendations, resume podcasts, search your library, or even create a Prompted Playlist with AI. Spotify says removing the extra voice command will make hands-free listening feel more natural, as users can just focus on what they want to hear, not how to phrase the request properly to get their preferred music app to respond. This feature works because Siri can now learn your music app preference. If you consistently use Spotify, it will route your audio requests to that app automatically. The new feature is available globally for users with an iPhone 15 Pro or later, outside the EU, if Apple Intelligence is enabled in Settings. events.title: Bumble agrees to a $1.3B acquisition deal as online dating faces a reset
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Bumble is getting a new owner. The dating app announced Tuesday that it has agreed to a $1.3 billion acquisition deal with Ithaca Holdings, marking a major shift for a company that once looked like one of the biggest success stories in online dating. The deal would take the company private after years of declining subscriber numbers, falling revenue, and mounting pressure to rethink the online dating experience. The move may give Bumble a chance to work on its next chapter away from the pressure of public markets. Founded in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble made a name for itself for its unique approach where only women made the first move. That helped it stand out in a crowded dating market, and the company eventually went public in 2021 at a valuation of roughly $14 billion. Since then, however, the dating app landscape has changed considerably. Bumble has faced declining paying users, weaker revenue, and growing dissatisfaction with the familiar swipe-based model. The company recently reported second-quarter 2026 revenue of $211 million, down 15.2% year over year, while its paying user base fell 16.4% to approximately 3.2 million. The acquisition follows a review of strategic options by an independent committee of Bumble’s board, which recommended the transaction after consulting outside legal and financial advisers. Wolfe Herd did not participate in the board’s discussions or vote on the deal, according to the press release. “In Ithaca, we have found a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future,” Wolfe Herd said in a statement. She also confirmed that she plans to stay actively involved in the business, working alongside Ithaca’s Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, and the Bumble team. Going private might give Bumble more flexibility to experiment with new features and make changes without having to answer to public-market investors every quarter. The company has been exploring AI-driven features and putting more energy into helping people connect offline, reflecting a broader shift in how younger users approach dating. One example is Plans , announced in July, which focuses on bringing people together through real-world activities. Wolfe Herd also recently revealed that the company is developing a new way for users to interact that could eventually replace the swipe-based model.
