events.title: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis
events.summary: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising O f all the drivers of the populist wave, one of the most powerful is the sense of inevitability that surrounds what we are told is the march of progress. In presenting the future as a fait accompli, it poisons the civic well by dealing us out of the game. While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI reality untethered to the will of the people . On the velocity and trajectory of the technology, Trump and the tech overlords have determined we must hit the accelerator and dispense with guardrails to “win” an ill-defined race to build a god in a box. This reckless exercise of power from a waning empire has created its own reality for all of us. In Australia, the government has determined that the only way we can exercise control in a world of such chaos is to grab on to this juggernaut. We become to US tech data what the Saudis are to oil; using renewables to power massive centres in the desert, converting solar into AI tokens and piping them up to Asia, a new export industry that will power our common wealth. Within the inevitability doctrine this strategy has logic. The alternative, we are told, is to become a client state to Silicon Valley. But in pursuing this vision we risk being blinded to the foreseeable consequences of what we are signing ourselves up to. The industry we are building derives value by replacing workers, it has been built on the stolen work of creators, its unregulated deployment is causing unconscionable harms particularly in theatres of war, it has an insatiable thirst for energy and water, while even its creators say there’s a not insignificant chance it will destroy humanity. The “inevitability doctrine” demands we concede rather than properly explore and negotiate these trade-offs. This facade of democracy leads to its populist backlash. We are seeing this in the US where the Bannon right and Sanders left are joining forces to block the scale out of datacentres, part of a broader and timely political reckoning. A few things have been happening over recent weeks to suggest something similar is starting to happen here. First, Australians who despite their high take-up of some AI tools remain among the world’s most sceptical, have a low tolerance for tech overlords. GetUp’s successful campaign against Coles’ partnership with Palantir, the data company that licenses its software to the US military who bomb children and immigration officials to track individuals, shows the vulnerability of public brands who lean in too close to the beast. Second, creators whose work has been stolen to train models that will diminish the value of their future careers are standing their ground. They are rightly aggrieved and won’t just wave through anything that feels like an amnesty. They are demanding compensation for the theft of their work as well as an ongoing model to give them control over the terms of its use. Even more significant may be the failure of the Firmus IPO , which was to have been the biggest Australian float since Telstra. The decision not to list the company followed the withdrawal of a datacentre in Sydney, the first major project to fall over due to local community pressure. There are a range of possible reasons the bid failed, including accusations of greed , but surely the growing community backlash to datacentres had some scratching their heads about the prospects of a hyper-scale out. Consumers, creators, communities are all challenging the “inevitability” storyline. Together they add up to a series of counter-punches that suggest our democratic faculties have not yet been fully exhausted. But the “inevitability doctrine” is durable and any pushback will need to be ongoing, because these companies have the resources, influence and bald self-interest to pursue their objectives with all the commitment of an AI agent gone rogue. The biggest danger to our democracy this technology poses is not in the cynical misuse of an untested and unregulated deployment (although this will be hugely destructive) but in the broader sense that we have no say in what is happening to us. Right now, its game on. In our parliament over the coming weeks there will be fights to land privacy reform, a digital duty of care, standards on datacentres and rules on how governments will use the technology on its citizens. In workplaces there will be struggles over usage, surveillance and displacement. In our schools and social circles, real negotiations on how we choose to use the bots and agents, or whether we need to use them at all.

The free plan will only offer limited chat and agent usage, and Premium or higher is required to access the latest Grok models. There’s another draw for existing X Premium+ subscribers: The comparable plan on the new X subscription costs the same or less, the company noted. Existing users can either switch from their subscription settings on X to upgrade to the new bundle, or maintain their current plan. The option to upgrade will roll out gradually, so interested customers will need to keep an eye on their billing settings for the offer to upgrade. events.title: Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry
events.summary: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned. Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday. Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026. Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta. Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad. However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad. Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES). The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it had been a tough year for the travel industry. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.” Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer. “We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.” He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Tanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.” Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays. Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain. Travel to the convention was provided by Abta

Apple’s new HomeView device was the center of the show at its smart home event on Tuesday, but the company also refreshed its HomePod mini smart speaker with a new chip and Siri AI integration, the latter of which will be available through a future update. The $149 update is $50 more expensive than the original version launched over six years ago in 2020 . The new HomePod mini has an S10 chip that helps improve optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. With the new HomePod mini, users can control their smart home devices through voice commands. Plus, the HomePod mini 2 speakers can be the default speaker for Mac for video calls or music playback instead of built-in speakers. The device has another new feature, as well: a visual canvas called “Sound Glow,” which uses the color scheme of the album art to turn the top of the HomePod mini into a visual canvas that will glow and pulse in sync with the music. Users can also pick soundscapes like rain or ocean waves to start animations. The new speaker comes in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight colorways and will be available starting October 30. events.title: Apple’s new smart home lineup includes a smart lock, thermostat, and video doorbells
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Apple is getting serious about the smart home space. The company on Tuesday showed off its new Apple Home Collection, which includes a new smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor, and a range of security cameras. The new devices are designed to work with HomeView , the company’s new smart home hub which can be used to control connected accessories and interact with Apple’s software. This new range of smart home accessories could help Apple compete better with Amazon Ring and Google Nest, two established players in connected home security. The products will become available in December. Apple says the devices were built in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — an interesting move for the company, which has long sought to build and support every smart home accessory itself. The smart lock, priced at $349.95, stands out for its support for ultra-wideband (UWB), a wireless technology that enables more precise proximity detection than traditional Bluetooth. This could allow the lock to recognize when an authorized user approaches and automatically unlock the door, reducing the need to pull out a phone or reach for a physical key. The $249.95 wired video doorbell, meanwhile, will let homeowners see who’s outside, monitor visitors, and receive notifications when someone approaches their property. When someone rings it, a chime will sound through Apple devices like HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Users will also be notified on their iPhone or iPad. As for the temperature sensor, it can provide insight into conditions in individual rooms, helping users identify temperature differences between areas and make adjustments. For security, Apple is also introducing indoor and outdoor cameras, as well as a floodlight camera ($399.95) that combines exterior lighting with video monitoring. events.title: Dating app Bumble swipes right on US$1.3b buyout as users fall out of love
events.summary: Paying users of Bumble fell 16.2% to 3.2 million in the second quarter of 2026. NEW YORK – Bumble has agreed to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valued at US$1.3 billion (S$1.6 billion), as the dating app pushes forward with its months-long turnaround amid shifting Gen Z dating habits and declining paying users. Ithaca Holdings will pay US$6.05 per share, according to a statement on Oct 12. The deal price represents a 138% premium over Bumble’s closing share price on Oct 9. After the deal is completed, Bumble will remain based in Austin, Texas, with other major offices in London and New York. Bumble and larger rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have been grappling with weaker user engagement , particularly from younger users tired of endless swiping. Founded in 2014 by CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd , Bumble pioneered the “women-go-first” approach to online dating. Under Herd, who returned as CEO in March 2025 after stepping down in 2023, the company has doubled down on revamping its core product with AI-powered features, group dating and a redesigned member experience in a bid to revive growth. In August, Bumble ditched the women-go-first model, its latest move to boost user engagement. The company also introduced an artificial intelligence-powered assistant designed to act as a personal matchmaker, offering an alternative experience to swiping through user profiles. The efforts follow steep declines in total paying users and revenue. Total paying users fell 16.4% to 3.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, while quarterly revenue has been declining for nearly two years. Herd said she would “remain actively involved with Bumble”. Bumble’s market capitalisation has shrunk to about US$582 million as at Oct 12, a far cry from the US$14 billion valuation when it went public in 2021. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

events.title: Saudi attacks shake the confidence of foreign investors
events.summary: Oil prices ticked down on Tuesday as Saudi oil executives sought to reassure the market following a major attack on the capital’s airport. International energy bosses were largely absent from this week’s World Petroleum Council Energy Congress, held in Riyadh for the first time, after the Houthi attack. The CEOs of BP, Shell, and TotalEnergies, along with a host of international ministers, including US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, dropped out due to the strikes. That left a thinner-than-expected crowd, mostly made up of local executives, to hear the kingdom seek deeper international cooperation to secure energy supplies and trade routes. Saudi Arabia can build more pipelines and boost storage capacity, but “no one nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone,” Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said. His comments reflect the growing role of foreign investors in the region’s energy industry, already expanding even before the Iran war. Long relegated to minor roles, the Gulf energy companies increasingly see international energy firms and global investors as an integral part of their plans to lock in customers for their hydrocarbon exports, invest in their infrastructure, and bind other states into their security in a way that the old expectations of oil for security arrangements have failed to guarantee. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Trump’s Russian energy strategy could backfire
events.summary: Tim’s view The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for. On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators , who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference — equal to less than a day of US consumption — and extended a “financial lifeline” to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is “enough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.” As for the “ceasefire,” Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly . A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscow’s behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trump’s proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries , which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscow’s sights . Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy can’t accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it . Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Biden’s decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But it’s counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead. Notable A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of November’s midterms , a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

events.title: Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment and manage the home
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home A person cooking in their kitchen looks at HomeView. A person sits at their kitchen table and reads a book next to HomeView. A user’s HomeView sits on their living room countertop. HomeView is shown in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. A person touches the screen of HomeView and moves the hinge. The back of HomeView is shown, complete with ports and a color-matched charging cable. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence Siri AI pulls up information from a user’s Calendar app on HomeView. Siri AI is shown on a user’s HomeView and iPhone 18 Pro. Rich Entertainment Anywhere in the Home Connecting Users to What Matters Most HomeView shows a group of people on a FaceTime call. HomeView shows a recipe for butternut squash soup. HomeView shows a timer a user set for 15 minutes. Customers in Australia , Canada , India , New Zealand , the UK , and the U.S. can pre-order Apple HomeView in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray for $299 (U.S.), and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) in space gray and silver for $299 (U.S.), starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Customers in Singapore can pre-order starting Thursday, October 15, at 9 a.m. SGT. Both models will be available in these countries beginning Friday, November 13. Customers in South Africa will be able to pre-order Apple HomeView and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) through Apple Authorized Resellers, with availability beginning Friday, November 13. Apple HomeView is not available for sale in the European Union, as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward. HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (U.S.), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (U.S.), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (U.S.). Siri AI on HomeView is available in English in the U.S., Australia , Canada , India , New Zealand , Singapore , South Africa , and the UK. Canadian French-language support will be offered later via a free software update. Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI and built with privacy and security at its core CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today introduced Apple HomeView , designed to be central to the home and personal to everyone in it. With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core. 1 HomeView recognizes users by their faces, adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more helpful, personalized responses. 2 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Pre-orders start today, with availability beginning November 13. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. “It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.” Elegantly Designed for Any Space HomeView features a beautiful aluminum design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base by a stainless steel hinge that provides a smooth tilt for comfortable viewing on tabletops of any height. The perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table, HomeView comes in four beautiful colors — silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray — each finished with a matching cable. The elegant design and Liquid Retina display seamlessly blend into any space while remaining clearly visible from across the room. It features adaptive display technologies, including True Tone, that react to changing light throughout the day. Automatic brightness adjusts from 500 nits — bright enough to stay vivid and easy to see even in a sunlit room — down to just 0.3 nits, making it ideal for the nightstand. The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer. A separate wall-mounted HomeView model — available in space gray and silver — offers the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display, powerful set of features, and rich audio. It can be attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon. Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness. With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer.

events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever iCloud photos are displayed on Apple TV 4K. Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K , delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience. 1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free. 2 The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes. 3 The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13. “The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.” An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.” A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing. Faster Performance, Smarter Remote The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth. The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate. 4 Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match. 5 An Even Smarter Home Hub The new Apple TV 4K continues to serve as a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere. 6 With a compatible doorbell, notifications appear directly on the TV so users can see who’s at the door, speak with them, and control other accessories like unlocking the door — all without interrupting what they’re watching. Apple TV 4K supports automations, guest mode, and secure local processing of HomeKit Secure Video, now enhanced with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity video descriptions and summarized notifications. Users can also use Siri AI to control smart home accessories and turn scenes on or off hands-free. And with built-in Wi-Fi and Thread, Apple TV 4K can seamlessly connect and control a user’s smart home. More Ways to Enjoy the Living Room Apple TV 4K is more than just a way to watch — it’s a home essential that transforms the living room to reflect what users want in the moment.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces the next generation of HomePod mini with support for Siri AI, beautiful new colors, and rich sound With a profoundly more capable and conversational Siri AI, new ways to enjoy music, and a more immersive home theater experience, HomePod mini does more than ever before CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced HomePod mini 2 , featuring Siri AI, gorgeous new colors, and enhanced audio experiences. Siri AI, 1 coming to HomePod mini 2 in a future software update, is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge that powers tasks like richer music discovery, and the ability to tap into even more apps — bringing a whole new level of capability to HomePod mini. 2 Users can enjoy room-filling audio with a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or using multiroom audio. When paired with the new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2 supports four-speaker surround sound — Apple’s most immersive home theater setup yet. And HomePod mini makes it easy for different users to manage the connected home with just a voice command, securely controlling accessories and running automations. HomePod mini 2 can be pre-ordered starting today in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight, with availability beginning Friday, October 30. “HomePod mini 2 brings together Siri AI, gorgeous new colors, and incredible audio,” said Kaiann Drance, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Home Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, it understands you better than ever, drawing on personal context and broad world knowledge to make music discovery even richer. It fills a room with sound on its own, which gets even bigger in a stereo pair or with multiroom audio, and when paired with the new Apple TV 4K, it delivers our most immersive home theater setup yet. And with just your voice, HomePod mini makes it easy to securely control your accessories and run automations across the connected home.” Siri AI Transforms the HomePod mini Experience Powered by an entirely new architecture built on the latest generation of Apple Foundation Models, Siri AI transforms the HomePod mini experience and helps users get more done than ever before. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment. HomePod mini can recognize up to six users in a household by their voice and securely connect to their device across apps like Messages and timers, while playing their favorite music, and more. Siri AI can also privately act on this context across a user’s iPhone and iPad apps to complete tasks like finding a song a friend recommended in a text, setting a reminder tied to a calendar event or location, locating a recipe from an email, or adding ingredients to a grocery list. With broad world knowledge, Siri AI can answer questions on almost any topic by getting up-to-date information from the web. And users can go back and forth with Siri in a conversation like never before. Once Siri AI is enabled on a supported HomePod mini speaker, even users without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad will benefit from Siri AI’s broad world knowledge; its ability to have rich, natural conversations; and its improved music discovery. Immersive Audio Experiences HomePod mini delivers rich 360-degree sound from its compact footprint, whether it’s used as a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or as part of a multiroom audio setup. Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, it analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. Together, the four speakers and the new Apple TV 4K intelligently recognize each speaker’s position in the room, so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. 3 The new HomePod mini can serve as a speaker for Mac, delivering expansive sound for everything from movies and gaming to FaceTime and video calls. 4 Finished in complementary colors, the new HomePod mini creates a beautifully unified desktop setup with Mac. Introducing Sound Glow With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. 5 The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere. Effortless Smart Home Management HomePod mini makes controlling the connected home easy at an incredible value. With just their voice, users can conduct a series of smart home actions, including locking the front door; closing the garage when leaving the house; and lowering the blinds, adjusting the thermostat, or turning off the lights at bedtime. With the Home app, users can automate their smart home accessories and create scenes to control multiple accessories at the same time. As a home hub, HomePod mini also lets users securely control accessories from the Home app on iPhone, whether they’re at home or away. 6 Sound Recognition gives HomePod mini users peace of mind by listening for a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm and, if one is detected, sending a notification immediately to the user’s iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. Using the Home app, users can check in via HomePod mini and listen and talk to someone at home to make sure everything is all right. 7 The new HomePod mini also works seamlessly with smart home accessories, including Apple Home Collection 8 video doorbells and cameras, using Face Recognition to announce who is at the door. 9 Private and Secure by Design As with every Apple product, privacy and security are foundational to HomePod mini. Siri AI takes full advantage of the bold new architecture for Apple Intelligence. Siri requests on HomePod mini 2 can use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy of the device to the cloud.

Each product can be set up starting with a single tap with iPhone, controlled entirely from the Home app and using Siri, and work as either standalone accessories or together as a connected system. “LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president. “Working closely with Apple, we’ve co-created a more connected, intuitive, and convenient home experience for our customers.” “As a global leader in energy technology, we are proud to bring our experience in innovative and advanced climate control to Apple Home,” said Olivier Blum, Schneider Electric’s CEO.

events.title: A pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show reaches Frieze Masters in London 58 years later
events.summary: It took 58 years for a pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show to reach Frieze Masters in London. In 1968, two female artists hung their paintings at a school in Jeddah called Dar Al-Tarbia Al-Hadetha, in one of the first exhibitions women had ever held in Saudi Arabia. One of them, Mounirah Mosly , spent the decades that followed — long before Vision 2030 set off a boom in Saudi art — designing Aramco publications, helping run its children’s art competitions, and working dyes, snakeskin, and rope into collages about war and Palestine, until her death in 2019. This week, her creations go on display at Frieze Masters , Frieze London’s fair for art made before 2000, where a slot reads as a verdict that the work now belongs to history. Jeddah’s Athr Gallery is debuting with Mosly and a second pioneer of Saudi modernism, Abdulrahman Alsulaiman. Her work hangs in the fair’s Feminist Legacies section. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: AI is an inflation problem, Fed’s Goolsbee says
events.summary: The News Inflation tied to the AI boom is “jumping out of its lane” and starting to push up prices in unrelated corners of the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said. “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said on Semafor’s . “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” Prices for land, electricity, water, construction, and electrical components used in data centers have surged. Those spikes don’t appear to have yet hit consumer pain points — for example, the cost of groceries or a haircut — but economists are closely watching how AI’s wealth, from paper millionaires in Silicon Valley to higher-paid construction workers, is being spent. Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned last month about “some economy-wide pressure from AI-fueled demand” but said that so far the boom looks like “a shift in demand toward AI-related sectors rather than an increase in economy-wide demand.” Fighting that kind of sector-specific inflation with rate hikes “could be a mistake,” she said. Goolsbee isn’t a member of the Fed committee that sets interest rates, but will join it in 2027. He and other economists have been trying to parse how much of today’s stubborn inflation — 3.4% in August, with September’s numbers due out this week — is from higher oil prices triggered by the war in the Middle East, which the Fed can’t do much about, and how much is coming from hotter demand across the economy for goods and services. “If inflation remains persistent, then I think it’s clear what the Fed has to do,” he said, when asked whether the central bank should raise interest rates again when it meets later this month. Liz’s view The Fed’s problem is that its best tool for fighting inflation doesn’t seem to be denting the demand for AI inputs. Hyperscalers aren’t slaphappy consumers who might be deterred by higher interest rates. They are locked in a must-win battle and don’t seem to mind higher debt costs. Companies like Alphabet and Meta have cash-cow advertising businesses that can support a few extra basis points of interest. It’s a broader problem for the Fed: Big parts of the US economy no longer respond to rising interest rates. There may be a pain point for the hyperscalers, but it’s likely to be intolerable for the rest of us. Room for Disagreement The issuance of new AI-linked debt fell in August, according to Morgan Stanley, which could show investors tapping on the brakes, even if corporate executives don’t want to. Transcript Liz Hoffman: Austan Goolsbee, welcome to the show. Austan Goolsbee: Thank you for having me. Liz: You are a great communicator in a world of wonks, literally a champion talker. Kevin Warsh wants the Fed to talk less and to force investors to look at the numbers and make their own decisions. What do you think? I’m an old friend and fan of Chairman Warsh. I worked with him back in the financial crisis. Before he ever got there, I’m uneasy with people expressing what we’re now calling forward guidance, that is saying, “Here’s what I think will happen at the next meeting. Here’s what I think four months from now the interest rate should change.” Most of the discussion about communication seems to have been about that, and I kind of agree with we should phase out that kind of communication. I’m engaged in a demystification project about the Federal Reserve. Here’s what we do. We’re not the bad guys. We’re the Guardians of the Galaxy. I’m going to stay on that for sure. Liz: Getting to those numbers that you would all like the market to put more stock in and make their own decisions about, even if they were prepared to be weaned off the commentary, does the data that you’re seeing right now lay out a clear picture? I like how you phrased that. I would say no, not a super clear picture because inflation’s still way too high. I have been worrying publicly about the potential for supply shocks like tariffs, like oil prices to shove us into a stagflationary kind of a trade-off. There is one sense in which it hasn’t been ambiguous. It hasn’t been stagflationary. The job market still looks very stable to me. Growth has been solid, consumer spending solid. We’re falling down on the inflation side of the mandate. But the ambiguity comes, is the inflation getting better on its own as it might if a supply shock kind of worked through or if you had a tariff that was just a one-time increase in the level of prices that should fade away and it hasn’t really been fading away. And you’ve seen inflation in services kicking up and that’s not really from tariffs, that’s not really mostly from oil. So that’s where you start to get the ambiguity in it and it’s not totally clear. Rohan Goswami: How much of that is AI, which obviously it’s driving a huge investment boom that’s sending up the price of inputs, power, land up. But at the same time, there is this deflationary promise that it’ll make everything cheaper. How do you think about those two things? This dynamic where there is great promise to come that is factored into massive stock market valuations and massive incentives for companies to engage in business investment. All of those things, the bigger the hype, the greater the chance that you overheat the economy in the short run, that for the day job of the Fed, the more promise there is, the more temptation, the more tendency to spend today based on the promise of what is to come. And that you got to be careful about because that’s just old-fashioned overheating right now. Rohan: What would a financial unwind of that trade, of the AI trade actually look like from where you sit? If it’s a discovery that the fundamentals are not there and it’s a bubble, that we have had bubbles in US history in the past, including in the recent past, and their unwinds can get ugly depending how much leverage is associated with those bubbles. It could be more like the popping of the internet. Now, Rohan, you’re not old enough. You don’t remember it, but if you back up, if you’re older than dirt like me, you’ll remember we had an experience with the internet that they were building out the infrastructure premised on growth rates of 20% per year. And when the growth rate came in, well, it’s only going to be 7% per year, that’s still a pretty strong growth rate, but they were massively overbuilt. And so we kind of had this overhang. That’s slightly different than... Finding out the fundamentals are different is slightly different than just a old-fashioned bubble in my view. Liz: But Alan Greenspan, I think, said basically that the Fed cannot deflate a bubble in real time without making life miserable for everybody else. Do you think that’s still true? There is a very significant debate among economists about the question, should the Fed try to prevent bubbles, pop bubbles, just clean up after the bubble pops? All of those things. events.title: How the Houthis’ Zaydi heritage influences their strikes in Iran
events.summary: The Houthis firing missiles at Riyadh are not just Iranian proxies — they’re heirs to a 1,000-year-old Zaydi imamate that ruled northern Yemen on and off until the modern state was established in 1962. Zaydism holds that power belongs to the Prophet’s descendants, not elected officials. In an explainer video , Baraa Shiban, a RUSI fellow who sat on Yemen’s National Dialogue before being exiled for criticizing the group’s abuses, describes how, after a 1995 trip to Iran, the group’s founder, Hussein al-Houthi, fused the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam with Tehran’s revolutionary doctrine and built a militia in Hezbollah’s image. The group seized Sanaa in 2014, a decade after its founder was killed. Rather than replace the state, the Houthis hollowed it out, Shiban said, assigning a “supervisor” to sit over every ministry and neighborhood, extorting businesses, indoctrinating the public, and recruiting children as soldiers . They now rule most of Yemen’s population and sit on one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: UAE and Saudi Arabia account for almost 90% of $2.98 billion of startup capital raised in 2026
events.summary: The UAE and Saudi Arabia accounted for almost 90% of the $2.98 billion that regional startups raised in the first nine months of the year, according to venture capital tracker MAGNiTT. The two countries were also responsible for every round of $100 million or more. Regional funding fell 7%, and the number of deals dropped by a third. Take out the big rounds and the picture is bleak. Most of the money went to a handful of fintech and logistics companies that have already proven themselves. Early-stage deals have thinned out, which leaves fewer companies ready for growth rounds in 2027. Gulf money is filling the gap that other investors left: Investors from outside the region want to know they can get their money out, and right now that’s hard, with fewer startups being bought. — Ed Clowes

events.title: The IMF cuts its 2026 growth forecasts across the Gulf
events.summary: The IMF cut its 2026 growth forecasts across the Gulf and now expects the Middle East and North Africa to be the only region in the world to shrink this year. In April, the fund still forecast Saudi Arabia and the UAE would grow. Both will still do better than Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, whose emir said today that government revenue was down 42% in the first half of the year , because they can pipe crude around the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Fujairah. The fund expects a strong rebound next year, but only if the strait gradually reopens from March, a date it has already pushed back. Oman, whose ports sit outside the strait, is the only Gulf economy still expected to grow in 2026, though its growth will roughly halve next year as Qatar and Kuwait rebound by more than 17%. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Five things to watch after Trump's Russian diesel deal
events.summary: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The law. It's not clear if any Russian barrels will reach U.S. shores — or whether it's legal if they do. A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement , say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws." Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions. Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week. events.title: Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, regulators have announced. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. For some customers - especially if their contact details have changed - it could take many months before compensation is paid. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027 those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 to 26 February. It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes. The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme.

events.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
events.summary: Shoppers are much more inclined to buy misshapen produce if they can be assured the quality is good. Carly Reeves on Unsplash , CC BY There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills . But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early. Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity , but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste. In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products . I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better. What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first. Making ‘ugly’ food attractive A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%. Companies that sell ‘misfit’ produce have seen a surge of consumer interest in recent years. Jintao Zhang , CC BY Another example is Too Good To Go , an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores . And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals. Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before , while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation. This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “ Different Outside. Same Inside ” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food. The upcycling boom This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas . Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025. Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart. But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers. Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found . Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality. That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store. A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms. When logos matter The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality , while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations . The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare. Shoppers respond more favorably to logos that provide information and incentives, research has found. From Jintao Zhang. , CC BY We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference. It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there. Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. events.title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 10:42 BST Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed. Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News , external . But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk. This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said. Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees. The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition. However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working". The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers. The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said. Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout. Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added. However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail. "We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added. A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner. Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said there were "tough times" on the High Street for all retailers. She said retailers were struggling with "significantly subdued consumer confidence as prices continue to rise" due to higher fuel costs. Poundland itself faces intense competition from rivals including B&M, Aldi, Lidl and from online retailers including Temu and TikTok Shop. The business "lost its strong £1 identity leaving shoppers to think it was getting too expensive", Shuttleworth said, and a costly expansion into clothing and frozen food under past management had not been successful. events.title: Hobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer data
events.summary: Cyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackers The owner of Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles has said its websites and IT systems have been hit by a cyber-attack that may have compromised customers’ personal data. The South-African listed TFG London said it identified the “cybersecurity incident” at the three UK-based retail chains on Sunday. Its two other UK brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. TFG said its stores had stayed open and trading but some of its IT systems “remain unavailable” and it had paused all online orders as a “precautionary measure”. An “investigation is ongoing, including establishing whether any personal or other sensitive information has been compromised,” the company said. If the investigation establishes that any personal information has been accessed by hackers, TFG said it would “notify affected individuals or organisations”. “Some of our brand’s website capabilities may not be available as the investigation continues. We apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate,” the company added. In an email to Whistles customers, the company said any orders placed on or after 11 October may be delayed. Orders placed before that date are being processed normally. Returns can only be made via stores at present and Whistles told customers it was “working on a solution for postal returns”. TFG has engaged external cybersecurity specialists to contain the incident, which has been reported to the relevant UK authorities. The group’s operations in Africa or Australia run on separate systems and are not affected. The attack on the three UK fashion brands comes less than a week after a cyber-attack affected the online fashion seller Asos , in which the names, addresses and recent search data of millions of customers was accessed. H&M said on Monday that it was also investigating claims that its systems had been attacked. However, the fast fashion retailer said: “We have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning On Monday, it emerged that hackers had forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight , in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores. Several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer , the Co-op and Harrods , were hit by damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op faced stock shortages and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean. Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the digital security firm NordVPN, said: “Coming so soon after the Asos incident, this latest attack on TFG London is another reminder that the retail sector is firmly in hackers’ sights. These attacks are becoming a recurring nightmare for businesses, and there’s every reason to believe we’ll see more of them. “Retailers are particularly attractive targets because they hold valuable customer information and rely on a sprawling network of payment systems, suppliers and third-party technology providers. Every connection is a potential weak point, and attackers are increasingly adept at exploiting stolen credentials, human error and gaps in security.”

events.title: Du and etisalat unveil new services boosting UAE push towards 6G
events.summary: UAE telecoms operators du and etisalat have unveiled new services to boost mobile phone communications as the nation accelerates its push towards 6G technology . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . U6GHz – the new spectrum for the next generation of mobile connectivity – is expected to enhance the cloud, artificial intelligence, digital experiences and connected environments. The U6GHz band was identified for international mobile telecoms in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, several Asian countries, as well as China, Brazil and Mexico, according to global technology advisory Omdia. U6GHz combines a wide contiguous spectrum bandwidth with characteristics closer to that of existing bands than that of other higher candidate bands, making it the “sweet spot” that balances capacity and coverage, the UK-based research firm said. Placing U6GHz “into the hands of customers … [will be] unlocking new opportunities for consumers, businesses and emerging digital applications”, Saleem Alblooshi, chief technology officer of Dubai-based du, said in a statement. Separately, Abu Dhabi's etisalat said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. The company – which recently rebranded back from e& – is using 2x2 Mimo, a wireless technology that allows the transmission of two data streams between mobile devices and cellular base stations. That new capability is exclusive on compatible smartphones on etisalat UAE’s 5.5G network and will be useful in sending high-resolution photos, videos and large files faster, in addition to harnessing the abilities of AI-powered applications, the company said. “Mobile experiences are changing,” said Marwan bin Shakar, chief technology officer of etisalat UAE. “Smartphones are no longer primarily consuming content – they are creating, sharing and increasingly sending richer data to AI and cloud applications in real time. That changes what we need from the network. By bringing this capability … we are increasing upload capacity where it matters.” Last month, etisalat claimed it had launched the world’s first mobile network operating on U6GHz. Mr bin Shakar said this was key to “accelerating the nation's transition to the 6G era”. Sixth-generation technology , or 6G, will offer faster speeds and data transfers for users of smartphones, tablets, laptops and other devices. Though the announcement does not mean 6G cellular technology has officially arrived, the UAE telecoms company's U6GHz mobile network makes use of several innovations that “elevate the 5G-advanced experience” and pave the way for it to become standard. The announcements from du and etisalat are the latest in a series of developments in the UAE related to the eventual adoption of 6G. Last month, du and Khalifa University said they had carried out field trials for the new technology. In 2024, the UAE's Telecommunications and Digital Regulatory Authority announced plans to allocate 600MHz and 6GHz bands, a move that helped accelerate the development of 6G services in the Arab world's second-largest economy. South Korea's Samsung, one of the world's largest manufacturers of smartphones, has predicted widespread adoption of 6G networks by 2030, with “completion of standards and early commercialisation by 2028".
