events.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
events.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing. The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support. Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark: Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more. The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows. NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport. Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark. Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app. Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta . Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23. The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS.

events.title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology. Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems . —Grace Huckins This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here .  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places. Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out . —Eshan Raul Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from sustainable cement to shipping containers packed with old EV batteries.  The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets Temperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. One more thing A brain implant changed her life. Then it was removed against her will. Sticking an electrode inside a person’s brain can do more than treat a disease. events.title: Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’
events.summary: Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits The new Your First Home programme for first-time buyers could increase the number of houses British builder Bellway produces each year by 10%, its boss has said. Faced with a chronic shortage of homes, the government has made housing one of its top priorities and Andy Burnham’s surprise announcement of the YFH scheme a fortnight ago sent housebuilders’ shares soaring by more than 10%. Jason Honeyman, who has led Bellway since 2017, welcomed the new programme, which will be more targeted than previous help-to-buy initiatives. It features household income caps to exclude those with big salaries, and price caps to ensure people can only buy modest houses. Full details, including the launch date, are expected be announced by John Healey in his first budget as chancellor on 28 October. YFH applies only to England and is for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. They will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price and the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. While the scheme has the potential to “provide significant support for first-time buyers”, it could weigh on the market in the near term, Honeyman said, as some will want to wait for the initiative to be launched. However, he added that it could drive Bellway’s annual completions back to 10,000 homes, in the 12-month period from next September at the earliest. “Based upon our past experience with help to buy, the new scheme has the potential to boost volumes by around 10%, and with a market recovery, provide a path back to at least 10,000 homes a year and a return on equity of 15%,” Honeyman said. Bellway is targeting between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year, ​down from 9,695 ​last year, ‌given a lower order book and “ongoing pressures on customer demand” coupled with higher construction costs, running at between 3% and 4%. It has a forward order book of 4,981 homes worth £1.4bn, compared with 5,285 homes with a value of £1.5bn a year earlier. Bellway also expects the average selling price to be flat over the coming year at about £325,000. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The chief executive’s comments came after the company beat analysts’ expectations with revenue of £3.16bn for the year to 31 August, up 13% from the previous year. This lifted underlying profits before tax by 5.7% to £305.7m. Bellway shares rose 2% on Tuesday but are still down by more than a quarter so far this year. YFH is expected to give a shot in the arm to most big housebuilders, such as Persimmon, MJ Gleeson, Taylor Wimpey and Bellway. However, the upmarket builder Berkeley Group, which is focused on London, where prices are higher, and Vistry Group, which has pivoted towards building affordable and social homes, are not expected to get much help from the initiative.

events.title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
events.summary: Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF). What the IMF says matters – it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world. Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel. Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report. 1. The UK is weathering the Iran war better than expected The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran. The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise. To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months. Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI). And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true. 2. The UK is doing better than other major economies There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this. The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both. By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments. "So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said. Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany. Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context. "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are." While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year. While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest. In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%. "There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot. He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year. events.title: Blackstone-backed AirTrunk delays Singapore REIT IPO amid AI stock sell-off, sources say
events.summary: Data-centre operator AirTrunk was originally planning to launch the IPO in September or October. HONG KONG – Blackstone-backed data-centre operator AirTrunk has postponed a planned Singapore REIT initial public offering (IPO) that could raise about $1.5 billion, two people with direct knowledge of the matter said, as a tech and AI stock sell-off rattles markets. AirTrunk was originally planning to launch the IPO in September or October, but put it on hold because of market conditions, said the people, declining to be named as the information was confidential. AirTrunk has not decided when to launch the offering but is aiming to complete the listing by early 2027 , one of them said. The delay comes as Asian equities slid to more-than-two-month lows on Oct 13 , led by a rout in chipmakers that renewed investor scrutiny of the artificial intelligence trade. AirTrunk, which is owned by US investment firm Blackstone, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Blackstone declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported the delay on Oct 13 . The REIT was expected to be valued at about $15 billion, potentially making it one of South-east Asia’s largest listings in the coming months. The postponement also follows the scrapping of Firmus’ planned IPO, highlighting an increasingly difficult backdrop for large data centre and AI-linked equity offerings as investors reassess valuations, rising borrowing costs and the durability of demand tied to the AI boom. Singapore-based data centre operator DayOne is aiming to launch its US IPO before the midterm elections, Reuters reported in September. REUTERS

events.summary: File photo of a British Airways plane A British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window. Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick. AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert". A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey. "We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said. Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft. Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off. The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet. And in August Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock". Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object. events.title: El Niño supercharges storms, leaving thousands without power in US and Mexico
events.summary: Powerful hurricanes killed several people and left thousands without power in the US and Mexico, as experts warned that this year’s supercharged El Niño risked making storms longer and more destructive. The climate phenomenon, which originates in the Pacific and leads to warmer global temperatures, has upended weather across the world, fueling extraordinary storms in the Americas. “ It’s been berserk, ” an expert told the Associated Press. Elsewhere, however, this year’s record El Niño has been welcome news: Forecasts for a warmer-than-usual winter have eased pressures on European and Asian economies — including some of the world’s biggest LNG importers — which are scrambling to contain soaring winter energy bills as expanding global conflicts drive up fuel prices. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Key watchdogs signal they will step up AI regulation
events.summary: Key watchdogs indicated they would step up regulation of AI, though the technology’s superpowers — the US and China — showed little indication of increasing their own scrutiny. Banking regulators on both sides of the Atlantic were increasingly asking questions of institutions’ use of AI models , fearful the technology could threaten financial stability, Reuters reported, while the Financial Times said the UK’s AI minister was readying proposals for compulsory monitoring of frontier technology . Still, the Trump administration has shown little willingness to step up its oversight of Big Tech, and while Beijing has talked a good game on AI safety, the chip-focused outlet SemiAnalysis wrote recently that “we think China’s real approach to AI safety is speed-based, not safety-based. ” — Prashant Rao

events.title: US house sales drop to 12 year lows as borrowing costs spike
events.summary: US home sales plunged to a 12-year low after mortgage rates topped 7%, driven by soaring global borrowing costs. Increasing energy prices and higher-for-longer inflation expectations have sent debt costs to recent records, with US bond yields touching a 24-year high and European debt climbing to levels not seen in decades. Higher borrowing costs are impacting poorer nations, as well: The UN warned several countries were facing a “ liquidity crisis ” that could push millions into poverty, with developing countries now on average spending 9.5% of government revenues on interest payments, the highest share in a quarter century. “The global economy could soon test the limits of resilience, ” the IMF’s chief economist said. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: AI spending to drive global growth higher, IMF forecasts
events.summary: The global economy will grow more this year than previously expected, the International Monetary Fund said, with booming investment in AI outweighing a fast-growing debt pile — for now. In particular, the IMF said the world’s biggest economies had to take “urgent” action to rebuild their public finances , with deficits at their biggest since the pandemic. “The global economy has been resilient,” a fund economist warned, “ but that resilience is reaching its limits .” — Prashant Rao

events.title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
events.summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. Kerry Nelson, the director of Nexus Independent Financial Advisers Limited and Nexus Investment Managers Limited, and Jacqueline Stephens, the firms' business operations manager, admitted all charges brought by the FCA at Portsmouth Crown Court.They admitted defrauding clients between January 2019 and January 2023 and using false documents as part of the fraud. Nelson has also admitted a money laundering offence after money was withdrawn from the firms, which she used to fund her extravagant lifestyle.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'This was a serious breach of trust. Nelson and Stephens caused significant losses to clients who relied on them. We will continue to act where people exploit clients for their own gain.'Nelson and Stephens will be sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on 10 December 2026. The FCA will seek confiscation proceedings to deprive Kerry Nelson of any financial benefit from her criminal conduct.Notes to editorsThe FCA started criminal proceedings against Kerry Nelson and Jacqueline Stephens in February 2025. For more details see, FCA charges two individuals with multiple fraud charges. They pleaded guilty at Portsmouth Crown Court on 12 October 2026.Fraud by abuse of position is an offence under sections 1 and 4 of the Fraud Act 2006.Using a false instrument is an offence under section 3 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.Converting or transferring criminal property is an offence under section 327(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Confiscation proceedings will be pursued under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Nexus IFA and Nexus IM were authorised by the FCA. Nexus IFA had permissions to provide investment, mortgage and pension advice and Nexus IM to provide discretionary fund management services. Neither firm was permitted to hold or control client money.On 25 January 2023, the FCA imposed restrictions preventing both firms from carrying on regulated activity and from reducing the value of the assets they held. The High Court placed both firms into administration on 26 January 2023.

events.title: Family offices ‘kept captive’ by relationship managers turn to independent advisers, direct deals
events.summary: (From left) Sean Tan and Anupum Khaitan, who co-founded the Private Family Society in August, a community for family office principals, executives and chief investment officers across APAC. Singapore family offices are taking more control of investments, moving away from relationship managers and private banks towards independent advisers and direct deals. Speakers said scale matters: smaller offices often rely on banks, while larger ones act more like fund managers and still need third-party advisers for balance. Family offices are also backing AI more heavily, with Asia-Pacific the most bullish region; some expect AI allocations to rise from 10 to 20 per cent to 30 per cent. SINGAPORE – Family offices in Singapore are taking a more active hand in sourcing their own investment opportunities as the sector becomes increasingly institutionalised. This shift was evident at the Private Family Society’s inaugural event, the AI & Family Office Summit, on Oct 5. The society is an invitation-only community for family office principals, executives and chief investment officers in the Asia-Pacific. It was co-founded in August by Anupum Khaitan, managing principal at advisory firm Sophatych, and Sean Tan, director at business lifestyle firm Bespoke 81. “Some of the pain points that we’ve seen in the family office industry, particularly in Singapore, is that oftentimes, family offices are kept captive by relationship managers and private banks... looking to monetise the next transaction,” said Khaitan. He added: “Information arrives as a pitch, not necessarily as intelligence of what’s the best thing for the families to do.” As at end-2025, the Republic had more than 2,000 single-family offices that receive tax incentives , as reported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Khaitan told The Business Times on the sidelines of the event that allocators across the board are embracing a trend of “going direct”. However, he noted that while many allocators are making direct investments, “as their legacy starts to become more meaningful, performance requires them, at minimum, to also allocate professionally to those who can keep sharp eyes on their investments”. Similarly, Andrew Khoo, executive chairman and CEO of Bursa Malaysia-listed MUI Group, who also helps to manage his family office, noted that while he expects direct investment sourcing to rise as the industry becomes more institutionalised, there is a need for a “balanced approach”. “While there is always going to be direct deal flow based on connections and network opportunities, third-party advisers will continue to play a critical role and (be a source of) where most investment opportunities will arise from,” he said. Yee Tuck Meng, partner at Singapore-based single family office JRT Partners, told BT that the extent of this shift, from siloed operations to institutionalised set-ups, largely depends on a family office’s scale. “(There are) families that run their portfolio like a fund, as opposed to running it like their personal investment portfolio, which is very different,” he said. He noted that smaller operations largely function on an advisory model, where investments are typically executed through private banks. Meanwhile, institutional family offices, which he defined as those that operate “more like fund managers”, largely employ internal teams with discretionary mandates to invest directly or through funds. Beyond using artificial intelligence in their operations, industry players at the AI & Family Office Summit noted that family offices are increasingly allocating capital towards it. However, for Asian family offices, most opportunities to invest in AI are still found in the US, said Yee of JRT Partners during a panel discussion on investment and asset management. This sits at odds with where JRT Partners’ beneficiaries reside: Only two are in the US, while most are in Malaysia, Singapore and Australia, creating an asset-liability mismatch, he noted. “Even if I think that there’s better value in Asia (or) better value in Europe, the reality is, at least in terms of short-term to medium-term... that the weight of money... is still very much in US dollars. “So I, like most of my peers, have overinvested in the US right across the entire tech spectrum,” he said, adding that JRT is invested in SpaceX. “That is good, so far, and that is also very bad when the correction comes, and I don’t know when that correction is at the end of the day.” According to Citi Wealth’s 2026 Global Family Office Report launched on Sept 22, Asia-Pacific’s family offices are the world’s most bullish on AI, with 80 % identifying it as a primary sector of interest for direct investments – the highest of any region. Khoo of MUI Group noted that AI-related investments across the company and his family office have grown steadily over the past five years, to around 10 to 20 % of total allocation. He added that this could go up to 30 % in the future.

events.title: Tencent draws strong demand for US$4.5 billion debt sale, defying AI scrutiny
events.summary: The sale comes as technology firms globally raise billions of dollars to finance AI investments. Tencent drew nearly four times its US$4.5 billion debt target, showing strong investor trust despite worries over AI spending and higher borrowing costs. The company will use the money for general corporate purposes as it keeps investing in AI infrastructure and products, with capital spending more than doubling in the first half of 2026. Demand was strong for both dollar and offshore yuan bonds, with orders far above supply, suggesting capital is still available for AI firms with strong cash flow and clear plans. HONG KONG – Tencent Holdings has received investor demand worth nearly four times the Chinese tech giant’s plan to raise at least US$4.5 billion (S$5.7 billion) via US dollar and offshore yuan debt offerings even as AI spending jitters hit global markets . Tencent plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, according to the deal term sheet, and the latest borrowing comes as the company increases investment in AI infrastructure and products. The sale comes as technology firms globally raise billions of dollars to finance AI investments , although investors have become more selective about companies funding costly AI infrastructure amid elevated borrowing costs. Despite those concerns, investor demand for Tencent’s 10-year and 20-year US dollar notes topped US$5.6 billion, including US$1.4 billion in interest from the joint lead managers, according to an updated term sheet issued on Oct 13 . Order books for the 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan, or dim sum, bonds exceeded 77 billion yuan (S$14.7 billion), the sheet showed. The total demand worth US$17.1 billion is significantly higher than the figure of at least US$4.5 billion that a person with direct knowledge of the deal had told Reuters on Oct 12 the company was looking to raise. The company last tapped the bond market in June, raising about US$4.66 billion through dollar- and yuan-denominated notes. Its return to the bond market so quickly suggests capital remains available for AI, particularly for companies with strong cash flows, balance sheets and credible monetisation plans, said Allspring Global Investments portfolio manager Gary Tan. “We are seeing a more definitive shift in sentiment around the pace of AI spending, as investors increasingly view financing availability and the cost of capital as potential bottlenecks to a further acceleration in AI investment.” Tencent has not responded to a Reuters request for comment on its debt issuance. The deal term sheet did not say how much it was looking to raise via the sale of US dollar and offshore yuan notes. Tencent set initial guidance for the 10-year dollar notes at about 115 basis points over comparable US Treasury bonds. The 20-year notes were set at about 140 basis points over Treasuries, according to the term sheet. It set initial yield guidance at around 2.90% for the 10-year offshore yuan notes and 3.50% for the 30-year notes, the sheets showed. The final coupons for all the bonds are expected to be determined later on Oct 13 , according to the sheets. Tencent’s capital expenditure more than doubled to 96.3 billion yuan in the first half of 2026 from 45.9 billion yuan a year earlier, according to its offering documents. The spending included computing equipment, software and data centres. The bonds are expected to be rated A1 by Moody’s and A+ by S&P. Tencent is rated A1 by Moody’s, A+ by S&P and A by Fitch, according to the term sheet. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and Morgan Stanley are joint global coordinators for Tencent’s dollar bond offering, the sheet showed. ICBC (Asia), Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, CITIC Securities, HSBC and JPMorgan are coordinating the offshore yuan sale, according to the sheet. events.title: Xi’s ‘death watch’ will become a global spectacle
events.summary: Andy’s view The Australian sinologist Geremie R. Barmé wrote that “autocrats and patriarchs share a fateful dilemma”: Once in power “the countdown to their demise is on.” Mao Zedong’s long descent into ill health and madness brought China to the brink of civil war. Deng Xiaoping went out peacefully, though the decade before he died was marked by political upheavals, including the Tiananmen Square protests. Now, the Xi Jinping “death watch” has begun. Of course, the big difference is that today China is at the center of everything. As it drags on, the Xi “death watch” will become a global spectacle, moving markets, affecting investment flows, and shaping defense priorities. China’s internal risks are now the world’s risks. Xi’s physical condition is one thing. At 73, he’s visibly slowing; he looked fragile descending the stairs of his plane at Air Base Andrews when he arrived for a summit with US President Donald Trump last month, clasping the hand of his wife, Peng Liyuan, for support. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese officials made a highly unusual request for a “ hold room ” for Xi at the White House where he could take breaks between meetings, and his talks with Trump were surprisingly brief. But the pressures building inside the Chinese system are largely unseen: Leadership politics, including the health of the top man, are as much a black box today as they were in the Deng era. But we can assume that from now on, everything that happens behind the high red walls of the leadership compound in Beijing will be connected, one way or another, to the vexed issue of how a post-Xi China will be governed. Political transitions are the midnight hour for all autocratic regimes. But Xi’s dilemma is particularly acute: If he names a successor now to carry forward his policies and protect his legacy, he risks triggering a political knife fight years before he’s ready to relinquish power. Wait too long, though, and he creates a dangerous political vacuum. Either way, Xi will have to pick a relative unknown — all the current members of the Politburo Standing Committee are too old to step into his shoes — raising a host of troubling questions. Would a designated successor catapulted to the top be strong enough to command the loyalty of the powerful military? Could he hold the Party together? Or could Xi himself turn on the chosen one? One of Mao’s designated successors, Liu Shaoqi, died of diabetes and pneumonia in solitary confinement, lying in his own filth. Deng cycled through two successors before settling on Jiang Zemin. Xi has grown paranoid about those around him, his ruthless purges targeting some of his oldest, and most trusted, comrades. That doesn’t bode well for any potential second-in-command. China now faces a period of prolonged political uncertainty. Carl Minzner, a US legal scholar and senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, predicted a “ long twilight ” with the economy sagging, social discontent rising, and the state using “grid management” — surveillance techniques used to maintain control over Xinjiang and other restive border areas. A succession struggle is unlikely to remain within China’s borders, Tyler Jost, a professor at Brown University, and Daniel Mattingly of Yale University argued in Foreign Affairs last year, noting that Xi’s prize goal is unification with Taiwan and “if he hears the succession clock ticking, he could become more willing to gamble on war .” I’m betting that the end of the Xi era will look a lot less like Deng’s, whose passing created hardly a ripple — by then, he’d handed over power and put in place a system to ensure smooth leadership transfers — and more like Mao’s, a drama that involved a bloodless coup (the arrest of the so-called “Gang of Four” led by Mao’s widow), intervention by the People’s Liberation Army, and show trials. We had a foretaste of this kind of turmoil when Xi took power in 2012. A carefully constructed power transfer was upended by the arrest of Xi’s main Politburo rival, and there were wild internet rumors of a military coup, tanks in the streets of the Chinese capital, and gunfire near the leadership compound. Xi has wrenched China back to an era of one-man rule. But having attained the pinnacle of power — next year he’ll likely get a fourth five-year term in office — Xi now has to reckon with the consequences for his country. As Deng himself warned, “building a nation’s fate on the reputation of one or two people is very unhealthy and very dangerous. Notable In 2025, during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Beijing, a hot mic picked up a conversation between Putin and Xi in which the two discussed organ transplants and the possibility of living forever. Musing on such procedures, Putin told Xi (through a translator) that with modern technology organs could be transplanted again and again so that “ (you can) even achieve immortality .” While a largely hypothetical conversation, it hinted that staving off old age and death — maybe for eternity — is top of mind among the world’s most powerful autocrats.

events.title: More than 300 scientists say AI oversight needed after 'preventable' hacks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More than 300 scientists call for greater AI security through new international body The open letter says immediate change is needed as future AI-related incidents may expose critical infrastructure. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) More than 300 scientists from across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania are calling for greater AI safety measures in an open letter. The letter gave three recommendations, including establishing an international body to record and publish security incidents caused by AI. The federal government is finalising its national AI standards and plans to legislate new rules in 2027. A group of 350 scientists from more than 30 countries has written an open letter calling for greater AI security by establishing an international body to record and publish security failures due to AI. In several incidents in recent months, both overseas and in Australia, AI models have hacked into the systems of external organisations, including startup Hugging Face and multiple government websites . "[These incidents] can also be seen as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures," the open letter reads. The scientists are from 31 countries, including Australia, and are based across Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, and said that without immediate change, future incidents could expose critical infrastructure. It had three recommendations, including: adopting high-assurance containment systems, and initially defaulting to air-gapping, which means disconnecting from the internet for cyber-capable AI models creating an international body to record and track AI containment failures reporting security incidents to the body and making them public. Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the University of New South Wales AI Institute, was among the signatories and said now was the time to act. "But you can imagine what would happen if an AI [model] was trying to hack into the air traffic control system. It could easily cause significant harms to our day-to-day lives." Safeguards will ensure incidents won't repeat Following the Hugging Face hack, where an AI model broke into the company's systems, OpenAI described it as a "warning shot", saying without proper safeguards AI agents could take "dangerous actions" without human direction. But Professor Walsh said one of the recommendations in the open letter would have prevented the hack entirely. "We wouldn't have had the Medicare hack if they'd been careful about giving the agents minimal permissions for the task it was needed to do. "I mean, these are all incredibly basic things." Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises Are cracks beginning to emerge in the glittery AI facade? White House demands transparency over Anthropic AI's false murder tip-off As One Nation looms over Victoria's election, voters ask chatbots for poll info Professor Walsh said the most important element of the open letter was the creation of an international body to provide both information sharing and oversight of incidents. He said similar bodies existed for industries such as banking, aviation and pharmaceuticals. "Every time there's an aviation accident, independent inspectors go in and find out what happened, so that everyone can learn and not make that same mistake again," he said. "We could do the same with AI because it's advancing rapidly and we need to make it as safe as possible." International cooperation needed to prevent incidents Last week, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton echoed those sentiments surrounding regulating AI similar to banking and aviation in a speech . Regulate AI like banks and airlines The federal government is looking to banking and aviation regulation as it develops laws that would make AI companies demonstrate they can identify and manage risks. The government is finalising its national AI standards, and plans to legislate the new rules next year. But Professor Walsh said there needed to be broad international consensus on AI because the technology was not being developed in isolation. "So we need to cooperate internationally … in terms of perhaps reporting of incidents and sharing of information that doesn't mean that we have to regulate internationally," he said. Cyber security improved after it became a requirement for companies to report incidents, Professor Walsh said. "[Otherwise] no-one knew what was happening and we weren't able to learn from all of the mistakes that companies made," he said.

events.title: Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?
events.summary: The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections There is a manic quality to Donald Trump ’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away. The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested . He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas.) In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere . In the face of such setbacks, maybe Trump felt he had to demonstrate he still can get something done. Still, it is somewhat counterintuitive that the administration, in the shape of Vice-President JD Vance, decided to broadcast the one initiative it did manage to bring to fruition: ejecting more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act (ACA) health insurance marketplaces, on grounds that they are not entitled to federal subsidies. Trump could argue that the cuts fit within the administration’s promised commitment to restore fiscal discipline. But that part of the platform – which came as Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, promised to trim the budget deficit to 3% of US gross domestic product – was never more than a rhetorical feint. The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees by Trump’s “fraud taskforce”, by contrast, looks a lot like political madness, given the persistent economic anxieties articulated by Democratic and Republican voters across the country. The savings from the ACA maneuver, estimated by the administration at $2.2bn per year, are chump change compared to the centerpiece of Trump’s fiscal policy – the One Big Beautiful Bill Act from 2025 that is expected to add $4.1tn to budget deficits over the next decade, largely due to tax cuts benefiting the most affluent Americans. Pace Bessent, the budget deficit is growing rapidly, expected to rise to some $2tn in the fiscal year of 2026, roughly 6% of GDP and some 18% more than in fiscal 2024, the last year of the Biden administration. Rather than stem budgetary red ink, it’s as if Trump’s objective is to spread misery beyond the 3 million Americans who had to drop their health insurance after the administration last year cancelled subsidies offered by the Biden administration. The effort is something out of the playbook of Elon Musk’s Doge . His promise to rid the government of “waste” and “fraud” probably caused the deaths of millions of children in the developing world after the dismantling of USAID, but proved largely irrelevant to the task of saving money for the government. It may serve as a masterclass in trolling. But it is not a vote-winner. Part of Trump’s brain seems to understand this. Trump paid in part for the “beautiful” bill’s colossal tax cut by cutting funding to Medicaid and the Snap food stamp program for low-income Americans. But he engineered most of the cuts to kick in after the midterms to minimize the political cost. The thinking was that lower-income Americans would happily vote for the Republicans out of gratitude for their somewhat bigger tax refund checks this year and tax breaks for overtime and tips (cleverly designed to expire at the end of Trump’s term) and not notice the cuts rushing down the pike on federal programs they relied on. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning But the new evictions from the ACA suggest that his brain’s darker side is winning. Indeed, it underscores Trump’s belief that hitting poor people might work for him. Rather than a commitment to sound fiscal policy, a helping hand for American families treading water or an economic platform of any kind, Trump’s latest exercise in “fraud prevention” points to a strategy revolving around punishing people he can define as “bad”. Deep underwater in the polls for his nutty stewardship of the economy, among other things, Trump seems to believe that his one remaining winning card is to do violence against constituencies that his base may not like. Top of the list are immigrants and low-income people. And so it is that ICE is also doubling down, announcing it will hire another 5,000 agents by the end of the year. The president is on to something.

events.title: Germany scrambles jets after airline radio glitch sends false hijack alert
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Germany's Nuremberg Airport reopens after glitch causes hijack alert An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( AP: Tizian Gerbing ) An aviation emergency has halted flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system". The airport said flight operations have returned to normal. One of Germany's biggest international airports says that flight operations have resumed after they were suspended following an aviation emergency. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system", according to the airline. Corendon Airlines said it wanted to "emphasise that no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger". The incident forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, where the plane was planned to land, the airport said. Flight operations later returned to normal. "From the cockpit, the code '7500' (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio," police said earlier on X. "For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered." The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet flying from Dubai to Israel attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe. An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( Reuters: Michaela Rehle ) The airline said the emergency code had been transmitted on Tuesday while the plane, a Boeing 737-800, was in Croatian airspace "due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system". "The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made. The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport," it said. An airport spokesperson had no additional information. Crash axe used in flydubai attack on pilot The co-pilot who allegedly attempted to down a flydubai plane had been barred from flying in his home country of Oman. German authorities have also been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia. A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday, the airport said in a separate statement. Three pilots independently reported an object they had seen during take-off or landing, the German media outlet Bild reported. An airport spokesperson said six flights were delayed and two inbound flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution. Authorities across Europe have stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks amid an increasing number of mostly mysterious drone incidents. Germany says Russia responsible for Leipzig airport drone attack Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that after assessing the technology used and other intelligence information "the government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack". In August, a drone disrupted flights overnight at Hanover Airport, located in northern Germany. The incident came a week after an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport . Runways at the airport were closed for 90 minutes before normal operations resumed. The Der Spiegel weekly, citing an internal police report, reported that "the possibility of a hybrid activity cannot be excluded". The drone went undetected by authorities and airport staff, flying freely for about two hours. German authorities use the term "hybrid attack" to describe a wide range of incidents — including sabotage and espionage as well as propaganda operations — that have increased since the start of the war in Ukraine and are mostly blamed on Russia. According to the magazine, the police report concludes that it is "currently impossible" to link the Hanover incident to the explosive drone found at Leipzig Airport. Following the Leipzig incident, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned of "a new dimension of threat" and mentioned a potential "hybrid attack scenario" without blaming anyone or any state in particular. Germany has become Ukraine's leading military backer in Europe following the 2022 Russian invasion.

events.title: UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
events.summary: Price of chocolates falls in run-up to Halloween, while supermarkets use special offers to draw in sales Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween. Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said. Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets. “More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances. Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.” However, in some good news for households stocking up on trick or treat supplies for Halloween, chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago. About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee. McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike. “After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.” While sales of hot chocolate and soup surged in September compared with August, by 41% and 35% respectively, they fell sharply when compared with last year, by 20% and 4% respectively. A separate report from NielsenIQ showed total till sales at major UK supermarkets grew 1.4% in the four weeks to 3 October, down from 1.8% growth in the previous month, as shoppers remain cautious about spending. Summer favourites remained popular as September was unusually warm this year, with strong sales of mineral water (+17.4%) and ice-cream (+11.7%). Asda was the only big grocer to report a drop in sales, of 0.5%, in the 12 weeks to 4 October, Worldpanel said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The German discounter Lidl led in market share gains and now controls 8.6%, on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine. Sales at the online grocer Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing online sales across the sector at 5.5%. Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively. Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year. Beyond the supermarkets, grocery sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.9%.

events.title: Alibaba unveils US$450 AI glasses in expanding push into gadgets
events.summary: With prices starting at 2,999 yuan (S$573) before discounts, they are no cheaper than industry leader Meta Platforms’s Ray-Ban smart glasses. Alibaba launched new Qwen Glasses N1 smart glasses in Hangzhou, deepening its push into consumer gadgets as part of its wider AI strategy. The glasses start at 2,999 yuan and include better cameras, sensors, eye-tracking on the Pro model, and up to 25 hours of standby time. Alibaba wants the glasses to be a gateway to Qwen AI tools, with features for shopping, payments and health tracking, and has also launched Qwen Clip AI earbuds. HANGZHOU – Alibaba Group Holding on Oct 13 unveiled the new generation of its smart glasses, deepening its foray into consumer electronics as an extension of its artificial intelligence strategy. The company, which models itself as China’s full-stack AI provider spanning everything from data centres and software to end-user products, detailed its new Qwen Glasses N1 series at an event in Hangzhou. With prices starting at 2,999 yuan (S$573) before discounts, they are no cheaper than industry leader Meta Platforms’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, showing Alibaba’s effort to compete on quality and features rather than just price. Mirroring Meta’s strategy, Alibaba is endeavouring to turn smart glasses into an entry point for its AI tools and agents. In September , Meta expanded its line-up of smart glasses with a simplified, camera-free model priced at US$349 (S$446) , designed primarily for interaction with the new Muse AI assistant. The new Alibaba glasses include improved 50-megapixel cameras and sensors, with a Pro edition priced at 3,499 yuan featuring new eye-tracking functions, said Wu Jianjun, general manager of Qwen AI hardware products. The new glasses will offer 25 hours of standby time or nine hours of music playback from one charge, Alibaba said. Coming roughly a year after November’s first edition, the new glasses more tightly integrate Alibaba’s Qwen AI assistant and expand on its functionality. Users will be able to speak to the AI agent via bone-conduction microphones, and the glasses also support shopping functions, payments and health tracking. In September , Alibaba chief executive officer Eddie Wu reiterated the company’s ambition to develop all-stack AI, from large language models and chatbot apps to AI chips and hardware. To provide a more affordable way to access Qwen, Alibaba also started sales of its new AI earbuds named Qwen Clip. These were jointly developed with headphone maker Bose and are priced at 1,299 yuan. events.title: IMF warns UK of risk of inflation ahead of government’s first budget
events.summary: The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday. The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget. It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies , said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023. “The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported. Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported. The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported. The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal. Energy crisis Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter. The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy. Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility. Inflation impact In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back. The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month. Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned. “Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels. The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added. “The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs. “Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.” Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said. The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

events.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
events.summary: Alex Gibney’s Musk Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says. Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk , which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed. “Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.” Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies. Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film. I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today. This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk , Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film? Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character. I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it. One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do. By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him. I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and … It is kind of a two-day growth of beard. Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was? It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually. Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices. That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made. When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens. I think it really worked for the film.

The eight-storey mixed-use site in Singapore has commercial shops, homes and an open terrace, with 999-year leasehold and approval for serviced apartments. It is the third collective sale attempt after failed bids in 2018 and 2019, though ETC says its location near schools could support hospitality and co-living uses. SINGAPORE – Mixed-used development Beauty World Plaza is up for sale again at $165 million, or $2,231 per sq ft of gross floor area, said real estate advisory firm ETC on Oct 13. The eight-storey property stands on a 24,817 sq ft site, with commercial shops on the first three floors, flats above and an open terrace on the fourth floor. It was built in the early 1980s and has 61 retail and 30 residential units. The 999-year leasehold development site is zoned for commercial and residential use, and has a gross plot ratio of 3 under the Urban Redevelopment Authority Master Plan 2025 . Preliminary approval has been granted for serviced apartments to be developed in the residential component of the development, which could accommodate about 108 keys, based on a minimum unit size of 35 sq m, said ETC. “Beyond a conventional redevelopment play, the buyer can also consider asset enhancement for the existing development,” said Swee Shou Fern, head of investment advisory at ETC. “The property’s proximity to educational institutions enhances its potential for hospitality, serviced apartment, co-living and other accommodation concepts catering to academia.” ETC, the sole marketing agent, is conducting the sale through a public tender exercise, which closes at 3pm on Nov 19. The development’s second attempt at a sale en bloc in mid-2019 at an unchanged reserve price of $165 million failed to draw any takers. Its first bid was in November 2018. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
events.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla . And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones?
