events.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
events.summary: Why Germany is backing tougher EU trade defenses against China Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base. Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices. In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate. Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue. Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week. Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent . Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026. Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries. Why Berlin's China policy is changing German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025. Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures . In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports. "After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW. Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments." Industry pressure grows for trade defenses Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt: "We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August. According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026. While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home. Business groups question industrial policy proposals The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies. Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory. How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials? The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally." Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

events.title: Market turns cold on luxury after LVMH’s China letdown
events.summary: LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue. LVMH’s weaker-than-expected quarterly fashion and leather goods sales, hit by a deterioration in Chinese consumer demand for its flagship Louis Vuitton brand, have raised fresh doubts about the luxury industry’s recovery prospects. Four sell-side analysts have cut their target price on LVMH shares by an average 9% following the results, the first quarterly report by a major sector player, expecting the miss to also signal weak performance at some of its competitors. LVMH shares were down 1.5% by 7.30am GMT ( 3.30pm Singapore time) . Its peers Hermes, Kering and Richemont were down by a similar degree. Europe’s leading luxury groups, mired in a three-year slowdown, have lost around €330 billion ( S$472.79 billion ) in market value since the start of 2026 , with LVMH alone shedding roughly 40%. “Despite the recent share price weakness, we expect some further pressure on the space as a whole today, with confirmation that the Chinese cluster seems to have taken a material (and bigger than feared) step down”, JPMorgan analysts said in a note to clients. LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue, missing expectations in a Visible Alpha consensus for a 1.8% decline. The group said a “less buoyant environment” in China impacted its revenues, contributing to 1% organic sales growth overall, excluding currency swings, to €18.5 billion, below expectations for 1.3% growth. Asked about Louis Vuitton’s recovery prospects in a call with analysts, the group’s Chief Financial Officer Cecile Cabanis said: “It takes a bit of time, but I don’t think there are a lot of shortcuts here”. Adding to investor concerns, growth in LVMH’s watches and jewellery division, home to brands including Bulgari and Tiffany, slowed to 6% from 9% in the first half of 2026 , marking a changing trend in one of luxury’s few bright spots. events.title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’
events.summary: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’ John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain. Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. “The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.” Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok. Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January . But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”. In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.” The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July . UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise. However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%. Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer. The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets. The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher. Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive. “There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said. The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year. It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs. Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter. A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

events.title: What to know about the Nord Stream pipeline explosions trial opening in Germany this week
events.summary: A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago BERLIN -- A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War. The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors . The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies. While international observers initially blamed Moscow, there are now increasing suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. According to German privacy rules, the suspect will be identified in court only as Serhii K., although he was publicly named as Serhii Kuznietsov in extradition proceedings in Italy . Here's what we know about the alleged ringleader of the attack and one of the most politically charged court cases of wartime sabotage that will be heard at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg starting this Wednesday. The explosions on Sept. 26, 2022, damaged pipelines that were built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that set off from the German port of Rostock. It had been hired from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The suspect allegedly organized and carried out the detonation of at least four bombs between 14 and 27 kilograms (around 31 to 62 pounds) at a depth of 70 to 80 meters (230 feet to 263 feet) near the Danish island of Bornholm. He was detained in August in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow where he was staying with his family. Police said he surrendered without resistance. He was extradited to Germany in November. A second suspect was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. He has applied for asylum in Croatia to fight his extradition to Germany. The pipelines were long a target of criticism by the U.S. and some of its allies, which warned that they increased dependence on Russian gas. Russian officials, however, have claimed that U.S. and British intelligence agencies were involved in staging the explosions, which Moscow declared “an act of international terrorism,” and have launched their own investigation. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Russia has also accused NATO of involvement in the attack, while several Western countries initially blamed Russia. More recently, the Kremlin has expressed hope that those who orchestrated the explosions will be held accountable. Asked what Moscow expects from the trial, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that “we expect objectivity.” “We expect … that both the perpetrators and those who ordered it will be named. That would be very important. I think no one doubts who it really is,” Peskov said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts. He also told reporters in August that Ukraine’s prosecutors and Foreign Ministry were already cooperating with partners and that Kyiv was “absolutely open to joint steps on the investigation,” stressing the importance of keeping Europe’s trust. Nonetheless, “all the evidence points very clearly to the fact that Ukraine blew up the Nord Stream pipelines, not the Russians, whom they initially tried to pin the blame on,” says Joachim Weber, a security expert at the Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies at the University of Bonn. “This is, of course, highly explosive politically, because, as is well known, Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies, supporting the country on a massive scale with huge sums of money and also by taking on considerable political risks,” Weber said.

events.title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
events.summary: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments. Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not. Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work. I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness. You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit. You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged. It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July. You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way. A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September. The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600. I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss. You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record. Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively? The small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French. Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted. The experience here echoes that of author Tansy Hoskins, whose latest book, Charity Shop World , paints a picture of a charity retail sector in crisis. She spent 16 months working in a London charity shop, sorting through “daily avalanches” of clothing, which swamped “all the other categories put together”. Everyone Hoskins interviewed said similar: “quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste.” The problem is nationwide. Since the book came out, she’s “been contacted by managers of charity shops around the country – for example, Nottingham, Accrington, Newcastle – all saying that most of what they’re getting is waste.” It is, of course, our waste. According to Jose Baladron of Traid, which has 12 shops across London, shopping for new clothes is “through the roof – the UK is the highest consumer of clothing in Europe by far ”. “That obviously translates to more donations, which is far too much to process in small shops.” Hoskins routinely found that ultra-fast-fashion donations would “still have tags on – it was clear people had received their online purchases and gone, ‘What the hell is this?’ It wasn’t even wearable so they’d just donate it.” On average, charity shops only manage to sell about 25% of clothing donations, according to Baladron (a figure replicated by a University of Southampton study ). “So they rely heavily on the ragman” to shift the rest. Yet the price of rag has “plummeted”, according to Merryn Haines-Gadd of the environmental action charity Wrap, “due to the saturation of low-quality fast fashion”. Ten years ago, a charity might have been paid 50-60p per kilo. “Now you’re lucky to get 10p,” says Baladron. Plus there’s only so much the ragman can take. For anything they can’t take, charity shops have to pay to have it collected as waste. At St Raphael’s, some of that has included, according to Worley, saucepans with food still in the bottom, babies’ soiled sleep-suits and used sanitary products. “[Staff] can get a bit worn down when people are donating stuff that isn’t saleable,” says Libby Gordon, CEO of Fara, which has 39 charity shops in London. “Plus there’s a time cost for us to process it all.” Factor in rising utility costs and national insurance payments, and “charity shops are in a perfect storm”, says Hoskins. In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its 651 stores; its latest accounts indicate that its retail arm lost £3.3m last year. Cancer Research is part-way through a 190-shop closure programme, and rumours are swirling that up to 100 Oxfam shops might close (which the charity has denied ). Some are fighting back. Fara’s new in-store poster campaign advises would-be donators: “If you’d be happy to give it to a friend, we’d be delighted to receive it.” Items should be “clean, complete, and in good condition” , states their online guide . But just as people “wish cycle” by chucking unrecyclables into the recycling, so do people “wish give”. I certainly struggle to accept that something with life left in it, however worn, can’t be useful to someone. This mentality, however, creates unpleasant work and costs for charities – even more so when people leave donations outside a closed charity shop (technically, it’s fly-tipping, and charity shops do often check their CCTV, record numberplates and report such crimes). These bags are often soiled by foxes or dogs, ripped open and/or rained on. At St Raphael’s, staff have found soiled mattresses, ripped sofas and even an old toilet dumped outside: “It leaves us with a big problem,” says Worley. Disposal at scale is an expensive business.

events.title: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China
events.summary: Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa won approval from the People’s Bank of China to prepare a domestic bank card clearing business, after seeking entry since 2017. The firm must finish preparatory work within one year before applying for a licence, joining Mastercard and American Express in China’s huge payments market. The move ends a long trade dispute issue, but Visa faces a market now dominated by Alipay and WeChat Pay, with 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation in 2025. BEIJING – Visa received approval to begin preparations to establish a domestic bank card clearing business in China, as the firm follows rivals Mastercard and American Express in serving the country’s massive payments market. “We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” Visa chief executive Ryan McInerney said in the statement. The company’s Beijing unit won the green-light from the People’s Bank of China, the official Xinhua News Agency reported on Oct 13. It must complete preparatory work within one year before applying to commence operations and obtaining the clearing business licence, Xinhua added. Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion (S$184 trillion) payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa applied for the licence in 2017, local media reported. Competitor Mastercard received approval to establish its bank card clearing business in 2020, and Amex’s joint venture in the country was approved to start bank card clearing services several months after that. For years, the battle for entry into China’s massive domestic clearing market was a primary friction point in the broader trade dispute between the world’s two largest economies. Earlier in 2026, US President Donald Trump said he brought up Visa’s request for access to China’s market during a meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing . Visa’s CEO McInerney accompanied Trump on that May trip to China. Xi later met his counterpart in Washington in late September, with both agreeing on a trade truce extension . The two are scheduled to talk again in person on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November. China first signalled an opening in the sector in June 2015, announcing that foreign bank card clearing providers could apply for licences by establishing local units or through acquisitions. The move was designed to dismantle the longstanding monopoly held by state-run China UnionPay. While the approval marks a significant milestone, Visa is entering a market that looks very different from the one it first sought to enter. China’s payments ecosystem is now dominated by domestic mobile platforms Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have largely bypassed traditional card networks and become the primary channels for everyday transactions. China had 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation at the end of 2025, with transaction value totalling 963.6 trillion yuan (S$184 trillion) in 2025, according to the People’s Bank of China. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Cost of living struggles inspire 'social supermarket'
events.summary: Thomas Cliffe and Laura Steele welcomed customers into the store for the first time on Monday Published 13 October 2026, 06:32 BST "Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy." Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity". Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets. Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store. Newcastle's first 'social supermarket' Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety. Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support. "It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'" "We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills." Cheryl Peeper found that the store was helpful to keep her ticking over to the next big shop without spending to much. The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday. Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices. "It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said. Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed. "One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000." "There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said. Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant". "The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said. Fiona Morris was one of the first to purchase items from the store. Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets , external backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity. But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity." The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table. Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming. After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff. "It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said. events.title: Singapore firm eyes hub in Japan for start-up talent in Asia
events.summary: Insignia Ventures Partners’ Yinglan Tan said the academy will train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to bridge the two regions. Insignia Ventures Partners and Iwate Prefecture plan a start-up academy in north-eastern Japan to train talent from South-east Asia and Japan and link the two regions. Yinglan Tan and Governor Takuya Tasso are due to sign an agreement in Morioka, but the opening date has not yet been decided. Iwate hopes the project will boost regional revival and offset ageing, while the site in Hanamaki may need housing, transport and renovation support. SINGAPORE – A Singaporean venture capital firm is planning to launch an academy in north-eastern Japan in partnership with a local Japanese government to develop start-up talent in and around Asia, according to sources familiar with the project. Insignia Ventures Partners and the Iwate prefectural government are crafting a plan to create a start-up hub in Iwate Prefecture by drawing international talent into the broader Tohoku region – a development the two sides hope will lead to increased investment in Japan by fast-growing South-east Asian economies. Yinglan Tan, founding managing partner of Insignia Ventures Partners, and Iwate Governor Takuya Tasso are scheduled to sign an agreement for the project on the sidelines of the Iwate International Convention, set to take place from Oct 29 to Oct 30 in Morioka, the prefectural capital. However, the two sides have yet to decide on a date to open the hub. Founded in 2017, Insignia Ventures Partners has invested in more than 90 companies in Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore and Taiwan, among other markets, and manages $1 billion in assets. The firm and the Iwate government started talks on the project after Tan and Tasso met during the Summer Davos forum in Dalian, north-eastern China, in 2024. Tan said the academy aims to train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to serve as a bridge between the two regions by combining knowledge of Japanese business culture with an understanding of the diversity of South-east Asian markets. According to prefectural officials, Iwate hopes the project will spur regional revitalisation and ease the impact of its ageing population. The facility will serve as the Iwate campus of the Insignia Ventures Academy, which is based in Singapore. According to the plan, the Iwate campus would offer in-person programmes. Insignia Ventures Partners reports that the Singapore academy has produced more than 250 graduates through its 12-week core programme on venture investment fundamentals. Graduates have joined portfolio companies or launched businesses, and the Iwate campus would be its first base outside Singapore. According to Iwate officials, the planned site of the academy is in Hanamaki, which is south of Morioka. The Iwate government plans to sell the 41,900 sq m Towa High School property, which closed in 2010, to the Singaporean firm. The Iwate government is considering earmarking renovation subsidies for the project, the officials said. Serving as a transportation hub in the Tohoku region, Hanamaki features Iwate Hanamaki Airport, Shin-Hanamaki Station on the Tohoku Shinkansen Line and the Tohoku Expressway. Tomokazu Sugawara, the executive director of the Management Support Division of the Iwate prefectural government, addressed the host prefecture’s need to develop accommodation and transportation for prospective students and faculty. “We recognise the need for such infrastructure so that instructors and students can travel from Singapore and other parts of the world to stay at the school,” Sugawara said. events.title: NVIDIA Lands in Europe for GTC Berlin
events.summary: NVIDIA is in Europe, showcasing the future of technology together with the region’s developers, researchers and industry leaders. It all leads up to NVIDIA GTC Berlin, taking place October 20-22. This is the place to find the latest — stay tuned for rolling coverage of the events and news. October 12 – 24, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers NVIDIA Brings Build-a-Claw to the Heart of Paris On the afternoon before NVIDIA's France Ecosystem Reception, hundreds of developers gathered at Pavillon Vendôme to build physical AI — and get a surprise visit from NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Pavillon Vendôme sits just off Place Vendôme in the 1st arrondissement — one of the most storied addresses in Paris. On Tuesday afternoon, it was full of claws. NVIDIA’s Build-a-Claw came to France with developers from the nation’s startup community and big companies alike packing into the pavilion. The excited crowd was lined up around the block to try their hands (and brains) at building AI-powered robotic claw machines using open models and NVIDIA’s platform. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang dropped in on the robotic fun chatting with the crowds inside and outside, and showing off NVIDIA DGX Spark and RTX Spark AI computing powerhouse machines. “The world’s first computers that unite all the software the world has ever created,” Huang said. Huang then raffled off one of each of the machines, signing the DGX Spark and handing out an autographed “IOU” for the wildly popular RTX machine, since it’s sold out at the moment. The crowd of developers did not miss a beat, claws were waiting, and went back to building. The Paris Build-a-Claw was NVIDIA's second event of the day, after a morning Build-a-Claw in Barcelona drew another big crowd at the Palacio de Pedralbes. He next headed to the nearby Salle des Tirages for an evening ecosystem reception with France's AI leaders. A single day, and already there is a sense of the huge excitement and ambition across the tech ecosystem in both countries. More news, and more countries to come. At GTC Berlin’s First Stop, Barcelona’s Builders Put Physical AI to Work Before NVIDIA's keynote in Berlin, the road to GTC began in Barcelona — with a royal palace, hundreds of developers and a very particular kind of robot. The Palacio de Pedralbes sits at the edge of Barcelona on land that once belonged to the Spanish royal family. On Tuesday morning, it belonged to builders. NVIDIA's Build-a-Claw brought together hundreds of developers, researchers and AI enthusiasts from across Spain and Europe for a morning of hands-on AI at the historic site. Using open models and NVIDIA's platform, participants built robotic claw machines capable of picking up objects — physical AI, made from scratch, in a few hours. The crowd was rapt as it watched robotic arms perform grasping tasks, learn from their own failures and improve over the span of time it takes to eat breakfast. For the crowd on hand it was an example of how to build and train robots using open models not just quickly, but safely and securely, something Spain's developer community is embracing. events.title: From Earth to Orbit, France’s Ecosystem Delivers Agentic Computing at Scale With NVIDIA
events.summary: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in France’s Startups Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack. NVIDIA has been investing in France’s startup ecosystem, having previously invested in leading technology companies including Alice&Bob, Gradium and Scintil Photonics . Across all of Europe, NVIDIA has committed nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Doctolib, Entalpic , Genesis AI and Pigment . These startups are innovating to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI and business planning. Doctolib , a European healthcare technology company, builds agents that free up healthcare professionals to deliver better care, while providing patients with a digital health companion that improves access to care and supports more preventive, continuous medicine. Entalpic , a Paris-based startup, accelerates the engineering of advanced materials at the atomic scale, with particular expertise in surfaces and interfaces for semiconductor manufacturing and next-generation electronics. Genesis AI is a global robotics company developing general-purpose robots with frontier intelligence and capabilities through its foundation models, data collection systems, simulation infrastructure and robot hardware. Pigment , a Paris-based enterprise software company, builds a planning platform that helps businesses forecast performance, model scenarios and make decisions across finance, sales, workforce and operations. France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks , a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space , the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit. NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement , making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA. Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries. events.title: NutryFarm shareholders demand CEO’s immediate suspension, CFO to take over in interim
events.summary: The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended on the SGX since April 11, 2022. On Oct 9, shareholders holding at least 10% of paid-up capital asked to remove Niu from the board and all group roles, and to consider Charlie In as CEO. NutryFarm is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. The row comes as the company stays suspended from trading, despite leaving judicial management in February. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to oust NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have stepped up their demands, calling for his immediate suspension and the appointment of the company’s chief financial officer as interim CEO. The former durian distributor said in an Oct 12 stock exchange filing that it had received an urgent demand notice from shareholders identifying themselves as acting on behalf of the group seeking a special general meeting. Their demands included suspending Niu as CEO and executive director, and appointing the current CFO to temporarily lead the company. NutryFarm’s notice did not name the CFO, but filings on the exchange show that Derek Ong Chee Beng, 60, was appointed group financial controller on June 8. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the notice and seeking legal advice. It also did not detail the grounds for suspension or announce any management changes. The Oct 12 demand follows several letters concerning Niu’s position at the firm and his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder. On Oct 9, shareholders identifying themselves as holding at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital requested a special general meeting to remove Niu from the board as well as his appointments across the group. They also sought to elect shareholder Charlie In as a director, and asked the board to consider appointing In as CEO. In another Oct 9 letter, the shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from executive positions and his recusal from board discussions and voting on the matter. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations, which its announcement did not detail. The company subsequently received an objection to Niu’s proxy voting rights granted by shareholder Jia Lijie, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement, on Oct 11. Under a share pledge arrangement, Niu has a deemed interest in NutryFarm through Jia’s 21.7 million shares and another 13.3 million belonging to Cheng Meng, according to the company’s 2024 annual report. Including his own 360,000 shares, his direct and deemed interest in the company is 25.72%. Niu also has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to place NutryFarm under judicial management in June 2022 . He became executive director and CEO in December that year. The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended since April 11, 2022 .

events.title: Jardine Matheson raises 2026 earnings guidance as high as US$5.65 per share
events.summary: Jardine Matheson raised its 2026 EPS guidance to US$5.50-US$5.65, above its earlier US$5.33 estimate, as portfolio performance improved. It bought Balfour Beatty’s 50% stake in Gammon Construction for £250 million, becoming sole owner. The deal should be “modestly accretive” from year one. Gammon will strengthen Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure, which aims to grow through targeted M&A. CEO Lincoln Pan wants to double JE&I earnings across Asia. SINGAPORE – Jardine Matheson expects its 2026 earnings per share (EPS) to come in between US$5.50 and US$5.65, reflecting stronger than previously expected portfolio performance , it said on Oct 13. The company, which previously expected EPS of about US$5.33, said the new range will be a 3% to 6% increase over its 2025 EPS when adjusted for disposals and reclassifications that year. Jardine Matheson on Oct 13 also said that it has acquired a 50% stake in Gammon Construction from Balfour Beatty, making it the sole owner, for £250 million (S$423.2 million). The cash will be paid in three tranches: at completion on Oct 13 , on Dec 31, 2027, and on Dec 29, 2028. The transaction is expected to be “modestly accretive” from its first year, said Jardine Matheson, adding that pricing is not subject to post-closing adjustments. The company will also acquire the Gammon Construction business inclusive of all future dividend entitlements and cash on balance sheet. Gammon Construction, an Asian construction and engineering company operating primarily in Hong Kong and Singapore, “enhances growth and scale for Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure (JE&I)”, said Jardine Matheson, which has been a Gammon investor since 1969. JE&I combines the wholly owned Jardine Engineering Corporation and Gammon Construction with two joint venture assets, Jardine Schindler and Hactl, into a new platform. It is led by Kevin O’Brien, former chief executive of Gammon Construction and Jardine Engineering Corporation, and has plans for growth supported by “targeted” mergers and acquisitions – starting with Gammon Construction. O’Brien said he expects a “significant opportunity” for Gammon to continue its growth trajectory through capturing broader regional growth trends, including demand from artificial intelligence for supporting infrastructure, energy and sustainable solutions and accelerating industrialisation across Asia. Lincoln Pan, CEO of Jardine Matheson, said: “Our goal remains doubling the earnings of JE&I in the coming years by focusing on strategic investments that expand controlled earnings and capabilities across Asia.”

events.title: ACCC takes egg 'cartel' to court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACCC takes civil action against egg companies for alleged cartel behaviour Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Sunny Queen is alleged to have breached competition laws. ( Facebook: Sunny Queen Farms ) The ACCC has launched legal action against 12 egg producers and suppliers, alleging they coordinated on production and supply decisions. The consumer watchdog alleges "widespread anti-competitive conduct" has affected egg supply in Australia since at least 2020. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen, Australia's largest egg supplier, has denied all allegations. Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers, alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour. Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since 2020. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions. The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it. The legal filing comes more than a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi. The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years". ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers. "When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition, so lower prices," she told Victorian Country Hour. "Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together … consumers can ultimately miss out. Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the ACCC is concerned consumers could miss out on lower prices. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco. The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia. The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies. The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it. "We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations. "Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said. The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts. Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie have been contacted for comment. Sunny Queen is one of 12 egg producers named in the Federal Court matter. ( Supplied ) It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017. A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions. "It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. "It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making.

events.title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Arab world's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

events.title: S’pore investors take stock risks abroad, but why not at home? SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee weighs in
events.summary: SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well-supported in Singapore. Singapore investors take risks overseas, but SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee says local shares still lack liquidity and sustained demand, so investors stay cautious at home. Koh says Singapore may need more capital injections, including the $6.5 billion EQDP, but warns these are not a natural, lasting flow like pension-backed markets in the US. He says Singapore must support more start-ups and growth firms, or they will keep listing overseas, which weakens local capital recycling and slows long-term economic growth. SINGAPORE – Singapore investors are willing to take risks on volatile growth stocks overseas, but are unlikely to make similar bets here, where the local market still lacks flow and liquidity, said Singapore Exchange chairman Koh Boon Hwee. The problem, in his view, is that the Republic has yet to create a level of sustained demand for local shares that gives investors enough confidence to take risks here, and, until then, further capital injections will be needed to sustain demand in the stock market. Koh was speaking to The Straits Times on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 8. “Do they here have the appetite for risk? The answer is yes,” he said, pointing to younger investors who buy overseas stocks such as Tesla and even SpaceX, which is loss-making. But would they back similar businesses on SGX? “My honest answer is, right now it’s unlikely, because they understand the constraints here as well,” he said. This could help explain why many initial public offerings on the local bourse have recently struggled to gain traction after listing, despite efforts by the central bank, the stock exchange and fund managers to revive the local equities market and attract new listings. Asked whether Singapore would need continued capital injections in the meantime, Koh said “personally, I would think so”, but noted that the decision was beyond him. While he commended the Government’s move to allocate $6.5 billion of investment capital to the local stock market through the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP), he noted that it is a “stochastic injection, and not a natural flow”. He distinguished such injections from the regular and sustained capital flows that pension systems generate in other countries. In the United States, for example, multiple pension funds make independent investment decisions and help circulate capital through the public markets, private equity and venture capital. An allocation under the EQDP, by contrast, leaves the question of what follows after the money has been committed. “You have to think about how much more for how much longer,” Koh said. While he stressed that the EQDP funds are being invested rather than spent, he noted that the wider concern is that the repeated allocations do not establish the recurring demand flows needed to sustain the market. “Our challenge right now is to create something that is circular and sustainable,” said Koh. “If you don’t have constant demand creation, it’s hard to sustain liquidity. And with no liquidity, there is no proper valuation.” Convincing investors to recycle capital here Koh explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well-supported in Singapore, but these investors eventually need a way to realise their investments and recycle the capital into other start-ups and ventures. A public listing can provide that route, but for it to work, the market needs investors willing to buy into a company’s next stage of growth. Without an attractive domestic market, founders must consider overseas listings to fulfil their obligations to their backers, regardless of how committed they are to Singapore. Several prominent Singapore-funded companies have already taken that path over the years. Sea, the parent of e-commerce platform Shopee and gaming business Garena, for example, listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2017, while Grab debuted on Nasdaq in 2021 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company. Singapore-headquartered data centre operator DayOne is now pursuing a similar route, having filed for a proposed Nasdaq IPO in October. The result is that SGX misses out on potential growth stocks that could attract a broader pool of investors, while early backers realise their investments through overseas markets, leaving a gap in the domestic capital cycle. “You can’t blame them for doing that,” Koh said, adding that Singapore may have provided the research funding, business environment, stability and security that help young companies develop, but much more work needs to be done to offer a viable route for capital to be recycled here. “We need to create an environment that will not make it an automatic reflex that we list on Nasdaq or we list in Hong Kong.

events.title: Oil edges lower after rising on expanding Middle East conflict
events.summary: Oil has risen more than 70% in 2026 as the US war on Iran roils energy markets. Oil prices slipped after three days of gains, as traders weighed fears that the widening Middle East war could disrupt supply and lift energy costs further. Houthi drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia killed at least 16 people and wounded about 300, while Trump said he may back Saudi-led strikes and warned of violations of his “energy ceasefire”. Saudi Arabia is moving to reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, with Aramco planning extra export capacity soon and a bigger bypass pipeline within two to three years, showing how fragile oil flows remain. Oil edged lower following three days of gains that were driven by concern the widening war in the Middle East could hamper a recovery in supply from the region. Brent traded below US$106 a barrel after rising more than 6% over the previous three sessions, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$93. Diesel fell a third day in New York after Russia agreed to release more supply following a request by US President Donald Trump. A barrage of drone and missile attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia’s main airport has intensified pressure on Washington to step up its efforts in the conflict in Yemen. Meanwhile, Trump said there had been violations of his “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will continue attacks against Russia as his nation’s energy infrastructure is still being targeted. The attacks on Saudi Arabia came shortly after Riyadh-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held territory, while strikes on tankers in the critical Strait of Hormuz have escalated. That has led to a growing number of supertankers turning away from the Persian Gulf in recent days. “It’s been a dizzying few days of headlines,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP Group, pointing to issues including Trump’s claims of an “energy ceasefire” as well as the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. “We are off to a messy start this week.” Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s main airport over the weekend killed at least 16 people, including a US citizen, and wounded about 300. Trump has said he would consider joining Saudi-backed strikes against the Yemen-based group that is backed by Iran. Meanwhile, the kingdom is seeking to bolster its ability to ship oil without having to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco could add 1.2 million barrels a day of export capacity within seven to eight weeks by repurposing existing gas pipelines, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at a conference in Riyadh on Monday. The country also plans to expand a pipeline that bypasses Hormuz by 40% to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years. The push comes even after Middle East oil flows recovered sharply in recent weeks. Some Wall Street banks have said crude shipments from the region had returned to near pre-war levels. That recovery put downward pressure on prices, but has also left the market vulnerable to another major supply disruption, said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “Just because the system has found ways to keep oil moving doesn’t mean it can handle another major disruption. That’s the risk the market could be underestimating.” In Europe, Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that allowing Russian diesel exports was part of efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations to end the war, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. events.title: Malaysian King buys stake in miner expanding into rare earths
events.summary: Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar, bought 2.25% of the firm’s issued shares from its managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents per share. Malaysia’s King bought a stake in local miner Southern Alliance Mining, which is expanding into rare earths, including through a project in his home state of Johor. Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar bought 2.25% of Singapore-listed Southern Alliance Mining, an iron ore miner, for $6.1 million , the company said in a statement. He acquired the shares from the firm’s managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents each, almost a 12% premium to the Oct 12 closing price, the company said in the statement on the same day. Shares of Southern Alliance Mining rose 10.5% to 42 cents in Singapore early on Oct 13. Sultan Ibrahim has wide business interests spanning real estate, telecommunications an infrastructure, mainly through his shareholdings in various enterprises. He is serving a five-year term as Malaysia’s king under the country’s unique rotating monarchy, in which nine hereditary rulers take turns holding the throne. A representative of Malaysia’s national palace did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Oct 13. In September 2025, Southern Alliance Mining acquired 40% of MCRE Resources, which partnered China Rare Earth Corp. for a rare earth mining operation in Perak state. Southern Alliance Mining is also pursuing a proposed acquisition of Paramount Synergy for a rare earth project in Johor as it positions itself at the forefront of the emerging sector. It has maintained a mining presence in the southern Malaysian state for many years through its flagship Chaah Mine and continues to pursue mineral resources development opportunities in the country. Malaysia has stated ambitions to become a globally competitive player in the rare earths industry, drawing significant interest from foreign miners and refiners. The country hosts Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths, one of only two major producers outside China, with local conglomerates such as Berjaya Corp also exploring projects. France’s Carester SAS plans to build a rare earths separation plant ​in the northern state of Perak as part of a venture with Malaysia’s ‌Malaco Mining Group. Southern Alliance’s Pek remains the company’s controlling shareholder, with a direct interest of 55.74%. The firm said it was not a party to the transaction and did not receive any proceeds. The share transfer will not result in any changes to the company’s management, operations or strategic direction, it said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: US supermarket chain Kroger plans to eliminate 3,000 corporate roles, memo shows, as it expands AI use
events.summary: Kroger’s CEO said the company should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, as job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees. Kroger plans to cut about 3,000 corporate jobs over three years as it expands AI use, CEO Greg Foran said in a memo seen by Reuters. Foran said the cuts will remove duplicate work and help Kroger lower prices and invest more in store staff. The move affects about 37% of 8,200 corporate workers and comes after Kroger outlined its AI strategy and cut its sales target to compete with Walmart and Aldi. CINCINNATI, Ohio – Kroger plans to cut roughly 3,000 corporate roles over the next three years, chief executive Greg Foran told staff in a memo, seen by Reuters on Oct 12, as the grocer integrates artificial intelligence into its workflow. Kroger should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, Foran wrote in the memo, adding that the job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees. Foran took over as Kroger’s CEO in February. Companies have been rethinking corporate structures and cutting jobs as they increasingly turn to AI to streamline workflows and divert more resources towards the technology, fuelling concerns over widespread disruption across sectors. In September, the company outlined the company’s AI strategy, including the use of models to manage workflows and leverage customer data to power tools such as its AI shopping assistant. The grocery retailer had also lowered its annual identical sales target and said it is seeking to cut prices to better compete with rivals such as Walmart and Aldi as consumers grow more frugal under pressure from high gas prices. Details on the job cuts, which would affect about 37% of its 8,200 corporate employees, would be shared in the coming months, Foran said in the memo. Bloomberg News first reported on the job cuts on Oct 12. In June 2025, the company cut about 1,000 corporate roles. REUTERS

events.title: Basel Committee finds Australia, Japan, Korea, Switzerland compliant, and Canada, United Kingdom largely compliant with its leverage ratio framework
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) The Basel Committee has published assessment reports on the implementation of its leverage ratio framework (LEV) in Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland are assessed as compliant; Canada and the United Kingdom are assessed as largely compliant. This publication concludes the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published assessment reports on Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom’s implementation of the Committee’s leverage ratio framework (LEV). Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland were assessed as compliant with the Committee’s global standards, the highest overall grade. Canada and the United Kingdom were assessed as largely compliant, which is one notch below the highest overall grade. These assessments form part of the Committee’s Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which evaluates the consistency and completeness of Basel standards’ implementation across member jurisdictions. With the publication of these reports, the Committee has concluded the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. In line with its work programme, the Committee initiated in H1 2026 jurisdictional assessments of the Basel III revisions to risk-weighted assets and continues to assess the implementation of the leverage ratio.

events.title: Scoop: Top Trump operative enlisted to rescue Kansas senator's campaign
events.summary: A top Trump political operative has been tapped to help boost Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall 's campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the latest sign of how Republicans are scrambling to defend the red-state seat. Why it matters: The hiring of veteran strategist Chris Grant reflects the GOP's growing anxiety over Kansas' Senate race. Marshall is running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state President Trump won by 16 points in 2024. Republicans fear losing Kansas could be a domino in costing them their Senate majority. Driving the news: GOP operatives have become increasingly frustrated with Marshall's reelection campaign, which they believe hasn't been aggressive enough at a time when soaring fuel prices have particularly hurt farmers in Kansas and elsewhere in the Midwest. Grant, who helped lead the main pro-Trump super PAC in 2024 and has remained involved in Trump's political operation, will be a senior adviser to Marshall and help guide strategy in the final three weeks. Grant also worked on Marshall's 2020 Senate campaign. What they're saying: "Chris is an absolute pro who has been a longtime friend to Team Marshall. Having him help land the plane these last three weeks is a no brainer," Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, told Axios. Zoom in: Two GOP outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund and Club for Growth — are pouring millions into the Kansas race. SLF, the principal super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, is spending $14 million in Kansas after shifting resources from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has a significant polling lead over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley. Trump said in a social media post Monday that he would campaign for Marshall "very soon." A Democrat-aligned super PAC has announced plans to spend $5 million to help Hamilton. Between the lines: Marshall has faced damaging headlines recently, including a New York Times r eport that his medical practice sued more than 700 former patients over unpaid medical bills, and that 81 were later arrested for missing court appearances. The other side: Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has won endorsements from two former Republican governors in Kansas, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.
