events.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 00:37 BST The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

events.title: What we know about Lady Violet Bridgerton ahead of Netflix spin-off
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Netflix has announced a Bridgerton spin-off focusing on Lady Violet. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) This article contains spoilers from seasons one to four of Bridgerton. In previous seasons of the Netflix and Shondaland series Bridgerton, Lady Violet has expressed a great affection for her late husband Viscount Edmund Bridgerton. She experienced intense heartbreak and sorrow when he died. Now, fans of the television show will get to see their love story. In the same way Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story delved into the early life of Queen Charlotte, a yet untitled series will chronicle the early life of a young Lady Violet. It promises to tell the story of Violet's romance with Edmund (Rupert Evans). There have been two actors so far who have taken on the role of Lady Violet. Ruth Gemmell plays her in the main series and appeared in the Queen Charlotte spin-off, in which Connie Jenkins-Greig played a younger version in flashbacks as a then Violet Ledger. Lady Violet is depicted in Bridgerton as a kind, warm and wise matriarch with the interests of her family at heart. As we gear up for the spin-off, here's a trip down memory lane exploring some of what we already know about Lady Violet and her relationship with Lord Bridgerton. Violet Bridgerton (née Ledger) holds the title the Dowager Viscountess Bridgerton. Lady Violet is the family's matriarch and has eight children. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) A Dowager Viscountess is the widowed wife of a viscount who retains her aristocratic rank after her husband's death. Violet was pregnant with Lord Bridgerton's eighth child Hyacinth when he died from anaphylaxis. He'd suffered a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee. He was in his late 30s at the time. He'd been out hunting with eldest son Anthony and was picking hyacinths for his wife when it happened. In a conversation with Anthony in season two, episode eight of Bridgerton, titled The Viscount Who Loved Me, Violet tells her son she would go through the pain of losing her husband again because the beauty of love overpowers the risk of grief. "Losing Edmund was the most difficult time of my life," Violet said. "And the pain that I felt … beyond description. "But there is one thing that has given me at least some modicum of solace. "It's knowing that I would still choose the life I led with him, each and every time. "And I would undoubtedly feel the same pain I felt all over again if I had to because real, true love is worth it no matter what." Lady Violet is close friends with Lady Danbury (right). ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) Violet is keen to see each of her eight children marry, but she wants them, too, to experience true love, rather than marry for the sake of it. While no marriage is perfect, the union between Violet and Edmund is so idealised that each of her children aspire to live a similar fairytale. In season one, episode eight called After the Rain, Violet points out to her daughter Daphne that marriage is hard, and the reason why hers worked was because they chose to love each other through each obstacle. "It is a rarity, I have come to realise," Violet said. "That is not to say it was without its trials. "Your father and I faced many difficulties, indeed, but we overcame them. "We made a decision early on to do so. "We chose to love each other every single day. "It is a choice, dearest, one that is never too late to make." Lady Violet remains devoted to her late husband throughout the first few seasons of the television series. Lady Violet develops feelings for Lord Marcus Anderson, but not enough to marry him. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) That is, until Lord Marcus Anderson (Daniel Francis) catches her eye. He is Lady Agatha Danbury's (Adjoa Andoh) younger brother, and they meet in season three of Bridgerton. In season four, they kick it up a notch into a steamy, passionate, but secret dalliance. Finally, Violet is exploring her own desires after mostly focusing her efforts on matchmaking her children. Lord Marcus wants to marry her, but the "not yet" response to his offer of engagement turns into a "not ever" in his eyes. With Queen Charlotte being as juicy as it was stunningly heartbreaking, this author cannot wait for the Lady Violet spin-off, dearest gentle reader. The spin-off will be written by showrunners and executive producers Shonda Rhimes and Nicholas Nardini. Bridgerton is based on the popular historical romance novels written by Julia Quinn. The TV show debuted on Netflix in 2020 and captivated global audiences. Season five is currently in production.

events.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 00:02 BST Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Published 10 September Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick says heating his home now feels more like an investment than a regular household bill Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". events.title: Hong Kong investors are warming to US Treasury bonds as yields hit 20-year high
events.summary: Strong demand was seen at a US$22 billion auction of US government bonds last week, following the fast rise of Treasury yields The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield surged above 5.36 per cent on Wednesday, its highest in 24 years, before retreating to around 5.23 per cent on Thursday following strong demand at a US$22 billion auction of 30-year government bonds. Standard Chartered has turned more bullish, recommending an opportunistic long position in 10-year Treasuries after yields climbed above 5 per cent. The bank expects the 10-year yield to retreat towards 4.75 to 5 per cent over the next six to 12 months, citing expectations of moderating inflation and a shallower Federal Reserve tightening cycle than markets anticipate.

events.title: New report shows US chip industry's reliance on China
events.summary: More than 5% of equipment and materials supplied to US chipmakers originate in China, which also possesses some 90% of the rare earths required to manufacture semiconductors, a new report showed. The figures highlight the structural reliance of US tech on China, and the difficulties of erecting a materials and software firewall against Beijing. “We’re so deeply intertwined,” Brookings’ AI specialist Kyle Chan told The Washington Post: “ There’s a lot of actual dependency .” Beyond materials, the US tech startup ecosystem also relies on cheaper, open-source Chinese AI, so much that when the Trump administration considered banning it, nearly 300 US firms spoke out — marking “the moment open intelligence itself becomes a geopolitical dependency,” an analyst wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

events.summary: Meta released its latest Muse model on Monday, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg said his company had reached the “frontier” of AI capabilities. “Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment ,” Zuckerberg told the Financial Times, vowing to spend more. events.title: Cyberattack destroys food at hundreds of French grocery stores
events.summary: A cyberattack, affecting at least 400 French supermarkets overnight, raised refrigerator temperatures to more than 122°F (50°C) in some cases , forcing millions of dollars’ worth of food to be discarded Monday. “ The weaponization of food has become a reality,” the EU commissioner for agriculture said. The scale of the hack demonstrated “a certain level of sophistication ,” a cybersecurity consultant told AFP. The Élysée has recently called to harden France’s digital infrastructure amid rising security breaches. Monday’s attack may have been continental — a Dutch supermarket chain operating in several countries reported network outages at distribution centers Monday, with one source telling Dutch broadcaster RTL, “You’re going to see huge gaps on the shelves in the coming days.” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
events.summary: Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state. It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election, something the Justice Department has typically avoided . The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance. "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said. "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country." What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. DHS referred Axios to the DOJ. The other side: Omar's office blasted the search. "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong." House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration. Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details. Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. Between the lines: Trump has for years demanded that Omar leave the country or be deported , citing, among other things, unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother to help him circumvent immigration laws. Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors." Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somali population. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Trump, as well as statements from Omar, her House office and House Democratic leaders, and with more context. Andrew Solender and Torey Van Oot contributed reporting.

events.title: Uber struggles to solve Broome's late-night transport issues
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late-night transport issues remain in Broome despite arrival of Uber Travellers say they opt for e-scooters after failing to book an Uber. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Residents and tourists in Broome have long raised concerns about the lack of transport options late at night. The arrival of Uber was touted as a potential solution, but those in Broome say they have struggled to book a ride through the app. Police say the issues people have getting a ride home are no excuse for drink driving. Global rideshare giant Uber has struggled to fill the void of late-night transport in Western Australia's far north. Like many remote locations across Australia, transport options in Broome, 2,000km north of Perth, are progressively limited as the evening wears on. Buses cease at 7pm during the peak tourist season, and many taxi operators stop their service from a similar time. While some drivers continue throughout the night, residents say they face long wait times with expensive fares. Limited taxis operate during the night in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) Uber was touted as a potential solution during its July launch, but those in town said the app has had little impact. Jenny Antonipillai recently travelled to Broome from Perth, and attempted to find a ride home from the pub. "We tried to get a taxi or an Uber, but there's not much available out here. It's very hard," she said. "We went on the Beam [e-scooter] and my boyfriend fell, so not a good idea." Jenny Antonipillai says she was not able to order an Uber home from the pub, despite the app launching in Broome two months ago. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Travellers Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon said they had also had no luck with Uber and opted for e-scooters to get around. "There was nothing available at all in the area," Mr Clancy said. "We got taxis quite easily earlier in the day, but later at night it's a bit more trouble." Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon opted for the e-scooters to get around in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Resident Lili Walker said she was used to long waits and expensive fares costing up to $60 for a 10-minute ride. The state government increased the flexibility of taxi authorisation in 2020, resulting in a number of drivers offering a private service throughout the evening. But their contacts are not always readily available. Matty Arai says many people struggle to organise a taxi through automated answering services. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Pub security guard Matty Arai said it was common to see patrons huddled out the front looking for a way home after close. "There are a couple of good guys around town that will be out all the time, but then trying to pick them up is also hard," he said. Partygoers said expensive fares, long wait times and limited options created a dangerous incentive for drink driving. Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe says educating the community on safe e-scooter use is a priority. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) But Kimberley District traffic Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe said inconvenience did not justify breaking the law. "I understand there are difficulties … transport, distance, everything else like that, but it's not acceptable," he said. Sergeant Di Giuseppe said police had been working to educate community members they were subject to the same road rules on an e-scooter as they were driving a vehicle. Broome and Karratha were the first off the rank for Uber's regional WA expansion in July. Broome Private Taxis owner Paul Rewell said he was not surprised the rideshare service has reportedly struggled to take-off. "If people like our group are struggling to find drivers, Uber won't be any different," he said. Paul Rewell says he is not surprised the app has struggled to attract drivers. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Mr Rewell has been operating taxis in the town for the past six years, and said his business had trialled working throughout the evening. Repeated incidents of vandalism during the night led to the decision to close after 6 or 7pm. He said he welcomed Uber's arrival should they have enough drivers. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said she recognised the challenges of catching taxi services at night in remote towns. She said the government was committed to "providing accessible and affordable" public transport for regional communities, pointing to an expansion of Broome's bus timetable put in place for this year's tourist season. events.title: Phillip Island business operators prepare for MotoGP's final lap
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Phillip Island has relied on the MotoGP to bring in tourists and revenue. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP race at the end of October before the race moves to Adelaide in 2027. The GP and World Superbikes inject about $80 million into the island's economy each year. Businesses, councillors and the island's tourism board are calling for government support. Every October, Phillip Island emerges from a sleepy winter season and roars to life with the sound of motorcycles travelling in convoy to the MotoGP. The weekend of racing turbocharges the island's summer tourism season, culminating in the World Superbikes event in February. But Cowes and the broader island community are preparing to host their final MotoGP later this month at the picturesque cliff-side track, before the race moves to its new home in Adelaide from 2027. The loss has hit businesses and residents hard, with many reeling emotionally and financially. During the 1990s, Bass Coast Shire Council Mayor Brett Tessari worked at a caravan park on the island. "The vibe of the motorbikes coming in and the people, it was awesome," he said. Brett Tessari says the region's tourism future will need to rely on new ideas. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "I remember being stuck on the [Phillip Island] bridge, trying to get over back to Wonthaggi and people were starting up barbecues and cooking sausages on the side of the road because we were at a standstill," Cr Tessari said. "Things like that are just etched in your memory. "To be the mayor, unfortunately, at the last one, it's pretty surreal and quite sad." For the past decade, Samantha Hampstead has run a tattoo business in Cowes with her husband Jason. They are both members of the social motorcycle club Trust No One, and are key organisers of the annual community motorcycle convoy that heralds the start of the motoring weekend. "We do it because of the love of the ride," she said. "It's a full-blown rush when you have all these riders together. "You look in the mirror and you can see this full parade of bikes behind you and it just goes on forever." Samantha Hampstead organises a community motorcycle run in Cowes. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Ms Hampstead said for many business operators the weekend was their busiest time of the year. "It's part of the island," she said. San Remo Fisherman's Co-Op chief executive Wolfgang Platzer said the GP brought thousands of visitors to the island who may not otherwise have visited the region. Wolfgang Platzer says the community needs develop fresh ideas to attract tourists. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There would be a large portion of people that come here for the GP and see that the island and the area is very beautiful and then might think about, oh, we'll come back because we liked it and it was so beautiful," he said. Phillip Island is the state's most tourism-reliant region. According to Destination Phillip Island (DPI), more than $80 million in annual economic activity is linked to the World Superbikes and the MotoGP. The accommodation sector is the island's largest employer, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, accounting for almost 4 per cent of jobs. Cafes and restaurants are the third-largest employer. San Remo is the gateway to Phillip Island. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) DPI chief executive Kim Storey said while the event's loss had accelerated the need to broaden the island's outlook beyond motoring events, the role the track had played could not be understated. Economic uncertainty, a lack of infrastructure such as a car ferry and the potential toll of the H5N1 virus on the island's wildlife were all cited by DPI as upcoming barriers to success. "The MotoGP has provided that platform of security and the resource for businesses," Ms Storey said. DPI and Bass Coast Shire Council have called for government funding to help develop new events, such as The Hills are Alive music festival, the Island Whale Festival, the island hot springs, and a new festival of motorsports to capitalise on the island's motoring history. One Nation candidate for Bass Nikole Schellekens, Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead and Labor candidate Chris Buckingham were asked what commitments they would make to the island's economy if elected at the November state election. All three candidates stressed the importance of tourism for Phillip Island and support for ongoing development of the island's resources.

events.title: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange at the opening bell on Oct 5 in New York City. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Oct 12 as oil prices jumped nearly US$2 (S$2.6) a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport , and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week. The S&P 500 ended the session barely lower while the Dow advanced. Oil futures rallied after deadly strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend. The attacks overshadowed the prospect of increased supplies after US President Donald Trump hailed fresh Russian diesel exports and talked about a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy targets. In coming days, US investors will focus on corporate earnings, with major US banks including Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase reporting early on Oct 13. Analysts were expecting S&P 500 earnings to surge 30.6% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. Also due out this week are September readings for US consumer and producer inflation as well as retail sales data. While the US Treasury market was closed on Oct 12 for Columbus Day, stock investors have been wary of bond yields’ recent advance to 24-year highs as elevated energy prices have stoked inflation concerns. “Looking out further in the week, we have some big economic reports,” said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. He said investors were also cautious due to a lack of direction from bonds. “We’re also waiting on earnings and that’s significant. The four large banks reporting on Tuesday can have a big impact,” he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 195.60 points, or 0.38%, to 51,850.55, the S&P 500 lost 4.30 points, or 0.06%, to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 120.27 points, or 0.44%, to 27,245.90. Trading volume was relatively light with 12.67 billion shares changing hands on US exchanges compared with the 20-day moving average of 17.62 billion. “There’s a lot to be wary of,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut, pointing to upcoming data and earnings along with rising oil prices. “You’re walking down a train line and you don’t know, because it’s dark, if a train is coming and so, you know, you’re just being real careful,” he said. With oil prices rising, energy outperformed among the S&P 500’s 11 major industry sectors with a 1.5% advance. The defensive consumer staples sector rose more than 1% along with the S&P 500 communication services index, which was boosted by a more than 3% gain in heavyweight Meta. Technology, down 0.9%, and consumer discretionary, off 0.7%, were the biggest sector laggards. Technology’s weakness was most pronounced among chip stocks with the Philadelphia semiconductor index finishing down 2.7% after hitting a three-week low. In consumer discretionary, Chipotle Mexican Grill shares fell 3.8% after Starbucks said it was not buying the burrito chain. Starbucks shares closed up 1.7%. Microsoft finished up 1.1% with its market capitalisation climbing above US$4 trillion for the first time in a year after it announced plans for major deployment of its own AI chips. Salesforce shares added 2% after BofA Global Research upgraded the stock to “buy” from “underperform.” And eBay rose 2% after Morgan Stanley added the stock to its top-pick list. Meanwhile, Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said the US central bank should move “relatively quickly” to a more restrictive monetary policy stance to fight inflation, which she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms’ price-setting plans. Traders were pricing in an almost 22% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this month, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, up from 17.7% on Oct 9. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 149 new highs and 272 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 1,888 stocks rose and 3,008 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.59-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 318 new lows. REUTERS

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bridgeport Energy already has oil wells in the Cooper-Eromanga basin. ( Supplied: Bridgeport Energy ) An Australian oil company has won tenders to explore for more oil and gas in the Channel Country. Bridgeport Energy has been allocated 270,000 hectares of land with new supply to stay within the domestic market. Traditional owners and graziers want assurances that "significant" flood plains will not be damaged. The head of an Australian oil company says any fossil fuels taken from new land in Queensland's Channel Country will stay in Australia, but it could take years before oil or gas flows. Bridgeport Energy has been declared the preferred tenderer across an extra 270,000 hectares of land between Innamincka and Thargomindah along the South Australian-Queensland border. Bridgeport already has about 90,000 hectares of "oil-producing acreage" in the Cooper-Eromanga basin and processes oil at Queensland's only inland oil refinery in Eromanga. The land allocated for exploration is on the Queensland-South Australia border. ( Supplied: Google Maps ) The state government has been ramping up land allocations to mining companies since 2025. Bridgeport Energy chief executive Christian Lange said he wanted to work "very, very closely" with landholders including graziers and traditional owners before any exploration began. "We need to be cognisant that our disturbance on that land is zero effectively by the time we pack up and leave," he said. Agriculture-conservation alliance wants assurances Western Rivers Alliance is a cooperative between graziers, traditional owners and conservationists advocating to stop new oil and gas activities on Channel Country flood plains. The latest sites are not within the protected Channel Country flood plains where fracking was banned two years ago , but parts are within 5 to 10 kilometres of the boundary. Coordinator Riley Rocco said the alliance was "neutral" on mining outside the flood plains. "But the activity could come quite close to the flood plain and obviously we are keen to make sure that any oil and gas or any industrial activity stays managed well outside of the flood plain in order to not have an adverse impact on those significant river and flood plain areas." In May 2013, a major oil spill in the Channel Country at a Santos-owned well involved the loss of 250,000 litres of crude oil, which flowed for 2 kilometres before the leak was stopped. The Queensland Department of Environment did not prosecute Santos at the time but admitted damage could have been severe if the leak had occurred during floodtime. Mr Lange said impacts on groundwater, fauna, flora, roads and other "land disturbances" would be considered before new exploration begins. He said the small-scale company would use seismic waves to determine whether there were enough "commercial flows" of oil or gas underground. "I would anticipate that it's probably the best part of two years to obtain your authority to prospect, and then preparing to do seismic surveys, whether it's 2D, 3D or a combination of all those things," he said. Gas exploration was banned in some parts of the Channel Country in 2024. ( Supplied: Pew Charitable Trusts ) The latest round of tenders also included 62,500 hectares for the ASX-listed Vintage Energy in the Channel Country, while a four-business consortium won 30,600 hectares of land in the Taroom Trough. In a statement, Queensland Resources Minister Dale Last said increasing the supply of fuels was the "only solution to bring down the cost of energy". The state government has awarded 12 sites for oil or gas exploration since 2025.

events.title: Fortune’s AIQ Summit: The conversation has moved from experimentation to execution
events.summary: As companies race to adopt generative AI, agents, and new data tools, leaders face a more demanding question than whether to use the technology: How can they turn it into measurable value without creating new costs, risks, and organizational confusion? At the Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange, executives from the technology, finance, industrial operations, travel, and human resources sectors explored what separates meaningful AI transformation from scattered pilots. The discussion made clear that the strongest companies are not simply distributing AI tools. They are redesigning workflows, developing talent, strengthening governance, and building the data and operating discipline needed to scale responsibly. Together, we explored these key trends: Moving from experimentation to enterprise transformation Building an AI-ready workforce Managing governance, trust, and risk Applying AI in physical and regulated environments Measuring ROI, controlling costs, and creating growth From AI adoption to AI transformation THE MOST IMPORTANT AI QUESTION IS NOT WHETHER A COMPANY HAS DEPLOYED TOOLS, BUT WHETHER IT HAS CHANGED HOW WORK GETS DONE. Speakers warned that widespread access to AI does not necessarily create productivity, business value, or organizational maturity. Diana David, director of futures at ServiceNow , said leading companies distinguish themselves through their commitment to people and operational discipline, not technology alone. In ServiceNow’s Enterprise AI Maturity Index, 57% of “pacesetters” invest in ongoing AI upskilling, compared with 4% of other organizations. The widest gap involves attracting, hiring, and retaining AI talent: 68% of pacesetters do so, compared with 10% of other companies. “Talent investment. That was the biggest gap,” David said. David cautioned against treating broad employee access to AI as proof of success: “95% of everybody has X, Y, Z,” she said. “But it is not translating into productivity, and it’s often not with training, and that doesn’t equal maturity.” The work, she argued, begins with leadership, a clear vision, transparent systems, the right data foundation, and iterative redesign of specific workflows. Paul Fipps, president of global customer operations at ServiceNow, made a related point: The greatest gains will not come from automating old processes faster, but from rebuilding them around new capabilities. “If I just automate or drive autonomous agents to drive the current processes I have, that’s a choice that might get some productivity bump,” Fipps said. “But the ones that are actually rethinking and reimagining the business processes … are really making the difference.” Fipps said companies should deploy AI horizontally, across employee-facing functions such as HR, legal, and technology, rather than isolating it in one department. He cited Standard Chartered , where AI has helped deflect 77% of employee requests. “If you get 25% to 30% deflection in those use cases, it’s game-changing,” he said. “If you get 75% to 80%, it is life-changing.” Amy Webb, founder and CEO of Future Today Strategy Group, was more blunt about the gap between ambition and readiness. “Let’s be fair, Fortune 500 companies are pretty late to the party on this,” she said. “Artificial intelligence didn’t just show up a couple of years ago.” Webb warned that companies are pouring significant capital into pilots without sufficient strategy, leadership, or planning—creating isolated projects that fail to produce durable value. Building the AI-ready workforce AI TRANSFORMATION IS A WORKFORCE TRANSFORMATION. The summit underscored that organizations need more than new software: They need employees and leaders willing to rethink established processes, learn new skills, and make room for new ways of working. Stacy Dillow, executive vice president and chief people officer at HPE , said companies must resist simply inserting AI into existing systems. “We’ve got to force ourselves to think differently, because if we’re not trying to change how we work, we’re just trying to retrofit and put AI in a process that isn’t going to give us a different answer,” she said. For senior executives, she added, AI adoption and transformation have become central management responsibilities. Danielle Gonzalez, chief people officer at Palo Alto Networks , described how AI is already changing the employee experience. A custom AI agent has reduced IT tickets by 83% and supports workflows across HR, finance, and legal. Instead of turning to a human HR partner or business contact, employees can increasingly ask an agent for answers tied to their role and location. Gonzalez said companies should hire and develop people who can adapt rapidly—not only learning new skills but questioning assumptions that no longer hold. “We’re looking for curiosity,” she said. “We’re looking for agency, and we’re looking for those people who can not only learn something at a fast rate … but also unlearn what they thought to be true, so that they can make space to move forward.” Drew Holler, chief human resources officer at Lennar, stressed that the responsibility is shared. “We’re going to give you all the tools, but it’s your responsibility to upskill yourself as well,” he said. “We’re going to give you trainings, but you, as an individual, have to upskill.” The workforce implications extend beyond reskilling. Francis Shanahan, chief technology officer at Peloton , warned that AI-enabled creation can create its own challenge. Employees are “inundated now because they can literally build anything,” he said, and “burnout” is becoming more of an issue. Michelle Kwon, chief operating officer at Runway, urged leaders not to mistake volume for productivity. “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or for doing a good job at work,” she said. AI should improve how people work, she argued, without generating additional work for colleagues or overwhelming them with output that has not been properly assessed and synthesized. Governance, trust, and control THE CASE FOR AI MUST BE MATCHED BY A CASE FOR OVERSIGHT. In regulated industries and high-stakes applications, leaders emphasized that successful deployment depends on selecting the right technology, understanding the risk, and keeping human judgment where it matters most. Hari Gopalkrishnan, chief technology and information officer at Bank of America , cautioned companies not to reach for AI reflexively. “One of the biggest mistakes we see ourselves and others doing is rushing to AI as a solution, when deterministic models do a plenty good job,” he said. Bank of America begins with client needs and a detailed inventory of the relevant process; sometimes a conventional mobile feature or real-time decision rule is the better tool. events.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian government 'manipulating' planning laws to win critical minerals race, expert says Kane Busch and his family have been farming vegetables in the Lindenow Valley for 100 years. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) The Victorian government is assessing a mineral sands mine project it has already rejected. The global critical minerals race is behind the renewed attempt to green light the project, experts argue. The company behind the proposal says claims the project has not been altered since its previous rejection are "misleading and false". The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims. The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry". But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception". "The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said. Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Sean Warren ) Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal. The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes. GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government. Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s. Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. ( ABC Rural: Emma Field ) Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements. Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable. After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations. In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal. Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review. "The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said. Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said. "This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource." Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval. University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look. Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects. The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. ( Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals ) In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals. GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list. China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining. Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China. The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn. Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

events.title: Loophole allowing new coal and gas to avoid stricter climate laws
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coal and gas avoiding stricter laws by expanding existing mines, Climate Council warns Hunter Valley Operations was recently approved for an extension that will include mining new seams and additional emissions. ( ABC News ) Coal and gas mines have to follow less strict emissions laws when they are expanded compared to outright new mines. The Climate Council says that amounts to a "loophole" being used by the industry to add new emissions without having to follow "best-practice" limits. The Safeguard Mechanism, which sets emissions laws for heavy industry, is under review. Coal and gas mines are using what the Climate Council warns is a "loophole" to expand operations and add new emissions while avoiding stricter laws imposed on new coal and gas projects. The Climate Council says unless emissions from mine expansions are treated the same as emissions from new mines, it will cause an additional 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2035. Coal and gas mines are among the roughly 200 facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism — climate laws that require Australia's biggest polluters to cut or offset emissions by about 5 per cent a year or else face heavy penalties. Under the laws, which are currently being reviewed, new coal and gas facilities are required to follow more strict, "best-practice" limits that take into account the most efficient technologies available for mines. But existing facilities are not required to meet that higher standard when expanding or extending the life of an existing mine. Modelling by Reputex has estimated that across 22 planned coal and gas expansions and extensions over the next decade, which will be treated as existing facilities, they will be able to emit 11 times more than if they were treated as new facilities. The Climate Council says expansions are being used widely across the industry, taking advantage of that favourable treatment and leading to more emissions. "Companies have an incentive to characterise everything as an expansion rather than a new facility," chief executive Amanda McKenzie said. "We're arguing that is one of the loopholes that needs to be shut." Amanda McKenzie says less stringent climate laws for mining expansions compared to new facilities amount to a "loophole" that should be closed. ( Supplied ) The Safeguard Mechanism is under review and due to be revisited next year, when the government will decide whether to set a steeper trajectory towards net zero emissions by 2050. The Climate Council says when that time comes, "best-practice" CO2 limits should be applied to all new coal and gas emissions, regardless of whether they come from a new mine or an expanded one. It says fossil fuel facilities are not doing enough to transition to net zero, and those covered by the Safeguard Mechanism actually increased emissions in the most recent year. Most new coal and gas emissions from expansions The council says since the Safeguard Mechanism laws were amended in 2022, more than three quarters of all new coal development have been expansions or extensions to projects. It pointed to last month's approval for an open-cut coalmine in the Hunter Valley , which owners Yancoal and Glencore applied to extend by more than a decade. Its life extension into the 2040s, which includes the mining of deeper coal seams, represents an additional $2.7 billion capital investment and will add an extra 809 megatonnes of CO2 emissions — or a bit less than two years' worth of Australia's annual emissions. The NSW Independent Planning Commission approves plans that will allow Hunter Valley Operations to continue coal mining at a site near Singleton until 2045. Because the Yancoal-Glencore owned coalmine was already covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, the extension will be treated under rules for existing projects, which the Climate Council estimates will result in emissions 60 per cent higher than if it was treated as a new project. The NSW Independent Planning Commission, which approved the life extension, said while it would contribute to climate change and add to Australia's emissions, that was outweighed by its benefits, including supporting up to 1,400 local jobs and ongoing tax revenue from the mine. "Despite these new investments being significant enough to require a new environmental approval, the vast majority of their pollution will not be considered 'new' by the Safeguard Mechanism," the council said.

events.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
events.summary: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them. Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. The firm added in a statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date. "Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to." The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France. Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed. In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon. The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible". Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported. As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires. French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C. Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions. French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality." In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible". He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable". Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience . events.title: Tasmania's financial windfall from mine leads to creation of future fund
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Windfall from King Island tungsten mine shares to support new Tasmanian future fund The Dolphin Tungsten Mine recommenced operations at Grassy on King Island and in 2023 started commercial production of tungsten concentrate. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) In 2023, the Tasmanian government acquired 12 per cent of the shares of a struggling tungsten mine after its owner could not repay a $10 million loan. The price of tungsten has since significantly increased. A recovery fund will be set up to insulate Tasmanians in major industries from workforce impacts. The Tasmanian government will create a $20 million future fund to help regional communities "navigate economic disruption" and "attract new investment". It follows the government stepping in financially to save King Island Dairy, and industrials Bell Bay Aluminium and Nyrstar from collapse, as well as dealing with the loss of more than 200 jobs after Australia's last manganese smelter Liberty Bell Bay shut down. The money for the new Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will come from the government's $10 million investment in King Island's tungsten mine. The mine is on King Island's south-east coast. ( Facebook: Group 6 Metals ) The Dolphin mine, which boasts the largest tungsten deposit in the country, is owned by Australian company Group 6 Metals. The mine shut for more than two decades due to low tungsten prices, but reopened in 2023 with the help of the $10 million loan. Under new ownership, the initial $10 million loan was converted into shares, of which Tasmania's government holds 12 per cent. The mine has since experienced a significant financial turnaround, rewarding investors like the government. Tungsten is classified as a critical mineral used in heavy machinery and defence manufacturing. The state government also lent the mine a further $7.5 million last year. The Dolphin mine is Australia's largest mined tungsten deposit. ( Supplied: Group 6 Metals ) Mine proceeds to help reduce state debt Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the government's investment in the mine would allow it to reinvest in regional communities. Government issues loan to mine after becoming a shareholder A struggling tungsten mine couldn't pay back a $10 million loan as it sat on the brink of administration. So a state government became a shareholder — and issued a new loan. "Our regional communities are at the heart of Tasmania's economic success and they deserve the confidence that comes from knowing support will be there when it is needed most," Mr Rockliff said. ​"The strong investment made by the Tasmanian government to support the future of the King Island tungsten mine has allowed us to reinvest a significant portion of the windfall back into the very regions that helped generate that success. ​"This fund is about transforming a one-off financial return into an enduring asset for regional Tasmania." The government said the fund will be able to support communities experiencing significant economic disruption, including responding to major industry change, employer closures, workforce impacts and other economic shocks. "Too often, governments are forced to react after a major employer closes or an industry undergoes significant change," he said. ​"Instead, we are getting ahead of those challenges by establishing a fund that will help communities navigate economic disruption, attract new investment and create new opportunities for the future. ​"The Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will help support economic diversification, workforce transition, investment attraction and community-led recovery initiatives when communities face significant economic disruption." The government said proceeds from the mine investment would also go towards reducing the state's debt, which is estimated to peak at just under $10 billion by the end of the decade. Speaking on King Island on Tuesday morning, Premier Jeremy Rockliff shed more light on the significant windfall from the state government's investment in the mine. The original $10 million loan, which later became equity, is now worth in excess of $75 million in shares it will now look to sell, he said. "Well, at this stage we've got the $20 million fund for regional resilience fund, $5 million for the school, and we expect to put about $50 million back to paying off the debt," Mr Rockliff said. "Our expectation … was to see the revival of the mine and for us to recoup the funds that we invested, of course, but it's exceeded expectations," he said.

events.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
events.summary: Graduates pass the John Harvard Statue during Harvard University's commencement on May 29, 2025. Harvard was the school's first big donor. Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images In 1638, John Harvard , an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death. In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets . Based on our decades of experience as scholars , academic administrators and school fundraisers , we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times. In the crosshairs Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts , student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States . University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package . The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments . A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria. There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate . Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever , students and their families are still struggling to pay for college . Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone , including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont. And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College , which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network. A sticky note spotted at Hampshire College’s Harold F. Johnson Library on May 16, 2026, months before the school was slated to be closed for good, assured students that alumni would support them. Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Higher education giving Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before. The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025. Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research . On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities. It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University . And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million . The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes . The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities , those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades . In 2024 it slipped below 7% . Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025 . Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts. Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Computer, and his wife Susan have given more than $1 billion to the University of Texas at Austin, with much of that funding reserved for specific purposes. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Corbis via Getty Images How donors can help In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts. 1. Pooling donations Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference. In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns. Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors. Sweet Briar College alumni take a selfie in 2015 at a pop-up fundraiser to save the womens’ college in Virginia. Evelyn Hockstein/For The Washington Post via Getty Images 2. Donating with few or no strings attached Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs. Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change. Brandeis University , Indiana University , Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic. Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies , such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts. events.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
events.summary: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.” Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says. “I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it does
