events.title: Cosmetic surgery event cancelled after questions over doctors' registration
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South Korean company cancels cosmetic surgery event after ABC raises questions A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors. The company had been questioned about promotions featuring doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Women who travel to South Korea for procedures are documenting the process online. A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors, after questions were raised by the ABC. The two-day, appointment-only event was advertised by South Korean company Restory Plastic Surgery, featuring two doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Examples of some of the advertisements promoting the now cancelled Korean surgeons' visit. ( Supplied: Restory Plastic Surgery ) National laws prohibit doctors who are not registered in Australia from providing medical consultations or services in the country. Previous advertising stated both doctors would attend the event. ( Supplied ) In response to questions about the event and the legalities of foreign doctors providing medical consultations in Australia, the South Korean company pulled down its advertising. "Dr I Yung Moon and Dr Myung Joon Lee will not be travelling to Australia and will not be attending the Sydney event," the company told the ABC. "We acknowledge that the presentation of the promotional material may have created the impression that the doctors themselves would be travelling to Sydney, and we would like to clarify that this is not the case." Pia Marshall documented her procedure on social media. ( Supplied/ABC News: Pete Mullins ) The ABC understands similar medical expo events are held regularly, prompting warnings from Australia's peak plastic surgery body about the risks of overseas procedures and the rules governing medical advertising. Sunshine Coast woman Pia Marshall met a different Korean cosmetic surgery company in Melbourne last year at an expo similar to the one that was due to be held in Sydney. She said meeting patients at events like these appeared to be common practice, but after doing her own research, she decided to undergo the procedure with a different surgeon. The marketing specialist travelled to South Korea with her mother, Marion, for matching face lifts and documented their experiences online. The women, aged 41 and 69, travelled to Incheon, a city bordering Seoul, in June to undergo deep-plane face lifts, neck lifts and lower mid-face lifts. The procedures, performed under general anaesthetic, typically take several hours and involve repositioning the skin and underlying tissues to restore facial contours. The Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS) confirmed wound infection and haematoma, when blood collects under the skin, were the most common face lift complications requiring operative intervention. The mother and daughter said South Korea's reputation for skin care, known as K-beauty, and the growing number of social media testimonials made it an "obvious choice", even though the face lifts themselves were not significantly different from procedures available in Australia. Pia Marshall spent 14 days in South Korea for the procedures. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Australia is now the second-highest-spending K-beauty market per capita globally , behind only South Korea, according to data from Future Market Insights. Pia was quoted $36,000 for the procedures, including accommodation and 14 days in South Korea. However, she negotiated a social media agreement with the company but could not disclose the details of the arrangement. Testimonial-style advertising for cosmetic surgery is prohibited when promoting a health service provided by an Australian-registered practitioner, but the same restrictions do not apply to overseas practitioners. A face lift in Australia typically starts at around $25,000, according to the ASPS, with the cost increasing depending on the surgeon, procedure and complexity. Pia said she found overseas cosmetic surgery options more accessible than those in Australia, due to Australia's strict advertising rules. Influencers are advertising the surgery. ( Graphic: ABC News ) While Pia said she did extensive research before her surgery, other influencers documenting their experiences have taken a more casual approach to discussing the risks. Ruby Tuesday Matthews is a 33-year-old Byron Bay content creator who specialises in lifestyle and luxury content and recently documented her own face lift.

events.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
events.summary: By Ke Yang , PhD Student Chenglong Wang , Senior Researcher Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Chandan Singh , Senior Researcher Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher ChengXiang Zhai , Professor, University of Illinois Department of Computer Science Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721.

events.title: U.K. prime minister attributes plot against U.S. bomber base to Iran
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the U.K. House of Commons Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was "almost certainly" behind the suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford base where U.S. bombers were stationed. Why it matters: This was the first time the U.K. officially blamed Iran for the alleged planned attack . What he's saying: "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. Driving the news: 10 days ago, the U.S. evacuated a dozen B-1 strategic bombers from RAF Fairford in response to intelligence indicating an Iranian drone attack. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen move by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential to dramatically escalate the war in the Middle East. The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. It was unclear whether the people who were arrested were connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel provided the U.K. with intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. State of play: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the Iranian ambassador was summoned to the foreign office in London to denounce the alleged Iranian plot. The other side: The Iranian ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, told IRNA that Iran "categorically rejects" the allegations. After his meeting with the UK minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doty, Mousavi said Iran had no involvement in the incident and asked the British government to provide evidence to support its claims. He added that Iran is ready to cooperate with the British authorities in investigating the issue. What they're saying: The U.S., U.K. and 27 other western countries published a joint statement on Monday condemning Iran for "use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners." The group said the threat against RAF Fairford "demonstrates the IRGC's continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors."

events.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
events.summary: Microsoft to expand Azure Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. That density allows Microsoft to serve more simultaneous AI interactions and larger workloads from each rack, improving datacenter capacity and the economics of expanding AI services. Maia 300 will begin production deployments in 2027. For more information on Maia 300 architectural details, read our technical paper . Azure Maia is at the heart of our Frontier Transformation The future will not be defined by a single model or a single piece of silicon or a single innovation. Model and silicon choice are inherent in our vision for Frontier Transformation. Our focus is on developing responsible, affordable and scalable platforms that will help everyone amplify their intelligence to drive breakthrough outcomes that matter for them.

events.title: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem
events.summary: Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise. Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising. The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own. Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication. Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities. Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet. Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself. The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier. What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it." Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases. Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday. Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran." Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso , backed the deal. How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban. GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers , have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war. Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity. His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots. Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion . A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved. Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers. The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

events.title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
events.summary: When Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development. Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today. The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent . Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky , with some researchers not sticking around for long. Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups. But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models. Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark , in April of this year. The company has also released a small open-weight model called Muse Glimmer , and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained. Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities. Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models. Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors. Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts. A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically. Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month. Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race. events.title: Britain faces looming energy crisis as gas reserves dwindle
events.summary: Britain faces a deepening energy crisis as a result of dwindling reserves and the possible closure of its largest storage site. With a 150 per cent surge in European gas prices before the seasonal dip in temperatures, the prospect of another inflationary shock is casting a shadow over the October 28 Budget. The prospect of losing Rough, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, threatens to further weaken the country's ability to withstand supply disruptions as Europe heads into winter with depleted reserves. Underground gas storage in Britain was only 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to only 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity equals about seven days of average winter demand. The problem of limited UK reserves is compounded by uncertainty over the future of Rough, which could close next year unless the government backs a £2 billion redevelopment proposed by its owner, Centrica. Chris O'Shea, chief executive of Centrica, which also owns British Gas, stepped up pressure on the government on Tuesday, warning that the site, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, would close at the end of the first quarter without a plan to support investment. "The commercial decision will be that this facility will close at the end of the first quarter," Mr O'Shea told the BBC, rejecting the government's position that Rough's future was a commercial matter for the company. He said Centrica was seeking a regulatory framework similar to those available to other critical infrastructure operators, providing more predictable returns in exchange for lower investment risk. Mr O'Shea described Rough as "the biggest battery in the UK", saying the proposed investment could create up to 5,000 jobs while safeguarding almost 1,000 existing positions. The company has also offered to make the site available as a temporary strategic gas reserve this winter but has yet to receive a response from the government, he said. "Our system is not resilient. Without energy security, we have no national security," Mr O'Shea said, pointing to increasingly frequent electricity supply margin notices. Britain’s grid operator sought emergency assistance from France on Monday, requesting as much as 1,200 megawatts of additional electricity through an undersea interconnector to help maintain the security of the power system. Britain will probably not run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House. “The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said. Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”. European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group. “It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters. Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels. EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves. A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further. Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high. The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

events.title: HSBC moves to Wall Street bonus model, cuts fixed-pay deals
events.summary: The London-headquartered bank will switch to the new pay system at the start of 2028, according to a memo seen by Bloomberg News. LONDON – HSBC Holdings will phase out fixed-pay allowances for its senior staff and instead hand out a greater proportion of its compensation in the form of bonuses, becoming the latest British lender to switch to Wall Street-style remuneration to better align with performance. The approach “strengthens our ability to pay for performance, better differentiate, attract the best talent, and recognise” top performers, a spokesman for HSBC said in a statement. HSBC’s shift follows a similar update by Barclays, which said in July it would switch more of its employees’ pay toward bonuses after Britain changed its rules around compensation in 2025 to allow for higher variable pay in an effort to boost domestic competitiveness. Wall Street bankers have typically received the bulk of their pay through bonuses tied to performance, rather than fixed salaries. Fixed pay allowances were introduced more than a decade ago at major British banks to provide a way of topping the base salary of senior staff after the introduction of European Union rules capping the compensation of financiers. At HSBC, those allowances have taken the form of share awards in immediately vested stock, though these have been subject to a retention period to ensure alignment between an executive’s interests and those of the bank. These payouts are non-pensionable and have been capped at a maximum of 150% of an individual’s base salary under the terms of HSBC’s fixed-pay structure. In its most recent annual report, HSBC said fixed pay remained the largest part of its bankers’ compensation. The UK rule changes have now lessened the need for these fixed-pay allowances. The lender spent US$3.93 billion (S$5.03 billion) in 2025 on variable pay, up 10% from the previous year, according to the annual report. Gross compensation and benefits stood at US$21.5 billion in 2025. The planned compensation overhaul is part of a broader restructuring HSBC has seen since Georges Elhedery took over as chief executive officer in September 2024 . His shake-up of the lender has resulted in the sale, closing or merger of several businesses and hundreds of job cuts. The CEO has also led a cost-cutting programme that has included the paring back of long-time benefits enjoyed by some of the company’s staff such as education allowances and contributions to private club memberships for employees of its Hong Kong-based business. In the Asian hub, the lender ended a long-standing education subsidy covering 95% of school fees for the children of new hires and senior staff relocating to the city. Existing band-three employees and managing directors who already receive the benefit will retain it, Bloomberg News reported in September. It is also cutting a perk worth up to HK$200,000 (S$32,645) that subsidised some private club access for its bankers in the city. The share price of HSBC has more than doubled since Elhedery became CEO. BLOOMBERG

events.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
events.summary: The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached. Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us". Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents. The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system." In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe". AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023. But it was reported in September , external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed. The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing. Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation. On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released". He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported. Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little". "Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said. "There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers." The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems. On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown . However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals. Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules. "We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said. "What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer." On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments". "It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said. events.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
events.summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP 🔗 NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory 🔗 NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/ NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories 🔗 For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for.

events.title: NVIDIA and Cisco Introduce New Pluggable Optics Form Factor to Scale AI Factories
events.summary: Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) is designed to be the first module to support 400Gb/s-per-lane electrical signals, enabling capacity up to 12.8Tb/s so AI factory builders can scale Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a proven deployment model across multiple generations of data center networks. USFP delivers 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200Gb/s-per-lane optics so AI factories can connect more computing systems without adding network tiers, while using less power to move each bit of data. NVIDIA and Cisco are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build a multi-source hardware ecosystem around USFP. NVIDIA and Cisco today announced plans for Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a new high-density 400Gb/s-per-lane optical module designed to equip the hardware ecosystem for the next generation of AI factories using pluggable transceivers. As AI models grow and inference demand expands, AI factories must connect more computing systems while managing network complexity, power and costs. Moving more data per watt and per switch helps operators make better use of their infrastructure investments. Scaling AI factories requires more bandwidth per connection and more connections per switch. When a switch reaches its capacity, further network expansion can require additional switch layers and optical links, increasing latency, power consumption and costs. USFP is designed to enable AI factory builders to scale from 200 Gb/s per lane to 400Gb/s-per-lane Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a deployment model proven at scale across multiple generations of data center networks. With USFP, customers can embrace next-generation optical technology and meet the performance demand of AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. The first planned USFP-based transceivers will pack 16 full-duplex lanes in an octal small form factor (OSFP)-sized footprint supporting both switches and SuperNICs, with the ability to expand to 32 and more lanes in the future. By doubling both the lane count and bandwidth per lane, USFP enables AI fabrics to connect more 1.6Tb/s endpoints without adding network tiers. Customers will be able to achieve 12.8Tb/s of overall capacity with USFP. Comparable with an OSFP-sized module, it delivers 4x the bandwidth and front-panel bandwidth density, with approximately 1.3x the power efficiency, versus 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable modules. This means AI builders can increase their compute scale within the same network footprint, while decreasing networking’s share of the overall AI factory power budget. “Building the world’s largest AI factories starts with rethinking the smallest of connections,” said Gilad Shainer, senior vice president NVIDIA. “With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco are building an ecosystem to reinvent pluggable optics — connecting more computing with greater efficiency to power the next generation of AI factories.” “AI builders need an interconnect architecture that can scale performance without locking them into a more complex operating model,” said Bill Gartner, senior vice president and general manager of optical systems and optics at Cisco. “Cisco and NVIDIA recognized that scaling pluggable optics to 400Gb/s per lane would require more than another incremental extension of today’s module designs. Through our collaboration, USFP is designed to deliver a new level of bandwidth density while preserving the serviceability, deployment flexibility and operational simplicity of pluggable optics. By taking a full-stack approach — from silicon and systems to optics and the network operating system — we can optimize every layer to deliver the performance and scale the next generation of AI networks will require.” More AI Infrastructure From Every Switch Designed for electrical signals of 400Gb/s per lane, USFP uses a new two-dimensional array connector with a two-step insertion design that engages high-speed contacts after the module is inserted, reducing contact wear, improving signal integrity and making insertion force more predictable. The connector technology allows for further scaling of lane count to 32 full duplex lanes and more in the future. Because the connector is designed for 400Gb/s performance, it also offers improved performance at 200Gb/s per lane. USFP supports power dissipation of up to 100 watts without needing a separate, dedicated embedded cooling circuit within the transceiver, reducing switch design complexity and improving reliability. Together, these capabilities enable higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the mature deployment, serviceability and manufacturability of existing pluggable transceivers. All USFP configurations support optical designs that reduce latency and power consumption by simplifying signal processing. Support for a broad range of optical technologies and connection distances gives system designers the flexibility to meet unique AI factory deployment needs. A Hardware Ecosystem for Next-Generation AI Factories NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build USFP cages, connectors and modules, with additional partners expected to join. The shared form factor gives suppliers a common foundation for developing high-density pluggable infrastructure for 400Gb/s-per-lane fabrics to build a robust ecosystem for AI factory builders. The collaboration builds on NVIDIA and Cisco’s existing work to ensure NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet networks work together seamlessly, simplifying AI infrastructure deployment for enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign clouds. NVIDIA and Cisco plan to create an open industry specification for USFP through an upcoming community-led multi-source project. events.title: A charming and 'instructive' dispatch from Rome
events.summary: by Jason Horowitz. When he moved to Italy, Horowitz, an American who grew up in Queens, was sure that the country’s best days were behind it. But by covering neofascism, financial crises, immigration, and other topics for 25 years — a portion of which he spent as The New York Times’ Rome bureau chief — he found that Italy’s problems were a harbinger for the rest of the industrial world. Horowitz’s love for Italy gives the book “its charm and its instructive value,” Kirkus Reviews wrote, describing it as “a mix of forewarning and reassurance from someone with a distinct viewpoint.” Buy The Italian Job from your local bookstore . — Kate McKenna

events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support A screen on iPhone 18 Pro Max shows gameplay of Little Kitty, Big City. A screen on iPhone 18 Pro Max shows gameplay of 9 Kings. A screen on iPhone 18 Pro Max shows gameplay of Dome Keeper. A screen on iPhone 18 Pro Max shows gameplay of Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall. Text of this article October 12, 2026 UPDATE App Store Indie Games Week kicks off today Seven acclaimed indie games, including Sifu, Vampire Crawlers, and No Man’s Sky, make their App Store debut Today, Indie Games Week lights up the App Store with a celebration of the incredible catalog of imaginative games made by independent teams with big dreams. Players worldwide can jump into their next adventure with seven highly acclaimed indie games, available for download or pre-order on iPhone and iPad. All week, the App Store will spotlight these indie gems with daily features and curated collections. “Indie games are constantly pushing the boundaries of creativity to deliver unique gameplay experiences to Apple users, and we wanted to take a moment to celebrate these games and the teams that take creative risks to push gaming forward,” said Carson Oliver, Apple’s head of App Store Worldwide. “Whether from a solo developer or a growing studio, the App Store gives bold ideas a global stage — turning daring visions into worldwide hits. We’re thrilled with the incredible games launching on the App Store this week and amazed by their breathtaking artistry, brilliant design, and deeply moving stories.” There are whole new worlds to discover during Indie Games Week, from building empires, to brawling through cinematic combat, to getting lost in another universe entirely. With the critically acclaimed Sifu , Indie Games Week puts the art of combat front and center. This stylish third-person brawler follows a young kung fu student on a relentless path of revenge. Battles are ferocious and unforgiving, with enemies attacking simultaneously, forcing players to parry strikes, chain combos, and weaponize everything around them. Sifu arrives fully adapted for iPhone and iPad, with custom-tuned touch controls, a reworked camera system, and full controller support. For players looking for quick bursts of strategy mixed with dark humor, Vampire Crawlers is an invitation to rough up skeletons, bats, and other nefarious creeps in a gothic card battler. The spin-off of the smash hit Vampire Survivors cleverly trades dodging bullets for tactical deck building. Players conquer chaotic dungeon runs by discovering game-changing card combos, uncovering secret relics, and mastering the luck of the draw. After celebrating a decade of continuous evolution, Hello Games’ groundbreaking space odyssey No Man’s Sky makes its mobile debut on iPhone and iPad on October 28. The game includes every major content expansion to date, including the most recent Cosmos update, where players can command their own space stations. Set in an infinite, procedurally generated universe rendered entirely at runtime, No Man’s Sky lets players explore, trade, fight, and survive across an interconnected galaxy — all in the palm of their hands. Also this week, players can guide a curious feline through an open-world metropolis in Little Kitty, Big City , assemble card armies to conquer royal adversaries in the strategic kingdom builder 9 Kings , dig deep to fend off foes in the alien mining simulator Dome Keeper , or grapple with agonizing moral choices to save a crumbling empire in Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall . All will be featured throughout Indie Games Week and are available now to download on the App Store. To discover more of the App Store’s indie games catalog, explore this in-depth overview of indie gems curated by App Store editors. On Mac, players can browse a great catalog of standout indie titles too in this indie games guide . events.title: OPay readies $4B New York IPO
events.summary: The News OPay, the Lagos-based fintech firm backed by Softbank and Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, more than doubled its revenue in the first half of 2026 as lending overtook payments as its top source of income, according to a filing ahead of a planned New York listing likely set for next month. The company has applied to trade under the ticker OPAY, with a potential Nigerian secondary listing to follow. The filing lays out a business growing rapidly after jumping 137% to $467 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 while net income rocketed by over 300% to $91 million. OPay launched in Nigeria as a payments company in 2018 backed by Chinese investors and later funded by venture investors led by Softbank. OPay hadn’t disclosed an IPO price range or a listing date as Semafor was going to press but based on the normal sequence of filings and roadshows, investors will be expecting pricing to be revealed in mid-November. Previous reports have put the initial valuation estimates around $4 billion. The fintech firm also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. Know More A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise and presence to expand across Africa. Step Back OPay took off in 2019 in Nigeria with ambitions to be a super app that offered various features, including motorcycle taxi bookings, food deliveries, and quick loans. But it narrowed its focus to financial services in recent years and raised $570 million in venture funds between 2018 and 2021. A handful of African tech companies have successfully listed in the US, notably e-commerce platform Jumia and telecom towers provider IHS but have had mixed performances. An OPay listing in the US would be the first by a fintech company with a mostly Nigerian customer base.

events.summary: Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services. And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot. Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet. Read more: https://lnkd.in/g68XQtxE This is encouraging. If AI is going to become part of practically every product and workflow, the cost of running it has to come down significantly. More efficient hardware could open the door to use cases that simply aren't economical today. "Tokens per watt". What an absurd metric. As if there's a uniform, consistent definition of a token or a generic correlation to compute. Not. And such a metric would inherently reward verbosity. Utterly stupid. I'm assuming this is good news. Anyone else consider themselves "tech savvy" and dont understand much of what they just read? It seems great though! Good job Microsoft: more power is always good:) I’d love to be in the room for Microsoft’s next GPU pricing negotiation when NVIDIA knows Maia is already running Copilot workloads 😅 Having a credible alternative at that scale might be worth almost as much as the efficiency gains themselves. 40% more tokens per watt, but at what context length? The workloads you named, sustained multi-step agents, carry long contexts, and every agent's working memory grows with each step. At that point the binding constraint is memory, not compute, and the specs that lead this launch are memory specs. Tokens per watt measured on short contexts says little about tokens per watt once agent memory dominates. The bigger announcement may be co-design. With Maia as the primary engine, Copilot's models get shaped around Maia and each next Maia around Copilot's workloads. That's where the gain compounds, and it's very hard to copy from outside. It also splits the market: integrated model-plus-chip stacks on one side, open models on general-purpose GPUs on the other. As agents multiply token demand, that gap becomes the price difference between closed and open AI. Who gives open models what Maia gives Copilot? Spot on, Satya Nadella! Transitioning toward custom silicon and multi-gigawatt infrastructure deployments represents a fundamental milestone in redefining enterprise AI economics and operational scalability. Maximizing tokens per watt through proprietary hardware architecture is critical for mitigating latency and curbing the exponential energy demands of large-scale agentic AI. Integrating full-stack silicon efficiency directly into cloud services sets a new benchmark for sustainable enterprise IT. As hyperscalers aggressively pivot toward custom silicon to optimize inference economics, what core engineering or supply-chain challenge do you view as the primary bottleneck for scaling multi-gigawatt deployments over the next cycle? Incredible milestone, mr.Satya! As custom silicon scales to multi-gigawatt deployments with Maia 300, optimizing tokens-per-watt highlights a critical industry truth: physical thermal management at the hardware level is becoming just as vital as architectural efficiency. We’ve been tackling this exact frontier through advanced passive thermal architectures designed for high-density AI hardware. If you or your silicon team are ever open to a brief exchange on bypassing the thermal wall at scale, I'd love to share a few notes. Exciting times ahead for full-stack optimization!" events.title: Ecobank agrees to join Chinese payment platform
events.summary: Ecobank agreed a partnership with China’s payment system to enable transaction settlements in the yuan currency. The Togo-based bank, which operates in 34 African countries — more than any other continental lender — will sign an agreement this month to join the China Interbank Payments System (CIPS). South Africa’s Standard Bank and the African Export Import Bank have taken the same step in the last year. The move follows increasing demand from businesses on the continent to transact and settle deals using China’s currency. An 18% rise in China-Africa trade last year — marked by a surge in the continent’s imports of Chinese solar power equipment — underscored the growing commercial relationship between both parties, highlighting the appeal of financial systems that make transactions easier to complete. China this year removed tariffs for imports from all African countries except Eswatini. Its move to increase bank integrations with its payments system furthers a push led by the BRICS bloc against the US dollar’s dominance in international trade. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics
events.summary: STOCKHOLM -- American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. “The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise." For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. “This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view," Hall and Woodford’s research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’ Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. “If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote. “The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’ Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace.

events.title: First Utility-Scale Enhanced Geothermal Plant Goes Live
events.summary: This article was originally published by Canary Media . The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah—marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide. The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California. Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity. “Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” sa ys Dawn Owens , Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets. With the first unit online, Fervo sa ys it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 Jan uary , 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW—which is supported by a new agreement with Google —is under construction and slated to come online in 2028. Fervo’s Next-Generation Geothermal Journey Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens sa ys the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets. “This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she sa ys . Fervo , which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments. Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers —all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say. “ Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” sa ys Mitchell Smith , who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “ to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added. Enhanced Geothermal Energy Gets Cheaper Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per k ilowatt , the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per k ilowatt in 2025.) Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers . While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods—like in the evening, when solar output declines—to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “ behind the meter” to directly power data centers so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens sa ys . “We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she sa ys . On Cape Station’s powering-up, she add s , “ That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”
