events.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
events.summary: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land. Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow. In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. events.title: Heavy rain, hail and ferocious wind speeds of 96km/h lash Alice Springs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thousands of properties in Central Australia without power after sudden storm lashes Alice Springs A damaging storm cell has caused a blackout in Alice Springs after it raged through Central Australia this afternoon. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The Bureau of Meteorology says "severe thunderstorms" have brought heavy rains and damaging winds to Alice Springs. The Hilton DoubleTree is among the properties damaged, with parts of its roof collapsing in during the storm. The weather bureau says more storms are possible through the week and emergency services are urging locals to remain vigilant. Thousands of homes are without power after a surprise storm brought wind speeds of almost 100km/h to Central Australia, pulling down trees and damaging properties. According to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), heavy rain and hail fell on Alice Springs at 3:30pm this afternoon and wind gusts of 96km/h were recorded locally at 3:44pm. It's the second storm to rock Alice Springs in just a few short days. ( Supplied: Damien Ryan ) "A surface trough coincides with a warm and unstable air mass in southern parts of the Territory, which has resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms," the weather bureau said. The short-lived storm cell pushed trees onto roads, powerlines and roofs. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree was among the properties to suffer significant damage. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree sustained damage to its ceiling. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Power and Water Corporation said "approximately 9,000 properties" had lost power "due to damage caused by a sudden storm cell". "Our crews are assessing the damage and will work to restore services as quickly as is safely possible," the statement said. "The communities of Arumbera, Burt Plain, Ilparpa, Simpson, Hermannsburg, Hugh, Namatjira and Wallace Rockhole have also been affected. Territorians can check power outages via Power and Water's online tracker . Cars parked outside the hospital in Alice Springs were damaged in the storm. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The BOM's Robert Urbaniak said Centralians were "not out of the woods yet", warning another similar storm cell was predicted for Tuesday afternoon and evening. "Unfortunately another day of it, but after that should settle down somewhat." NT Emergency Services (NTES) said it had received 47 calls for assistance since the storm hit. Adam White from NTES said Alice Springs residents would need to remain vigilant in the coming few days and urged people to keep an eye on SecureNT for updates . "I've got some reports of multiple trees down, some damage from the hail and the winds," he said. It was the second storm to hit Alice Springs in less than a week. Two cells are moving east over parts of Central Australia and the Barkly region, according to the BOM, which are likely to persist through this evening. events.title: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
events.summary: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier. “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress . “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.” The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack. But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time. “Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.” The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added. He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline , which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd. The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added. “Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said. At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”. The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

events.title: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027
events.summary: Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year. IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday. A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules. A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added. “IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business." IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre. The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said. Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil , with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country. It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy. Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

events.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
events.summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Profound consequences Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. Impact on entry-level jobs World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

events.title: Startup Funding: Q3 2026
events.summary: AI dominated funding in the third quarter of 2026, with two inference companies each announcing $1 billion in funding. But with the data center buildout driving insatiable demand for memory, investors also rewarded startups with alternatives to costly, capacity-limited HBM. Some are building on commodity DRAM or holding models in on-chip SRAM, while others stack memory directly onto compute. Data movement at all levels of the stack remains a critical bottleneck, too. Interconnect technologies, networking chips, and photonics were the most active areas of the quarter, with startups tackling the problem with diverse approaches ranging from manufacturing-ready co-packaged optics, millimeter-wave RF signals over plastic waveguides, and ferroelectric glass modulators to optical couplers printed directly onto chips and coherent DSPs designed specifically for AI optics. Nearly $7.5 billion of the quarter’s total was directed to just 22 startups that raised $100 million or more, including eight that saw investors return within roughly a year, some more than doubling the previous round. events.title: UAE Property: 'Can my tenant legally list my apartment as a holiday rental without my consent?'
events.summary: Question: I own an apartment in Dubai Marina, which I've rented to the same tenant for two years. A neighbour recently contacted me because different people appear to be entering the apartment every few days with suitcases. I checked one of the holiday rental websites and, to my surprise, found what appears to be my apartment being advertised for short-term stays . I never agreed to this and my tenancy contract says the property is for residential use by the tenant. The tenant is paying the rent on time, so financially, I haven't lost anything, but I'm uncomfortable with strangers continually using a property I'm responsible for. Can a tenant legally do this without my permission, and could I as the owner face problems if something happens? Ahmed, Abu Dhabi Answer: I wouldn't ignore this simply because the rent continues to arrive on time. There's an important distinction between a tenant occasionally having friends or family stay and somebody commercially offering another person's property as short-term accommodation. Dubai's holiday-home sector is regulated, and properties being used for this purpose need to comply with the relevant licensing and registration requirements. Separately, your tenancy agreement determines what your tenant is permitted to do with the apartment. Subletting in Dubai is not illegal; however, the landlord must be informed and agree to the subleasing. Since you were not informed, his actions are illegal and he cannot simply decide to turn your property into his own short-term rental business. Before taking any action I suggest you document what you've discovered. Save screenshots of the advertisement, including photographs that clearly identify your apartment and keep any messages from neighbours or building management. I would then write to the tenant and ask for an explanation rather than immediately making accusations. I'd also establish whether the apartment has actually been registered as a holiday home and, if so, how this was done without your knowledge. There's another practical concern: short-term occupation can mean considerably more wear and tear than a conventional tenancy, as well as possible issues with access cards, building security and insurance. For landlords, this is a useful reminder that receiving the rent doesn't necessarily mean everything is fine with the property. Sensible asset management means knowing how your investment is actually being used. Q: My former partner and I bought a villa in Dubai several years ago in both our names. We have now separated. I want to sell the property so we can both move on financially, but my ex refuses. He says that because he owns half of the villa I cannot force him to sell his share. Neither of us can realistically afford to buy the other person out, and there is still a mortgage on the property. What happens when two people jointly own a Dubai property but one wants to sell and the other simply refuses? Are we effectively stuck owning it together indefinitely? Emma, Dubai A: This is unfortunately one of the complications of joint property ownership that people rarely think about when they're happily buying together. You cannot ordinarily sell your former partner's ownership interest simply because you want the whole property sold. Equally, however, joint ownership doesn't necessarily mean two people must remain financially tied together indefinitely. The first thing I'd establish is exactly how ownership is recorded on the title deed and the respective ownership percentages. Then have the property independently valued. Once you know the realistic selling price, deduct the outstanding mortgage and likely selling costs so both parties can see what equity would actually be available. Sometimes having a real number on the table makes negotiations considerably easier. Possible solutions include one party refinancing and purchasing the other's interest, an agreed sale on the open market or another mutually acceptable transfer arrangement, subject of course to the lender and Dubai Land Department requirements. I'd also check who has been paying the mortgage , service charges and other property expenses since the separation because those contributions may need to be considered when the financial position is ultimately resolved. If agreement genuinely cannot be reached, this moves beyond estate agency advice. You should speak to a Dubai lawyer experienced in property and co-ownership disputes about the legal mechanisms available to bring the joint ownership to an end. The wider lesson for unmarried couples, friends and relatives buying together is simple: discuss the break-up before the purchase. A written co-ownership agreement setting out what happens if one person wants to sell can prevent an enormous amount of difficulty later. events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." The White House referred Axios to Trump's Truth Social post last week last week, in which he described the ads as a "positive promotion" for the U.S. Representatives for the DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Tuesday to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs and the White House's response to a request for comment.

events.title: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows
events.summary: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network’s name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox’s opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox’s coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network’s news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading “The case for data centers,” Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged “real concerns,” but argued that “saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don’t build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.” On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities’ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers “are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,” MS NOW’s Katy Tur said in May. “Politicians beware.” Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment , Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max’s view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. events.title: Hack reveals Netanyahu campaign's media ties
events.summary: The News Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aides’ close ties to the media. The incumbent prime minister’s reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections. The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had “verified” the leak. The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the country’s leading broadcaster, and host of the program , an analogue of the US show of that name. In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaign’s videos and its messaging: Netanyahu’s management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahu’s campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give. Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didn’t respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyers’ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israel’s Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means. Ben’s view Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks — including this one — is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his country’s response to the October 7 attacks. But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu — but he’s also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senor’s widely-followed podcast, as an independent analyst. One Israeli journalist compared Segal’s role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segal’s version of that image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister. Room for Disagreement Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a “very delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.” He added that “any people I’ve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, ‘This will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?’” Notable The region’s politics have been buffeted — and illuminated — repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

events.title: ABC News offers contradictory explanation for vanishing Anduril story
events.summary: The News When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trump’s sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published “prematurely.” Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece , used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece. But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes. On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trump’s son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which “claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.” After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company — which had not responded to ABC News’ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source — wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Anduril’s latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total. “Today, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or ‘major stake’ in Anduril is inaccurate,” Anduril’s spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor. After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story. “I have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,” Lee said in a note. “We had pulled the ‘major stake’ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.” Anduril’s PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capital’s investment in Anduril’s fundraising round. “It’s still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,” a spokesperson wrote. In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC News’ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece. “Apologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. I’ll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,” Lee said. But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been “published prematurely and removed from our website.” On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline . An editor’s note did not include language that the initial piece was published early. “Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.” A network source told Semafor: “We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.” The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story. Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the network’s regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, “suggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,” and it “circulated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.” Max’s view ABC News’ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the company’s mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident. But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors. Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC News’ initial piece, complained that the network’s handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the president’s administration. “It’s destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,” Velicovich said. “The damage is already done.” The Trump family’s mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC News’ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the president’s son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets. If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories? Room for Disagreement Remove the numbers, and the most basic version of the story — the Pentagon is paying very large sums to a defense contractor in which the president’s sons have invested, and whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is a high-dollar Trump donor — is correct . It also follows a pattern congressional Democrats have promised to investigate should they retake power after the midterms.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary . Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. events.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
events.summary: Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire. Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes. Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture. Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good. Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers. 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak . Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details. 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary ( including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team. 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." ( More on the film .) 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports . The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity." These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists. "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast." "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically." Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry. Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling . "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many." The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says. They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein." Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment. The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."

events.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
events.summary: America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields. Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time. The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures . Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change. As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry , more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago. "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of " Take Back the Game : How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore." By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found. Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play . Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found. State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity , massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams. Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor. How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region. Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships. That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending. Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches. Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found. What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times. "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship." Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender. Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field. Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels. Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said. Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said. The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven. For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

events.title: The Inside Brief: Menzies chief on aviation’s recovery and a lifetime of navigating crises
events.summary: When you look out of the aircraft window on the apron, the people turning your flight around probably work for Menzies . Its chief executive, Hassan El Houry, manages 65,000 of them across 65 countries and joined me for the launch edition of season two of The Inside Brief . This was days after the security incident on flydubai flight FZ1073 , which diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia on September 30 and is now under investigation by UAE authorities. He said the industry's next task is clear. “Airlines need to reinstall confidence in the general public,” he said. What most people do not know, he explained, is how thoroughly staff are screened. “After September 11, airports and airlines introduced an array of security measures for passengers,” Mr El Houry said. “While there are security measures for people that work at airports and airlines, they’re not so much in the spotlight like taking off your shoes and your belt.” That is about to change. “I think what we’ll end up seeing is that a lot of the security measures that are applied to pilots, to cabin crew, to our staff, to airport staff ... will come to the spotlight because it is quite thorough actually.” Every Menzies employee is background-checked and passes through “the same security measures that a passenger does”. And no new bill is coming. “All those security measures are already there,” he said. The bigger pressure is cost. Impact of a deal on the Strait of Hormuz Jet fuel has risen by 50 per cent or more since the war began, and ticket prices are “two, three, four times more expensive than they were pre-crisis”, Mr El Houry said. Asked whether fuel prices would fall straight away if a lasting peace reopens the Strait of Hormuz, he replied: “Every time there’s been an aviation crisis, we’ve recovered fairly quickly”. After September 11, “it was just a year and a half or two years, and aviation recovered”. Covid-19, the longest crisis, took “about three and a half years”, he said. “When there is some sort of peace and more clarity, I think we’ll recover fairly quickly.” The reason is demand. “Every airline that I’ve been talking to has been telling us that there isn’t a demand problem," he said. “Passengers are still flying. There’s a cost problem.” About five billion passengers will fly this year. “Five billion, that’s a record,” Mr El Houry said. Yet airline profits are expected to halve, from $50 billion last year “to about 25 billion this year”. ‘Quitting is permanent’ Mr El Houry learnt about risk early. His privileged childhood in Kuwait ended with the Iraqi invasion in 1990. “We were made refugees literally overnight,” he said. The family drove to Baghdad, then Amman, and spent two years in Cyprus. “At any moment you can have a black swan event. You can have a binary event from one to zero literally overnight, and you just have to be resilient enough to overcome it.” Compulsory military service in Lebanon followed. “I would spend 10, 12, 14 hours a day on my feet, and the one idea that kept going through my mind was the pain, the discomfort is temporary, but quitting is permanent.” His tolerance for complaining today? “It’s very low. It’s very low.” The fork in the road Wharton had been his dream since he was 19. It taught him to ask when he does not know. “You have to be humble. You’re not expected to know everything about everything.” Then came the choice: a New York investment bank, with the draw of “walking down Wall Street every day, going up to the 50th floor”, or Agility in Kuwait. “It wasn’t a cash decision,” he said. He chose Agility. “It was probably one of the best decisions I’ve made in my life.” At 28, he was running National Aviation Services, with 200 employees in one country. “Leadership is not a right that you have. You have to earn it.” Today, the combined business is the largest of its kind in the world, and Mr El Houry has the Gulf in his sights. “We don’t need to IPO,” he said. “The barriers to entry in the region are pretty high, but our resolve is much higher.” The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and other major platforms.

events.title: Hawkish sentiment returns to IMF and World Bank meetings
events.summary: The world’s finance ministers and central bankers are set to gather for this year’s IMF and World Bank annual meetings as a new set of inflationary drivers descends on the global economy. This year, representatives from the IMF and World Bank member countries will meet in Bangkok, Thailand, from Monday. The meetings are typically held in Washington for two consecutive years and in another member country every third year. The 2029 annual meetings will be held in Abu Dhabi . During the meetings, the Bretton Woods institutions’ board of governors hold discussions on how international monetary issues should be addressed, while other talks are held on emerging economic trends and regional programmes. This year's meetings come amid a renewed threat of inflation. Supply disruptions from the Iran war are pushing up energy prices, with the Strait of Hormuz’s prolonged partial closure driving the price for Brent crude roughly 30 per cent higher than prewar levels. The expansion of artificial intelligence is placing additional pressure on electricity demand, and the massive debt issuance it requires partially accounts for the recent rise in bond yields , also driven by the US national debt reaching $40 trillion. The global economy is still grappling with the inflationary after-effects of the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Inflation has remained above 2 per cent in the US for more than five years. “While this rise in inflation pales in comparison with what we saw in the immediate wake of the pandemic, it is large enough to be of real concern to central banks, many of whom hadn't wrestled inflation back to its target before this episode had begun,” Karen Dynan, non-resident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute, said during a round-table discussion on Tuesday in Washington. Speaking in Singapore on Tuesday, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said the environment was right for most countries to adopt a “prudently hawkish” posture. The US Federal Reserve , the world’s most influential central bank, entered a new tightening cycle in September after it raised interest rates by a quarter point. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan have also recently raised rates due to rising inflation. The Bank of England is expected to hike rates next month. Meanwhile, US government borrowing costs have reached multi-decade highs. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, recorded a 24-year high this week. Bond yields in Germany, the UK and Japan are also on the rise. Against this backdrop, Ms Georgieva suggested austerity was back on the menu for advanced economies. “After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, populations have grown accustomed to state support. Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” she said. Meeting the moment? The question persists whether the IMF and World Bank have done enough to support low-income and conflict-afflicted countries facing higher funding costs, slower growth and shrinking aid flows. “We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries,” said Marina Zucker-Marques, a senior academic researcher at Boston University's Boston University Global Development Policy Centre. We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries Senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative Since the Iran war broke out at the end of February, the World Bank has pledged up to $60 billion in financing to help countries absorb the impact of the conflict's energy shock. The African Development Bank Group has launched a $5.1 billion framework to offset the impact of the war's energy and fertiliser crisis on the continent. The Asian Development Bank said it is mobilising $4 billion in financing to help countries withstand the war's impact. The IMF last week said it would provide non-financial support to war-torn Yemen, and reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that would unlock $1.21 billion for the country that is dependent on Gulf energy imports. Bangladesh has also requested a programme due to the war's impact. “The international financial institutions are weathering these crises remarkably well compared to other multilaterals,” Rachel Glennerster, president of the Centre for Global Development, said during a webinar. However, Ms Zucker-Marques questioned how eager low-income countries might be for more funding from the IMF, citing the fund's conditionality for programmes. Ms Georgieva said in April that the fund expected at least a dozen countries, including several in sub-Saharan Africa, to seek new loan programmes to respond to the war's impact on energy prices and supply chain disruptions. The US central bank's new tightening cycle is also expected to lead to higher borrowing costs for low-income countries seeking loans. The Federal Reserve's rate-setting activity directly influences borrowing costs from the IMF, World Bank and other multi-development banks. Traders anticipate the Fed will raise interest rates three more times by July 2027, according to CME Group data. “A lot of people are talking about the bond yields, which is quite important for countries that have access to markets, but also we need to pay attention that the interest rate hike in the US is actually increasing the tide to all types of lending,” Ms Zucker-Marques said.

events.title: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
events.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed Saturday to force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases, challenging President Trump's diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. Why it matters: Trump has touted the deal as a way to lower fuel prices, but it could also provide revenue for Russia's war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Fitzpatrick, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said he would introduce the "Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act" and force a vote through a discharge petition. "It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," Fitzpatrick wrote on X . Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) tells Axios he has "already agreed" to sign the petition. Catch up quick: Trump said Friday Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more shipments to follow. Energy analysts are skeptical the additional diesel will meaningfully lower prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal "not fair and not honest," telling Axios it amounted to a gift to Putin. Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with a leader willing to reach a deal with Russia. The White House has not yet responded to Axios' request for comment about Fitzpatrick's bill. The big picture: Fitzpatrick is the latest Republican lawmaker to break with Trump in a high-profile way, as the party fights to keep control of Congress amid mounting disapproval of the president. Zoom out: Fitzpatrick is turning to a tactic lawmakers have increasingly used to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.): a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures to bring legislation up for a vote without House leadership's approval. Fitzpatrick and Bacon forced a House vote on Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions earlier this year; it passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Reality check: Fitzpatrick has little time to pass the bill before this Congress ends in January. The House isn't scheduled to vote again until after the Nov. 3 midterm. Any legislation that passes the House would still need Senate approval and could face Trump's veto pen. What they're saying: Another House Republican, speaking anonymously to offer their candid thoughts, tells Axios: "Being that Congress won't be in session for another four weeks, any prudent lawmaker would probably not make a commitment to this prematurely." One House Democrat tells Axios that they will personally sign the petition and that "most" of their colleagues probably would as well, but unanimous support from Democrats is not guaranteed. "Leadership may not want people to help him," the Democrat said, though they added that may change after the midterms. Ben Geman contributed.

events.title: Attacks on Riyadh threaten Saudi confidence
events.summary: The News Several people were wounded in another likely Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, the third strike this week on the gateway to Saudi Arabia’s capital. Earlier attacks killed four people. Flights were canceled or diverted, and airport operations were suspended. Hours of silence and speculation in the aftermath added to a sense of fear in Saudi Arabia and across the region. Rumors of injuries circulated in the afternoon, flights were canceled, Canada’s embassy warned citizens to avoid the airport at 5:34 p.m. The US followed at 8:03 p.m. Al Arabiya TV, which usually switches to breaking news if firecrackers are heard in other countries, was airing reruns. Saudi authorities finally acknowledged the incident at 8:34 p.m. There are definitely security considerations to withhold information during an attack. But the insistence on projecting calm is starting to backfire. Firms in Riyadh were telling their employees to work from home tomorrow, and people have been spooked for weeks. Since the US-Iran war began on Feb 28, Gulf governments have restricted media coverage and criminalized social media posts, even as everyone living here could see and hear explosions themselves. For months, Riyadh seemed relatively insulated from the war (sorry, “conflict,” as many officials in the region prefer to call it). Its airport remained open as travelers fled attacks elsewhere in the Gulf, and Saudis rallied around the flag, deeming any expressions of concern as unpatriotic. The messaging also seemed coordinated, with official statements followed by a flood of pledges of allegiance on social media. Now this confidence appears to be fraying. And in a war that is as much about economics as explosives, this may be the vulnerability that the Houthis, and Iran, are banking on. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had pushed back the Houthi advances around Bab el-Mandeb, the Red Sea shipping chokepoint this week. But in a similar move to the substantial losses that Iran had been dealt by the US and Israel earlier in the war, the Houthis chose asymmetric targets. The Iran-backed group has escalated attacks on Saudi oil facilities and civilian aviation, declaring Saudi airspace a military operations zone. The timing matters. Riyadh hosts the World Petroleum Congress this week, with CEOs from ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, and BP expected, followed later this month by the Future Investment Initiative and Wall Street’s billionaire financiers. Organizers insist both events will proceed , according to Reuters. But it’s certain that some of these executives — or their boards — will have second thoughts. Some US officials who were planning to attend the events in Riyadh this month are reconsidering. At stake is not just some meetings, but a questioning of the kingdom’s pitch as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries. The repeated airport attacks provide a sense that a major escalation is close. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the US may join strikes on the Houthis and will decide quickly. If that happens, it’s likely the region will remain the punching bag for any Houthi or Iranian response. Notable Ambulances and helicopters were sent to collect the wounded from Saturday’s attacks. The kingdom may be short on missile interceptors or are “struggling” to take out the Houthis’ rockets, The Wall Street Journal reported .
